i.294691192:
LPH performed a comprehensive electrical system check throughout the home. The evaluation included reviewing the electrical service and main panel, panel condition and labeling, breakers and overcurrent protection, grounding and bonding, wiring and visible connections, receptacles, switches, GFCI protection, exterior electrical devices, lighting, and other accessible electrical components throughout the home. LPH also checked for visible signs of damage, deterioration, overheating, loose or compromised connections, improper installations, and potential electrical safety concerns. All findings and available repair options were reviewed with the homeowner.

Overall, the home’s electrical system was found to be in great condition, with only a few items identified that would be beneficial to address for improved safety, reliability, and continued protection.

Findings & Recommended Options

Exterior Receptacle – Corrosion, GFCI & Weather Protection
The exterior receptacle was found to be significantly rusted and corroded. The corrosion has deteriorated the receptacle to the point where the internal connections are beginning to lose their ability to maintain a reliable connection. The receptacle was also not currently provided with GFCI protection or a proper in-use bubble cover.

LPH recommended replacing the damaged receptacle with a new weather-resistant GFCI receptacle, installing a proper bubble cover, and sealing the enclosure to help prevent additional moisture intrusion. This repair improves both the safety and reliability of the exterior electrical connection.

Washing Machine Receptacle – GFCI Protection
LPH recommended replacing the existing washing machine receptacle with a new GFCI-protected receptacle. Washing machines combine electrical equipment and water, increasing the potential for an electrical fault if moisture reaches electrical components or connections. There are also exposed water-pipe connection points located above the receptacle, making appropriate GFCI protection an important additional layer of shock protection.

Three Arcing/Popping Switches – Replacement
LPH identified three switches that are arcing and popping when operated. This can occur as switches wear with age and their internal contacts and connection points begin to deteriorate. The existing switches also utilize back-stab connections, which can become less reliable over time due to repeated heating, cooling, and normal operation. Replacing these switches would provide more reliable connections and eliminate the existing arcing and popping concerns.

Work Approved & Completed – Exterior Receptacle

After reviewing the inspection findings and available options with the homeowner, she elected to move forward at this time with only the replacement of the rusted and corroded exterior receptacle. The homeowner would like to save the remaining recommended options for future visits while she plans and budgets for additional work throughout the home.

LPH removed the existing damaged receptacle and cleaned out the exterior electrical box to remove accumulated corrosion and debris. The siding surrounding the enclosure was carefully trimmed to provide proper clearance and allow the new in-use bubble cover to fit correctly.

LPH installed a new GFCI-protected exterior receptacle and proper weather-resistant in-use bubble cover. All accessible openings around the top and sides of the enclosure were sealed with silicone to help prevent water from entering around the enclosure and causing future corrosion or deterioration.

The newly installed GFCI was tested, and proper power was confirmed. The receptacle was verified to be operating correctly at the completion of the repair.

Payment was collected at the completion of today’s visit. Today’s invoice and electrical system evaluation will be emailed to the homeowner for her records.

Thank you for choosing LPH!

e.336907415:
Washing Machine Receptacle – GFCI Protection

LPH will replace the existing washing machine receptacle with a new GFCI-protected receptacle. Washing machines combine electricity and water, creating an increased potential for an electrical fault if water reaches electrical components or wiring. A water leak or internal component failure can create an unintended path for electrical current, making GFCI protection especially important.

There are also exposed water-pipe connection points located directly above the receptacle. Providing GFCI protection helps reduce the risk of electrical shock should moisture, leakage, or an electrical fault occur in this area. The GFCI is designed to quickly disconnect power when it detects current leaving the intended electrical path, providing an additional layer of protection for the occupants and the equipment.

Three Arcing/Popping Switches – Replacement

LPH will replace three switches that are currently arcing and popping during operation. These symptoms are commonly associated with switches that have experienced wear over time. As switches age, their internal contacts and connection points can deteriorate or loosen, which can create a less reliable electrical connection and result in arcing when the switch is operated.

The existing switches also utilize back-stab connections, which rely on spring tension to hold the conductor in place. These connections can become less reliable as the device ages and is repeatedly heated, cooled, and operated. A weakened connection can create additional resistance and heat at the connection point, accelerating wear on the device.

Replacing the switches and establishing secure, reliable connections will eliminate the currently observed arcing and popping and provide a safer, more dependable connection for the lighting circuits.

LPH found that the exterior receptacles originally installed with the home are rated for indoor use only and are not designed for continued exposure to outdoor moisture and weather conditions.

While testing the receptacles, LPH noticed corrosion inside the devices that was making the plug connections increasingly difficult to insert and remove. i.301232734:
LPH completed an electrical system check of the home. During the inspection, we evaluated the electrical panel and breakers, visible wiring and connections, switches and receptacles, GFCI protection, exterior electrical devices, smoke and carbon monoxide detection, and overall visible safety and operating conditions of the electrical system.

Bathroom Exhaust Fan / GFCI Investigation:
LPH also investigated a reported issue with the bathroom exhaust fan causing the GFCI to trip when the fan is turned off. The homeowner reported that this has only occurred twice. Due to the limited number of occurrences, there is currently not enough evidence to confirm a consistent electrical fault.

LPH pulled the wiring down at the fan and inspected the wiring and connections at the fan, switch box, and GFCI. We verified that the wiring was properly positioned and that no conductors were touching where they should not. During our inspection, nothing was found that would cause immediate concern or indicate an obvious ground fault.

The wiring has been inspected and repositioned as necessary in an effort to eliminate the possibility of an unintended ground fault at the connections. We are hopeful this resolves the issue. However, because the GFCI trip has occurred specifically when the fan is being turned off, there is also a possibility that the fan motor may be contributing to the occasional trip.

As a motor ages, small amounts of electrical leakage can potentially develop. When power to a motor is interrupted, the magnetic energy stored within the motor can also create a brief electrical transient. In some circumstances, this can result in a momentary current imbalance that a sensitive GFCI detects and responds to by tripping. Since this has only happened twice and no visible wiring problem was found, LPH recommends monitoring the fan for now. If the GFCI continues to trip, further troubleshooting may be necessary, including evaluation of the fan motor and potentially replacing the fan if it is determined to be the source of the issue.

Four-Way Switch – Arcing:
One four-way switch was found to be arcing when being turned on and off. Arcing can create excessive heat at the switch connection and can eventually damage the device or surrounding wiring. LPH recommends replacing the switch to restore a secure electrical connection and prevent continued arcing.

Exterior Receptacles – Corrosion:
Three exterior receptacles were found to be corroded from exposure to outdoor moisture and weather conditions. LPH recommends replacing these devices with weather-resistant receptacles designed to better withstand the outdoor environment and provide improved long-term reliability.

Mechanical Room Smoke/Carbon Monoxide Detector:
The combination smoke and carbon monoxide detector located in the mechanical room with the furnace is over 20 years old. Smoke/CO detectors have a limited service life, and their operation should not be relied upon once they are past their recommended service period. LPH recommends replacing this detector with a new combination smoke and carbon monoxide detector to provide reliable detection in an area containing the home’s heating equipment.

Panel Breakers – Shared Neutral Concern:
LPH found two tandem 20-amp breakers serving circuits that are sharing a neutral in a configuration that presents a safety concern. The associated circuit conductors need to be properly configured so the circuits can be safely disconnected together when required. LPH recommends replacing the two existing tandem breakers with the appropriate 20-amp quad tandem breaker to provide proper circuit disconnecting and maintain safe operation of the circuits.

LPH reviewed the electrical system findings and recommended corrections with the homeowner. The recommended work is intended to address the identified safety concerns, improve reliability, and update aging or deteriorated electrical components.

Today’s invoice and electrical system evaluation will be emailed to the homeowner for their records.

Thank you for allowing LPH into your home. We appreciate the opportunity to service your electrical system and look forward to servicing you again in the future.

e.338178484:
Four-Way Switch Replacement:
LPH will replace one four-way switch that is currently showing signs of arcing when being turned on and off. Arcing occurs when electrical current jumps across a connection instead of flowing cleanly through the switch. Continued arcing can create heat and damage the switch and surrounding wiring, increasing the potential for a more serious electrical issue. Replacing the switch will restore a secure connection and provide reliable operation.

Exterior Receptacle Replacement:
LPH will replace three exterior receptacles that are showing corrosion from exposure to the outdoor environment. The existing receptacles will be replaced with new weather-resistant (WR) receptacles designed to better withstand moisture and temperature changes. This will provide improved protection and reliability for the home’s exterior electrical system.

Carbon Monoxide/Smoke Combination Detector Replacement:
LPH will replace one combination smoke and carbon monoxide detector located in the mechanical room containing the furnace. The existing detector is over 20 years old, which is well beyond the typical recommended service life of a smoke/CO detector. These combination detectors use sensors designed to detect hazardous conditions, and their operation should not be relied upon once they are past their service life. Replacing the detector will provide the home with current, reliable smoke and carbon monoxide detection in an area containing fuel-burning equipment.

Quad Tandem Breaker Replacement:
LPH will replace two existing tandem 20-amp breakers with one properly configured 20-amp quad breaker. The existing tandem breakers are sharing a neutral in a configuration that does not provide the proper disconnecting arrangement for the associated circuits. This creates a safety concern because the circuits can remain energized in an unsafe condition even when one breaker has been turned off or has tripped. Installing the appropriate quad breaker will provide proper circuit separation and disconnecting protection while maintaining the necessary electrical capacity within the panel.

These recommendations are intended to correct existing safety concerns, improve the reliability of the electrical system, and provide updated protection where the existing equipment has reached the end of its useful service life.

i.302697740: This afternoon I arrived at the sessions family home to perform their annual electrical system and safety check. I have also provided an option to install a whole home surge protection device at the main breaker panel, needing two tandem breakers to make room for the surge protectors double pole breaker. i.304806635:
LPH arrived at the home to perform a comprehensive electrical system check. During today’s evaluation, we inspected the home’s electrical service, meter base, service entrance equipment, main electrical panel, grounding and bonding system, circuit breakers, receptacles, and GFCI protection. We also evaluated the condition and operation of the accessible electrical components throughout the home and looked for visible signs of corrosion, moisture intrusion, deterioration, improper wiring, and potential safety concerns.

Electrical Service & Meter Base – Finding

LPH found the outside meter base to be extensively corroded internally. Upon inspection, an opening was found in the seal at the top of the meter base where water has been entering the enclosure. The meter base is also not properly sealed around the top and sides, allowing additional moisture to penetrate through the rear of the enclosure and into the service equipment.

The moisture intrusion has allowed water and humidity to enter the service entrance cable feeding the electrical panel. Continued exposure to moisture can cause the conductors, particularly the neutral conductor, to slowly corrode internally. As corrosion progresses, the conductor can lose its ability to reliably carry the electrical load of the home.

A compromised service neutral can create a serious voltage imbalance between the two incoming service legs. This can cause voltage on one side of the electrical system to rise while voltage on the other side drops depending on the loads operating throughout the home. If severe enough, this condition can place excessive voltage on connected appliances, electronics, and other electrical equipment.

The corrosion inside the meter base is also extensive around the service lugs and connection points. Corroded electrical connections can develop increased resistance and heat, potentially leading to further deterioration or failure.

Due to the condition of the meter base and its internal connections, replacement is recommended rather than attempting to repair or reseal the existing equipment.

Service Replacement & Code Update Option

LPH provided an option to address the meter base, service conductors, grounding, bonding, and associated service equipment as a complete system. This option would include:

* Installation of a new service head.
* Coordination of the electrical service disconnection as required.
* Replacement of the upper and lower service cable drops with new service conductors.
* Installation of a new outside emergency/service disconnect.
* Installation of a new properly sealed meter base.
* Installation of updated grounding and bonding components.
* Installation of a new bonding bridge at the appropriate service location.
* Reconfiguration of the electrical panel wiring to properly separate grounded neutral conductors from equipment grounding conductors where required.
* Extension of the grounding electrode conductor to the metallic water service and termination at the appropriate grounding location.
* Installation of two new exterior ground rods to provide the home with a proper grounding electrode system.
* Installation of the new service using PVC conduit to provide additional protection for the service conductors and help prevent future moisture exposure and physical damage.

This option would address not only the visibly corroded meter base, but also the moisture intrusion, deteriorated service conductors, grounding deficiencies, bonding concerns, and service-disconnect requirements associated with the existing installation.

Shared-Neutral Circuit Breakers – Finding

LPH identified four circuit breakers serving circuits that share neutral conductors. These circuits should be properly paired using common-trip two-pole breakers.

The recommended correction would include:

* One 2-pole 15-amp breaker for the two 15-amp circuits.
* One 2-pole 20-amp breaker for the two 20-amp circuits.

Using properly paired two-pole breakers allows the associated circuits to disconnect together if either circuit trips. This helps eliminate the possibility of one circuit remaining energized while the other circuit sharing its neutral has been disconnected.

GFCI Protection – Findings

LPH also identified locations where additional GFCI protection is recommended.

Exterior Receptacle:
One exterior receptacle should be provided with GFCI protection to help protect against electrical shock in an area exposed to moisture and changing weather conditions.

Basement Washing Machine Receptacle:
The washing-machine receptacle in the basement should also be provided with GFCI protection. GFCI protection monitors for unintended current flow and quickly disconnects power when a ground fault is detected, providing an additional level of protection for occupants and electrical equipment.

Overall Electrical System Recommendation

The primary concern identified during today’s inspection is the extensive corrosion and moisture intrusion at the outside meter base and associated service equipment. The condition of the meter base and the potential for continued moisture exposure warrant correction to help prevent further deterioration and reduce the possibility of future electrical service problems or equipment damage.

LPH has provided multiple options so the homeowner can determine the appropriate level of correction for the home. The homeowner will review all of the options provided today and will contact LPH when they are ready to schedule the recommended work.

No additional work is being scheduled at this time.

Today’s invoice and electrical system evaluation will be emailed to the homeowner for their records.

Thank you for allowing LPH the opportunity to inspect your electrical system and provide our recommendations. We appreciate your business and look forward to assisting you when you are ready to move forward with the work.

e.336337904:
Whole-House Sediment Filter:
Technician flushed the existing water heater and found a significant amount of sediment buildup inside the tank. Excessive sediment can accumulate in the water heater and plumbing system and may reduce equipment efficiency and contribute to premature component failure. Technician recommends installing a whole-house sediment filter on the home’s water distribution system to help capture sediment before it enters the home’s plumbing and water-using appliances.

The sediment filter would be installed after the water meter and before the existing water softener. Technician would need to shut off the water supply to the home to complete the installation. The filter cartridge should be inspected regularly and replaced approximately every 6 months to 1 year, depending on water quality and usage.

High Water Pressure:
While checking the home’s water pressure, technician found the static water pressure to be approximately 110 PSI. This is significantly higher than the recommended residential water pressure range of 40–60 PSI and exceeds the generally accepted maximum static pressure of 80 PSI. Plumbing fixtures, appliances, and other components may not be designed to withstand prolonged exposure to pressure this high, which can increase the risk of premature failure, leaks, and damage.

Technician highly recommends installing a pressure reducing valve (PRV) on the home’s water distribution system to regulate the incoming water pressure and help protect the plumbing fixtures, appliances, and piping from excessive pressure.

Water Damage Prevention / Flood Stop:
Homeowner stated that the previous sump pump stopped operating, which resulted in water damage in the basement. As an additional measure to help prevent future water damage, technician recommends installing a flood stop device at the existing water heater. The flood stop is designed to detect water from a potential water heater leak and automatically shut off the water supply, helping limit the amount of water released if the water heater were to fail.

LPH completed a thorough electrical system check of the home, including an evaluation of the electrical service, main electrical panel, breakers, grounding and bonding, wiring, receptacles, switches, GFCI protection, AFCI protection where applicable, smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, lighting, exterior electrical devices, and visible electrical connections throughout the home. LPH also checked for signs of overheating, loose connections, damaged or deteriorated wiring, corrosion, improper installations, exposed electrical components, and other potential safety concerns.

Overall, the home’s electrical system was found to be in fantastic condition. The panel, wiring, devices, and accessible electrical components were all operating properly, with no significant issues identified during today’s inspection.

After reviewing the electrical system with the homeowner, LPH’s only recommendations are the following GFCI protection upgrades:

1. GFCI Protection – Washing Machine

LPH recommends installing GFCI protection for the washing machine receptacle. The washing machine is located in an area where water supply hoses, drain connections, or the appliance itself could potentially leak or become loose. If water were to reach the electrical wiring or components, it could create an unintended path for electrical current.

In certain fault conditions, energized wiring contacting water or the metal housing of the appliance could allow voltage to transfer onto the appliance housing, creating a potential shock hazard. GFCI protection is designed to quickly detect this type of unintended current path and shut the circuit off, providing an additional layer of protection for anyone who may come into contact with the appliance.

2. GFCI Protection – Garbage Disposal

LPH also recommends installing GFCI protection for the garbage disposal receptacle located underneath the kitchen sink. This is a moisture-prone location because the receptacle and disposal wiring are located near the sink’s water supply, drain plumbing, and disposal connections.

If a plumbing connection were to leak or come loose, water could reach the receptacle, wiring, or electrical components. GFCI protection provides additional protection by quickly disconnecting power if current begins traveling along an unintended path, helping reduce the potential for electrical shock or an energized appliance housing.

These recommendations are proactive safety upgrades rather than indications that the home’s electrical system is currently in poor condition. With the remainder of the electrical system found to be in fantastic shape, these upgrades would provide additional protection specifically at two locations where water and electrical equipment are in close proximity.

3. Whole-Home Surge Protection

LPH recommends adding a whole-home surge protection device at the electrical panel to provide an additional layer of protection for the home’s electrical system and connected electronics.

Electrical surges can come from outside sources, such as lightning strikes or utility-related events, but many smaller surges are actually generated inside the home when motor-driven equipment cycles on and off. Appliances and equipment such as air conditioners, refrigerators, heat pumps, furnaces, microwaves, dishwashers, washing machines, dryers, and garage door openers can create these smaller electrical disturbances.

Modern electronics are particularly sensitive to these fluctuations because many appliances and devices contain electronic control boards, circuit boards, power supplies, and LED drivers. A surge protector installed at the main electrical panel helps divert excessive voltage away from the home’s branch circuits and connected equipment, providing protection throughout the home rather than relying solely on individual plug-in surge protectors.

This is a proactive protection upgrade, not an indication that the electrical system is currently experiencing a problem. With the home’s electrical system otherwise found to be in fantastic condition, whole-home surge protection provides an added level of protection for the investment the homeowner has in their appliances, electronics, and electrical equipment.

e.337230869:
Premium Whole-Home Surge Protection
LPH will install a premium whole-home surge protection device at the home’s main electrical panel. This device is designed to protect the home’s electrical system and connected equipment from damaging voltage spikes and transient surges before they can travel throughout the home’s wiring.
Many homeowners think of lightning when they hear the term “surge,” but the majority of power surges actually originate inside the home. Everyday appliances such as air conditioners, refrigerators, heat pumps, furnaces, microwaves, dishwashers, washers, dryers, and even garage door openers create small electrical surges—known as microsurges—every time their motors cycle on and off. While each individual surge is small, thousands of these microsurges occur over time and gradually wear down the sensitive electronic components found in today’s modern appliances and equipment.
Whole-home surge protection helps absorb and divert these surges away from the home’s electrical system, reducing cumulative damage to expensive electronics and appliances. This is especially important in newer homes, where nearly every major appliance contains sophisticated circuit boards and microprocessors that are far more sensitive to voltage fluctuations than older equipment.
In addition to protecting against internally generated microsurges, whole-home surge protection also provides a critical first line of defense against larger surges originating from the utility company, switching events on the electrical grid, nearby lightning strikes, or power being restored after an outage.
Benefits of premium whole-home surge protection include:
	• Protects HVAC systems, refrigerators, ovens, dishwashers, washers, dryers, and other major appliances.
	• Helps safeguard sensitive electronics such as televisions, computers, gaming systems, networking equipment, and smart home devices.
	• Reduces the long-term effects of everyday microsurges that slowly degrade electronic components.
	• Can help extend the service life of modern appliances and equipment by reducing electrical stress on internal circuit boards.
	• Helps minimize the likelihood of costly repairs or premature equipment replacement due to surge damage.
	• Provides continuous protection for the entire home’s electrical system without relying solely on individual plug-in surge strips.
	• Offers added peace of mind during storms, utility switching events, and unexpected power outages.
As homes continue to rely on more connected technology and electronically controlled appliances, whole-home surge protection has become one of the most valuable upgrades for preserving the reliability, longevity, and performance of a home’s electrical equipment.

Premium Surge Protection Warranty & Replacement Coverage

The installed surge protection device also provides additional protection beyond the device itself. If the surge protector is ever sacrificed or fails as a result of a covered surge event, the device is backed by a lifetime warranty and coverage of up to $100,000 toward covered damage to the home’s electrical components and connected equipment, subject to the manufacturer’s warranty terms and conditions.

If the surge protector ever needs to be replaced under the warranty, the replacement device is provided at no charge. LPH will also handle the replacement installation for a $150 labor charge, helping make future warranty replacement straightforward and affordable for the homeowner.

This means the homeowner is not simply purchasing a surge protector—they are adding a long-term layer of protection to the home’s electrical system while also having manufacturer-backed coverage in the event of a significant surge.

As homes continue to rely on more connected technology and electronically controlled appliances, whole-home surge protection has become one of the most valuable upgrades for preserving the reliability, longevity, and performance of a home’s electrical equipment.

LPH recommends installing GFCI protection for the washing machine receptacle and the garbage disposal receptacle located underneath the kitchen sink. Both appliances are located in areas where water leaks, loose connections, or plumbing issues could potentially allow moisture to reach the electrical components.

If a washer hose, drain connection, disposal plumbing, or other water connection were to leak or come loose, water could come into contact with the appliance wiring or electrical components. If energized wiring were to contact the water or an appliance’s metal housing, it could create an unintended electrical path and potentially place voltage onto the metal housing of the appliance through voltage bleed-off. This creates a potential shock hazard for anyone touching the appliance while also in contact with a grounded surface.

GFCI protection is designed to detect even a small difference in the amount of current flowing through the circuit and quickly interrupt power when electricity begins taking an unintended path. This provides an important layer of protection against electrical shock, particularly in areas where water and electricity are located in close proximity.

Washing Machine: The washer has water supply and drain connections that can potentially leak or become loose. GFCI protection helps protect the homeowner if water reaches the electrical components or creates an unintended path to the appliance’s metal housing.

Garbage Disposal: The receptacle underneath the sink is located directly alongside water supply, drain, and disposal connections. A plumbing leak could allow water to reach the electrical receptacle, wiring, or disposal components, making GFCI protection especially beneficial.

LPH recommends adding GFCI protection at both locations as a proactive safety upgrade. This helps provide faster protection if an electrical fault or water-related issue occurs, reducing the potential for serious electrical shock and protecting the occupants from an unexpected energized appliance housing.

i.320870176:
LPH arrived to begin the annual electrical system check. Upon arrival, no immediate concerns or questions were reported prior to our electrical inspection. 

We began our evaluation at the main electrical/distribution panel. This is where we assessed the internal conditions, age, connections and voltage readings. During this inspection, most of the inspected parameters meet the required threshold for a healthy panel. However, there are a few recommendations we assessed during this inspection. 

First we discovered that there are multiple locations where more than one wire is landed under one breaker termination screw, which increases the chance of loose connections. Second we noticed that this electrical system is currently within the “end of life” range, which means the longevity is in question. This main electrical/distribution panel is also maxed out and most newer circuit or electrical equipment could not be installed within this existing panel. We also discovered the presence of corrosion on the main neutral wire coming into this panel, which will continuously deteriorate this wire and create power loss/fluctuation issues. Lastly, there’s no system put in place to protect appliances/electronics from spikes of electric which target the sensitive components inside these units. A whole home surge protection device is recommended if the homeowners were interested in  protecting their main utility equipment with a one time investment unit.

Next, we inspected all of the protective systems for personnel and equipment in the home such as the smoke detectors, GFI protection devices, and the grounding system. First, we discovered that the water meter does meet today’s grounding standards to protect against any leakage of electricity from traveling on the pipes. The next was confirmation that all of the existing smoke detectors and carbon monoxide detectors are installed in the right locations and up-to-date. All other devices in the home were tested and functioning properly prior to leaving today.

We provided options to remedy all of our electrical recommendations, which was presented today. All of the options that were not approved will be emailed along with the electrical evaluation form and invoice for today’s visit. We thank you for allowing us in your home to service you and we look forward to servicing you in the future.

e.337791128:
Technician recommends adding a constant pressure switch to the existing well pump system. The constant pressure switch will provide more consistent water pressure throughout the home by allowing the well pump to adjust its operation based on the water demand. Technician would install the constant pressure switch and update the pump controls as needed to properly operate the existing well pump system. The system would then be tested to verify proper pump operation and consistent water pressure.

Technician performed water quality testing and found the home’s water hardness to be 7 grains per gallon (GPG). A hardness level of 7 GPG is considered hard water and can lead to calcium and magnesium scale buildup inside water heaters, plumbing fixtures, faucets, showerheads, and water-using appliances. Over time, this mineral buildup can reduce appliance efficiency, shorten equipment life expectancy, cause spotting on dishes and glassware, and leave soap residue on fixtures and surfaces. The presence of chlorine, while common in municipal water supplies, can contribute to dry skin and hair and may deteriorate rubber seals and gaskets within the plumbing system over time.

To improve water quality and help protect the home’s plumbing system, technician recommends installing a City Soft water treatment system. The system is designed to soften the water by removing the hardness minerals that cause scale buildup while also reducing chlorine levels throughout the home. Benefits of the system include improved soap and detergent performance, reduced spotting and scaling, softer-feeling water, and increased protection and efficiency of plumbing fixtures and water-using appliances.

The proposed installation location for the water softener system is near the existing water heater to allow for efficient integration into the home’s main water distribution system. The softener’s backwash drain lines will be routed and connected to the existing main drain located behind the washer. The system also requires a dedicated electrical outlet for operation and regeneration cycles. The home’s electrical panel is located approximately 5 feet away, and an outlet will need to be installed and provided at the equipment location prior to or as part of the installation. Once installed, the system will provide conditioned water to the entire home and help minimize the long-term effects of hard water and chlorine exposure on the plumbing system.

LPH completed a comprehensive electrical system check throughout the home. During the inspection, we evaluated the electrical panel and overcurrent protection, inspected accessible wiring and electrical connections, checked receptacles and switches for proper operation and signs of wear or damage, verified grounding and bonding, inspected GFCI/AFCI protection where applicable, checked for loose or improper connections, evaluated accessible electrical devices for heat damage or arcing, and reviewed the overall condition and safety of the electrical system.

Dryer Electrical Safety Issue

The homeowner reported receiving an electrical shock when touching the dryer while also making contact with another grounded surface. LPH investigated the dryer circuit and initially confirmed that the receptacle and connections at the wall were properly installed.

LPH then pulled the dryer away from the wall and inspected the electrical connection compartment on the appliance. During this inspection, we discovered a serious wiring and grounding issue at the dryer itself. The cable entering the dryer was not secured with a proper connector, and the conductors had been terminated incorrectly.

The dryer had been wired with the hot conductors connected to the incorrect terminals, including a hot conductor being connected to the dryer’s neutral connection and the neutral conductor being connected to one of the primary hot connections. Additionally, the dryer was designed to operate using a 4-wire configuration, which requires the neutral and equipment grounding conductor to remain electrically separated. Instead, the neutral conductor had been improperly bonded to the metal housing of the dryer.

This configuration created a significant shock hazard because the metal chassis of the dryer could become energized. LPH identified this condition as the likely cause of the homeowner’s reported shock.

Dryer Wiring Correction

LPH corrected the dryer wiring to restore the appliance to the proper 4-wire configuration. This included:

* Removing the improperly installed cable connection and installing a proper strain-relief/connector where the wiring enters the dryer.
* Correctly identifying and terminating both hot conductors on their proper terminals.
* Correctly terminating the neutral conductor on the dryer’s neutral connection.
* Removing the improper neutral-to-ground bond from the dryer housing.
* Installing the equipment grounding conductor onto the dryer’s designated bonding/grounding connection.
* Verifying that the neutral and equipment grounding paths were properly separated as required for a 4-wire dryer installation.
* Testing the corrected installation to confirm proper electrical operation and safety.

After the repair, LPH had the homeowner operate the dryer with a wet towel load to verify proper operation under normal conditions and confirm that the appliance was functioning correctly following the wiring correction. The dryer operated properly, and no additional issues were identified during testing.

Downstairs Bedroom Bathroom Switch

LPH also identified an arcing single-pole switch in the downstairs bedroom bathroom. The switch was replaced to eliminate the arcing condition and restore safe, reliable operation.

Whole-Home Surge Protection

As an additional protection option, LPH installed a Type 1 whole-home surge protective device directly underneath the main service lugs. This provides the home with an additional layer of protection against damaging voltage surges that can enter through the electrical service and potentially affect sensitive electronics, appliances, and electrical equipment throughout the home.

Options Provided / Work Completed

At the conclusion of the electrical system check, LPH reviewed the available options with the homeowner. The options provided included:

* Correcting the unsafe dryer wiring and grounding configuration — completed today.
* Replacing the arcing single-pole bathroom switch — completed today.
* Installing Type 1 whole-home surge protection — completed today.

LPH tested and confirmed proper operation of all completed installations and corrections.

Overall System Condition

The primary concern identified during today’s inspection was the improperly wired dryer, which presented a significant electrical shock hazard. LPH corrected the wiring and grounding configuration and verified proper operation after the repair. The additional switch replacement and whole-home surge protection were also completed and tested successfully.

Today’s invoice and electrical evaluation will be sent to the homeowner’s email for their records.

Thank you for allowing LPH into your home. We appreciate the opportunity to serve you and look forward to servicing you again in the future.

Premium Whole-Home Surge Protection
LPH will install a premium whole-home surge protection device at the home’s main electrical panel. This device is designed to protect the home’s electrical system and connected equipment from damaging voltage spikes and transient surges before they can travel throughout the home’s wiring.
Many homeowners think of lightning when they hear the term “surge,” but the majority of power surges actually originate inside the home. Everyday appliances such as air conditioners, refrigerators, heat pumps, furnaces, microwaves, dishwashers, washers, dryers, and even garage door openers create small electrical surges—known as microsurges—every time their motors cycle on and off. While each individual surge is small, thousands of these microsurges occur over time and gradually wear down the sensitive electronic components found in today’s modern appliances and equipment.
Whole-home surge protection helps absorb and divert these surges away from the home’s electrical system, reducing cumulative damage to expensive electronics and appliances. This is especially important in newer homes, where nearly every major appliance contains sophisticated circuit boards and microprocessors that are far more sensitive to voltage fluctuations than older equipment.
In addition to protecting against internally generated microsurges, whole-home surge protection also provides a critical first line of defense against larger surges originating from the utility company, switching events on the electrical grid, nearby lightning strikes, or power being restored after an outage.
Benefits of premium whole-home surge protection include:
	• Protects HVAC systems, refrigerators, ovens, dishwashers, washers, dryers, and other major appliances.
	• Helps safeguard sensitive electronics such as televisions, computers, gaming systems, networking equipment, and smart home devices.
	• Reduces the long-term effects of everyday microsurges that slowly degrade electronic components.
	• Can help extend the service life of modern appliances and equipment by reducing electrical stress on internal circuit boards.
	• Helps minimize the likelihood of costly repairs or premature equipment replacement due to surge damage.
	• Provides continuous protection for the entire home’s electrical system without relying solely on individual plug-in surge strips.
	• Offers added peace of mind during storms, utility switching events, and unexpected power outages.
As homes continue to rely on more connected technology and electronically controlled appliances, whole-home surge protection has become one of the most valuable upgrades for preserving the reliability, longevity, and performance of a home’s electrical equipment.

Premium Surge Protection Warranty & Replacement Coverage

The installed surge protection device also provides additional protection beyond the device itself. If the surge protector is ever sacrificed or fails as a result of a covered surge event, the device is backed by a lifetime warranty and coverage of up to $100,000 toward covered damage to the home’s electrical components and connected equipment, subject to the manufacturer’s warranty terms and conditions.

If the surge protector ever needs to be replaced under the warranty, the replacement device is provided at no charge. LPH will also handle the replacement installation for a $150 labor charge, helping make future warranty replacement straightforward and affordable for the homeowner.

This means the homeowner is not simply purchasing a surge protector—they are adding a long-term layer of protection to the home’s electrical system while also having manufacturer-backed coverage in the event of a significant surge.

As homes continue to rely on more connected technology and electronically controlled appliances, whole-home surge protection has become one of the most valuable upgrades for preserving the reliability, longevity, and performance of a home’s electrical equipment.

i.328112683:
LPH completed a comprehensive electrical system check of the home, including evaluation of the electrical service, meter base, service entrance conductors, grounding and bonding, main disconnects, electrical panels, breakers, wiring, receptacles, GFI protection, switches, and overall condition of the electrical system. We also checked for signs of overheating, corrosion, moisture intrusion, loose or improperly terminated wiring, overloaded circuits, and other potential safety concerns. The majority of the electrical service and distribution system is in good overall condition; however, several items were identified that LPH recommends addressing to improve safety, reliability, and protection of the home’s electrical system.

Electrical Service – Undersized Main Service Feed

The existing electrical service is utilizing 100-amp service cable feeding a split meter base that supplies two separate 100-amp panels. While each individual panel is rated at 100 amps, the existing 100-amp service conductors feeding the split service are being asked to supply the combined electrical demand of both panels.

LPH recommends upgrading the main service feed to 200-amp service conductors before the service splits into the two existing 100-amp panel runs. This provides a properly sized main service supply for the combined electrical demand and reduces the amount of stress placed on the existing service conductors. It also provides additional capacity for the home’s electrical loads and helps prevent the service from becoming a limiting factor as electrical demand increases over time.

The remainder of the exterior service is in good condition and has been installed in PVC conduit, so LPH is recommending addressing the service-feed concern without unnecessarily replacing components that are currently in good condition.

Upper Service Drop – Corrosion and Water Damage

LPH also found the upper service cable to be deteriorated. Corrosion is visible coming through the cable jacket at the neutral conductor. This indicates that moisture has entered or affected the cable and has begun compromising the conductor.

Because the condition of the conductor inside the cable cannot be fully verified without replacement, LPH recommends replacing the upper service cable, weather-tight connector, hub, and service head. The replacement would utilize 200-amp service cable, allowing this portion of the service to be properly sized while correcting the existing corrosion and improving the weather-tight integrity of the service entrance.

Addressing this now helps prevent continued deterioration of the neutral conductor and reduces the possibility of future heating, connection problems, or service interruptions.

Water Heater Breaker – Corrosion

LPH found one 2-pole breaker showing clear signs that it has been exposed to moisture at some point during its service life. Corrosion is visible on the breaker. Because the breaker supplies the water heater, which is a consistently loaded appliance, LPH recommends replacing the breaker rather than continuing to rely on a device with unknown internal moisture exposure.

Replacing the breaker provides a known-good connection and removes a component that may have experienced internal corrosion or damage that cannot be determined through visual inspection alone.

Double-Tapped Breaker / Tandem Breaker Correction

LPH found two wires installed underneath a single breaker terminal. The circuit is currently utilizing 12 AWG wiring on a 20-amp circuit, but a second 14 AWG conductor rated for 15 amps is also terminated underneath the same terminal.

Because the panel is currently full, LPH recommends correcting this by installing a 15-amp tandem breaker, allowing the 15-amp circuit to have its own properly rated overcurrent protection and terminal connection rather than sharing a breaker terminal with another circuit.

This correction ensures each conductor is protected according to its ampacity and provides a proper termination for the wiring.

Dedicated Patio Circuit Installation

LPH recommends installing a new dedicated 15-amp electrical circuit to the patio area. This includes installing a 15-amp tandem breaker in the existing electrical panel to supply the new circuit.

The new wiring will be routed through the basement, with the cable neatly stapled along the exposed joists where accessible and then continued through the secondary drop-ceiling area to reach the patio location. This provides a dedicated power source without relying on existing circuits that may already be serving other loads.

At the patio, LPH will install a weather-rated electrical box with GFI protection to provide a properly protected outdoor power source. The weather-rated enclosure is designed to better protect the electrical connections from outdoor moisture, while GFI protection provides additional shock protection in an area exposed to the elements.

This installation provides the homeowner with a convenient, properly protected outdoor receptacle while keeping the new patio power on its own dedicated circuit.

Basement GFI Protection

LPH found a faulty GFI receptacle in the basement that is no longer operating properly. LPH recommends replacing the GFI to restore proper ground-fault protection.

GFI protection is especially important in basement areas where moisture, plumbing, concrete, and other conductive surfaces can increase the potential for shock hazards.

Kitchen Counter GFI Protection

LPH recommends installing a GFI receptacle on the kitchen countertop circuit to provide the required ground-fault protection in this area.

Kitchen countertop receptacles are commonly exposed to water and other conductive materials. Proper GFI protection is designed to quickly disconnect power when it detects current flowing along an unintended path, helping protect occupants from electrical shock.

Bathroom GFI – Failed Test Function

LPH found the existing bathroom GFI receptacle is no longer tripping properly when tested. Because the primary purpose of a GFI is to provide rapid protection during a ground-fault condition, a device that fails its test function should not be relied upon for protection.

LPH recommends replacing the bathroom GFI with a new properly functioning device and testing it after installation to confirm the protection is operating correctly.

Secondary Apartment – GFI Protection

In the secondary apartment, LPH recommends installing two GFI receptacles underneath the sink to protect the receptacles supplying the dishwasher and garbage disposal.

These appliances are located in an area where water and electricity are in close proximity. Providing GFI protection helps reduce the risk of electrical shock if a fault occurs involving the appliances, wiring, or moisture.

Whole-Home Surge Protection – Both Panels

LPH also recommends installing whole-home surge protection on both basement electrical panels.

Modern appliances and electronics contain sensitive circuit boards and electronic controls that can be damaged by voltage surges. Surges do not only come from lightning or the utility company; many are generated inside the home when larger motors and appliances turn on and off, including air-conditioning equipment, refrigerators, heat pumps, furnaces, washers, dryers, dishwashers, and other motor-driven equipment.

Installing surge protection at both panels provides an additional layer of protection for the home’s electrical equipment by helping divert damaging transient voltage away from connected circuits and electronics. With two separate panels supplying the home, protecting both panels provides more complete coverage of the electrical system.

Overall Evaluation

Overall, the existing service and distribution system is in good condition, particularly the portions of the service that have already been installed in PVC conduit. LPH is recommending targeted repairs and upgrades rather than replacing components that are currently serviceable.

The primary priorities are correcting the 100-amp main service feed supplying two 100-amp panels, replacing the deteriorated upper service drop and weather-tight components, and addressing the corroded water-heater breaker. The dedicated patio circuit, GFI replacements and additions, proper GFI protection in the secondary apartment, tandem-breaker correction, and whole-home surge protection would further improve the safety, reliability, convenience, and protection of the home’s electrical system.

LPH reviewed these findings and recommendations with the homeowner so they could understand the condition of the existing system, the purpose of each recommended repair, and the benefits of addressing these items.

The homeowner would like some time to review the different options and decide which recommendations she would like to move forward with. LPH will email the completed electrical evaluation and all estimates to the homeowner for her review and consideration.

Thank you for choosing LPH!

LPH will install a premium whole-home surge protection device at the home’s main electrical panel. This device is designed to protect the home’s electrical system and connected equipment from damaging voltage spikes and transient surges before they can travel throughout the home’s wiring.
Many homeowners think of lightning when they hear the term “surge,” but the majority of power surges actually originate inside the home. Everyday appliances such as air conditioners, refrigerators, heat pumps, furnaces, microwaves, dishwashers, washers, dryers, and even garage door openers create small electrical surges—known as microsurges—every time their motors cycle on and off. While each individual surge is small, thousands of these microsurges occur over time and gradually wear down the sensitive electronic components found in today’s modern appliances and equipment.
Whole-home surge protection helps absorb and divert these surges away from the home’s electrical system, reducing cumulative damage to expensive electronics and appliances. This is especially important in newer homes, where nearly every major appliance contains sophisticated circuit boards and microprocessors that are far more sensitive to voltage fluctuations than older equipment.
In addition to protecting against internally generated microsurges, whole-home surge protection also provides a critical first line of defense against larger surges originating from the utility company, switching events on the electrical grid, nearby lightning strikes, or power being restored after an outage.
Benefits of premium whole-home surge protection include:
	• Protects HVAC systems, refrigerators, ovens, dishwashers, washers, dryers, and other major appliances.
	• Helps safeguard sensitive electronics such as televisions, computers, gaming systems, networking equipment, and smart home devices.
	• Reduces the long-term effects of everyday microsurges that slowly degrade electronic components.
	• Can help extend the service life of modern appliances and equipment by reducing electrical stress on internal circuit boards.
	• Helps minimize the likelihood of costly repairs or premature equipment replacement due to surge damage.
	• Provides continuous protection for the entire home’s electrical system without relying solely on individual plug-in surge strips.
	• Offers added peace of mind during storms, utility switching events, and unexpected power outages.
As homes continue to rely on more connected technology and electronically controlled appliances, whole-home surge protection has become one of the most valuable upgrades for preserving the reliability, longevity, and performance of a home’s electrical equipment.

e.336917502:
Technician performed water quality testing and found the home’s water hardness to be 15 grains per gallon (GPG) and the chlorine level to be 3.0 ppm. A hardness level of 15 GPG is considered hard water and can lead to calcium and magnesium scale buildup inside water heaters, plumbing fixtures, faucets, shower heads, and water-using appliances. Over time, this mineral buildup can reduce appliance efficiency, shorten equipment life expectancy, cause spotting on dishes and glassware, and leave soap residue on fixtures and surfaces. The presence of chlorine, while common in municipal water supplies, can contribute to dry skin and hair and may deteriorate rubber seals and gaskets within the plumbing system over time.

To improve water quality and help protect the home’s plumbing system, technician recommends installing a City Soft water treatment system. The system is designed to soften the water by removing the hardness minerals that cause scale buildup while also reducing chlorine levels throughout the home. Benefits of the system include improved soap and detergent performance, reduced spotting and scaling, softer-feeling water, and increased protection and efficiency of plumbing fixtures and water-using appliances.

The proposed installation location for the City Soft system is near the existing water meter to allow for efficient integration into the home’s main water distribution system. The softener’s backwash drain lines will be routed and connected to the existing main drain located above the water softener at the proposed installation area. The system also requires a dedicated electrical outlet for operation and regeneration cycles. The home’s electrical panel is located approximately 5’ feet away, and an outlet will need to be installed and provided at the equipment location prior to or as part of the installation. Once installed, the system will provide conditioned water to the entire home and help minimize the long-term effects of hard water and chlorine exposure on the plumbing system.

LPH performed an electrical system check of the home to evaluate the overall condition, safety, and operation of the electrical system. During the evaluation, LPH reviewed the electrical service, panels and breakers, grounding and bonding, receptacles and switches, GFCI protection, visible wiring and connections, exterior electrical equipment, and the overall condition and available capacity of the electrical system.

Main Electrical Service — 100-Amp Exterior Service

LPH found that the home is currently supplied by a 100-amp exterior electrical service that is approximately 36 years old. Evidence of long-term water and moisture intrusion was found within the existing service equipment.

Water-drop marks were observed inside the existing panel, and inspection of the exterior meter base confirmed visible water and moisture throughout the enclosure. Corrosion is also present on the neutral conductor where it exits its insulation jacket.

Water entry is presumed to be occurring through the upper service drop and/or the older seals, which have deteriorated over time and are no longer providing reliable protection against moisture. Moisture and water-drop marks were also observed above the main breaker, creating additional concern for continued corrosion and deterioration of the breaker and other service components.

The existing 100-amp service supplies two electrical panels, both of which are substantially populated with circuits. The current electrical demand leaves limited additional capacity for the home’s existing and future electrical needs.

Recommended Option 1 — Replace Existing 100-Amp Service

LPH recommends replacing the existing 100-amp exterior electrical service due to its age, water intrusion, corrosion, and overall condition. This option would maintain the home’s existing 100-amp service capacity while replacing the aging and moisture-damaged service equipment with new, properly sealed equipment.

The replacement would address the existing water-entry concerns and provide a safer, more reliable exterior service installation while bringing the replaced components up to current applicable electrical requirements.

Recommended Option 2 — Upgrade to 200-Amp Service

LPH also recommends considering an upgrade from the existing 100-amp service to a 200-amp electrical service. The home currently has two electrical panels that are substantially populated, and upgrading the service would provide significantly more available electrical capacity for the home’s existing circuitry and future electrical demands.

A 200-amp service upgrade would also provide additional capacity for future additions or larger electrical loads without placing the home’s service near its maximum available capacity. This option would replace the existing aging and moisture-damaged service equipment and provide a modern service installation with substantially greater capacity.

The 200-amp upgrade is recommended as the preferred long-term option based on the home’s existing amount of circuitry and the limited capacity of the current 100-amp service.

Exterior Garage Receptacle

LPH identified an opportunity to provide a properly protected exterior power source at the garage.

LPH would utilize the existing junction box located inside the garage as the source for a new exterior receptacle. A new electrical connection would be made from the existing junction box, with wiring routed directly through the rear of the box and through the exterior wall to supply a new outdoor receptacle.

LPH would install a new GFCI-protected exterior receptacle with a weather-resistant enclosure and in-use bubble cover. The bubble cover will protect the receptacle and plug connection from rain and moisture while equipment is plugged in, providing a safer and more reliable outdoor power location.

GFCI Protection — Kitchen

LPH found that the kitchen lacks adequate GFCI protection for applicable receptacles.

LPH recommends adding GFCI protection in the kitchen to provide additional shock protection in an area where electrical equipment is commonly used around sinks, water, and conductive surfaces.

GFCI Protection — Upstairs Bathroom

LPH found that the upstairs bathroom lacks appropriate GFCI protection.

LPH recommends installing GFCI protection for the applicable bathroom receptacle(s). GFCI protection is especially important in bathroom locations because electrical devices are used in close proximity to water.

GFCI Protection — Garage

LPH found that the garage lacks appropriate GFCI protection for the applicable receptacle(s).

LPH recommends adding GFCI protection to the garage receptacle circuit to provide additional shock protection in an area where power tools, extension cords, grounded surfaces, and potential moisture may be present.

Overall Electrical System Summary

LPH’s electrical system check identified several conditions that should be addressed to improve the home’s safety, reliability, and electrical capacity.

The most significant finding is the 36-year-old 100-amp exterior service with documented water intrusion and corrosion. LPH recommends either replacing the existing service while maintaining the 100-amp capacity or upgrading the home to a 200-amp service for increased electrical capacity. Based on the home’s two-panel configuration and the amount of existing circuitry, the 200-amp upgrade provides the homeowner with the greatest long-term electrical capacity and flexibility.

LPH also recommends installing GFCI protection in the kitchen, upstairs bathroom, and garage, along with installing the proposed new GFCI-protected exterior garage receptacle with an in-use bubble cover.

These recommendations are intended to address the conditions observed during today’s evaluation, improve electrical safety, protect the system from moisture-related deterioration, and provide the home with a more reliable electrical system for both current and future needs.

At this time the homeowner would like to go over her finances before moving forward with any work. LPH scheduled a call back on Friday to go over the job further. Thank you for allowing us into your home, all estimates and evaluations will be sent via email.

i.329376463:
LPH completed a comprehensive electrical system check of the home. During the evaluation, we inspected the electrical service and meter equipment, exterior service components, main electrical panel and breakers, grounding and bonding, visible wiring and connections, receptacles and switches, GFCI protection, and other accessible electrical components throughout the home. We also looked for signs of water intrusion, moisture exposure, corrosion, overheating, deterioration, loose or damaged connections, and other conditions that could affect the safety, reliability, or proper operation of the electrical system.

System Check Findings – Electrical Panel

During the system check, LPH found evidence that water had previously entered the homeowner’s new electrical panel, resulting in corrosion and deterioration of the electrical equipment. Corrosion was already beginning to form on the main lugs and other electrical surfaces.

The homeowner advised LPH that the electrical company that previously installed the panel had already been notified of the water-entry concern and had taken steps to seal the exterior areas where the water was entering. The areas have since been sealed; however, the corrosion and deterioration that occurred before the water entry was addressed remain present within the electrical equipment.

LPH explained to the homeowner that sealing the exterior areas helps prevent additional water from entering, but it does not reverse the damage that has already occurred. Water that previously reached the main breaker and electrical connections can cause corrosion and deterioration of the metal surfaces and lugs. Over time, this deterioration can increase resistance at electrical connections, create additional heat, and potentially contribute to premature failure of the equipment.

This is particularly important because the panel itself is brand new. Although the source of the water entry has been addressed, the damage caused by the previous water exposure could result in the newly installed equipment failing significantly earlier than expected. LPH recommends having the affected equipment evaluated and addressing any components that have already been compromised by the water and corrosion.

System Check Findings – GFCI Protection

During the system check, LPH identified several areas that would benefit from GFCI protection based on current applicable NEC requirements. GFCI protection is designed to quickly interrupt power when it detects current flowing along an unintended path, helping reduce the risk of serious electrical shock.

All-Season Room: The all-season room is an area where there can be some interpretation depending on how the space is classified due to the full-glass windows. However, because this room is not climate controlled and is exposed to significant temperature and humidity swings throughout the year, LPH recommends GFCI protection. These environmental conditions can contribute to moisture accumulation, corrosion, and premature deterioration of electrical devices over time.

Unfinished Basement: The receptacles located on the basement block walls are lacking GFCI protection. Block walls can allow moisture from the surrounding ground to migrate through the wall, resulting in condensation or “sweating” around electrical devices. The unfinished basement is also more susceptible to water intrusion or flooding. GFCI protection provides an additional layer of safety by quickly shutting down power when a ground-fault condition is detected, helping reduce the risk of shock if water comes into contact with energized equipment.

LPH also found that the receptacle supplying the water heater and water softener has already experienced water intrusion. Because this receptacle is supplied by its own dedicated circuit, LPH recommends installing a GFCI receptacle at this location to provide localized protection to the circuit and directly address the existing moisture exposure.

The remaining basement receptacles are supplied by a separate circuit and can be protected together with a 20-amp GFCI breaker, providing protection to the entire circuit.

Garage: The garage is another area requiring GFCI protection under current applicable NEC requirements. Garages present increased electrical shock hazards because receptacles can be exposed to moisture, concrete floors, tools, vehicles, and other conditions that can increase the possibility of a ground-fault event.

LPH also observed that some of the garage receptacles have already been affected by the higher humidity levels in this area. Corrosion has developed inside the receptacle contact points where plugs make connection. Corroded contacts can create poor electrical connections, increasing resistance and heat and potentially contributing to arcing or electrical failure. Providing GFCI protection and addressing deteriorated devices will improve the safety and reliability of these electrical connections.

Upstairs Bathrooms: The upstairs bathroom receptacles were found without GFCI protection. GFCI protection is required in bathroom areas because electrical devices are used in close proximity to water, and a person may simultaneously be in contact with water, plumbing, or other grounded surfaces. GFCI protection is designed to quickly interrupt power when it detects a potentially dangerous current imbalance.

LPH recommends providing GFCI protection to the circuit supplying the upstairs bathroom receptacles.

Kitchen: LPH inspected the kitchen countertop receptacles and found that the countertop receptacles are present; however, one countertop receptacle is currently not GFCI protected. Kitchen countertop receptacles require GFCI protection because portable electrical appliances are commonly used in close proximity to sinks, water, and other sources of moisture. GFCI protection helps reduce the risk of electrical shock if an appliance or electrical device develops a fault.

LPH recommends providing GFCI protection for the currently unprotected countertop receptacle and adding the recommended 20-amp GFCI protection for the kitchen.

Exterior Receptacles: LPH found that only one of the six exterior receptacles currently has GFCI protection with an appropriate in-use bubble cover. None of the exterior receptacles were installed with weather-resistant devices.

Several of the exterior receptacles were found to have significant corrosion and were deemed unsafe for continued use. Outdoor electrical devices are exposed to rain, humidity, temperature changes, and moisture, making proper weather-resistant equipment and GFCI protection especially important.

LPH recommends replacing the affected exterior devices with weather-resistant, tamper-resistant GFCI receptacles and installing extra-duty in-use bubble covers. These covers help protect the receptacle and plug connection from direct exposure to rain and moisture while the receptacle is in use.

Recommended Protection Plan

To provide comprehensive GFCI protection throughout the identified areas, LPH recommends:

* Weather-resistant, tamper-resistant GFCI receptacles at the exterior locations
* Extra-duty in-use bubble covers for the exterior receptacles
* GFCI protection for the currently unprotected kitchen countertop receptacle
* A dedicated GFCI receptacle for the water heater and water softener circuit due to the existing water intrusion
* 20-amp GFCI breaker protection for the remaining unfinished basement receptacle circuit
* 20-amp GFCI breaker protection for the all-season room
* 20-amp GFCI breaker protection for the circuit supplying the upstairs bathrooms
* 20-amp GFCI breaker protection for the garage
* Evaluation and replacement of any electrical components within the new panel that have already been compromised by the previous water exposure and corrosion

These recommendations address the moisture, humidity, corrosion, and electrical safety concerns observed during today’s system check while providing additional protection against electrical shock and premature deterioration of the electrical equipment.

Homeowner Follow-Up

All findings and recommendations were reviewed with the homeowner. The homeowner stated that he would like to look into completing these items as his own project. LPH still wanted to provide the homeowner with the option of having these improvements completed by qualified electrical professionals and will provide estimates for the recommended work.

The estimates and today’s electrical system evaluation will be emailed to the homeowner for his records and future review.

Thank you for allowing LPH into your home today. We appreciate the opportunity to assist you and look forward to servicing you again in the future.
