LPH completed a comprehensive electrical system check of the home, evaluating the electrical service, main disconnect, meter/service equipment, interior panel, grounding and bonding, branch-circuit wiring, breakers, receptacles, switches, GFCI protection, and visible electrical connections throughout the home. LPH also evaluated the bathroom ventilation and identified additional device concerns that should be addressed to improve the safety, reliability, and overall condition of the electrical system.

Primary Recommendation – 100A/200A Service Replacement

LPH found deterioration and water-related corrosion affecting the existing electrical service equipment. The existing service components, including the overhead service conductors, weatherhead, meter enclosure, service connections, and interior panel, are showing signs of age and deterioration that warrant replacement rather than continued reliance on the existing equipment.

LPH recommends replacing the service in its entirety. The homeowner may choose between a 100-amp service replacement or an upgrade to a 200-amp service, depending on the home’s present and future electrical demands.

The service replacement will include:

* Required electrical utility coordination, service shutdown, and inspections.
* Removal of the existing overhead service equipment.
* Installation of new properly sized overhead service conductors.
* Installation of a new weatherhead and properly securing/strapping the overhead service cable to the exterior of the home.
* Removal and replacement of the existing exterior meter base.
* Installation of a new exterior emergency/service disconnect sized for the selected 100-amp or 200-amp service.
* Installation of new PVC conduit from the exterior disconnect into the home.
* Proper sealing of the meter base, disconnect, conduit, and electrical entry points to help prevent future water intrusion.
* Installation of a new four-wire feeder from the exterior service disconnect to the interior electrical panel.
* Reconfiguration of the interior panel as a subpanel, with the neutral and equipment grounding conductors properly separated.
* Installation of a properly bonded grounding bar and isolated neutral bar within the interior panel.
* Establishment of the service grounding and bonding at the exterior service disconnect.
* Installation of the required grounding electrode system, including two ground rods.
* New grounding and bonding connections to the home’s water and gas systems as required by applicable code.
* Installation of a whole-home surge protection device as part of the service replacement.
* Removal of the existing interior panel and installation of a new Eaton CH loadcenter, sized appropriately for the selected service.
* Replacement/retermination of breakers and branch-circuit conductors as needed during the panel replacement.
* Properly labeling all circuits in the new panel.
* Completion of all required grounding, bonding, and electrical connections.
* Required inspections and final testing of the completed electrical system.

The goal of the service replacement is to provide the home with a properly reconstructed service, updated grounding and bonding, improved protection from water intrusion, additional breaker capacity, and a safer and more reliable foundation for the home’s electrical system. If the homeowner chooses the 200-amp option, the additional capacity will also provide greater flexibility for future electrical improvements and higher-demand equipment.

Upstairs Bedroom Receptacle

During the system check, LPH found an upstairs bedroom receptacle that is extremely corroded. Corrosion inside a receptacle can affect the connection between the plug and internal contacts, creating increased electrical resistance and heat at the connection point. Continued deterioration can lead to poor connections, intermittent operation, arcing, or overheating.

LPH recommends replacing this receptacle with a new properly rated device and testing the circuit to confirm proper operation.

Upstairs Bathroom – Premium Bath Fan & Ventilation

LPH also evaluated the upstairs bathroom and found that the bathroom currently does not have a properly installed exhaust fan for ventilation. Mold is developing on the bathroom walls, and the lack of mechanical ventilation allows moisture from showers and normal bathroom use to remain trapped in the room.

LPH recommends installing a new premium Panasonic bath fan to provide proper mechanical ventilation and help remove excess moisture from the bathroom.

The installation will include:

* Installation of a new premium Panasonic bath fan.
* Installation of new ductwork to properly discharge bathroom air to the exterior of the home.
* Routing the ductwork through the existing structure as needed due to the limited access and existing construction.
* Installation of an appropriate exterior termination to allow the moist bathroom air to discharge outdoors.
* Running new electrical wiring from the existing switch bank to establish a dedicated switch leg for the new bath fan.
* Installation of a new wall switch to control the fan.
* Proper electrical connection and testing of the new fan.
* Testing the completed ventilation system to verify proper operation and airflow.

Proper bathroom ventilation will help remove moisture at the source, reducing the amount of humidity that remains on the walls and ceiling after bathing. This is an important improvement for the bathroom because continued moisture accumulation can contribute to mold growth, staining, deterioration of finishes, and other moisture-related problems. The new fan and exterior ductwork are intended to improve ongoing ventilation; existing mold growth may require separate cleaning or remediation.

Due to the age and construction of the existing plaster/wall materials, LPH will take reasonable precautions to minimize unnecessary disturbance during the installation. If testing confirms asbestos-containing material or additional asbestos-related procedures are required before work can safely proceed, those services would need to be addressed separately by the appropriate qualified professionals.

Overall System Check & Estimate Review

LPH discussed the recommended electrical upgrades and improvements with the homeowner, including the available 100-amp and 200-amp service replacement options, the corroded bedroom receptacle, and the installation of proper ventilation for the upstairs bathroom.

LPH will provide the homeowner with the estimates for the recommended work, along with today’s complete electrical system check evaluation, via email for their review. This will allow the homeowner to review the available options, scope of work, and recommendations before deciding how they would like to proceed.

Thank you for allowing LPH into your home today. We appreciate the opportunity to inspect your electrical system and provide recommendations to help keep your home safe, reliable, and properly maintained. We look forward to servicing you again in the future.

e.339965112:
During today’s electrical system evaluation, LPH identified significant water intrusion and extensive deterioration affecting the home’s overhead electrical service. The condition of the service equipment presents a serious electrical safety concern and should be addressed as soon as possible.

The existing upper overhead service cable run is extremely weathered and deteriorated. Water is entering through the upper portion of the service entrance and traveling down the service cable toward the exterior meter enclosure. Upon opening the meter enclosure, visible corrosion trails were observed coming down from the service cable and running along the main phase conductors. This moisture has caused significant corrosion and deterioration at the service lugs and electrical connections.

The neutral block is also discolored from heat exposure, adding another concern at the primary service connection. The combination of water intrusion, corrosion, weathered service equipment, and heat discoloration is particularly serious because these connections carry the home’s entire electrical supply.

Water is also entering through the lower portion of the overhead service and continuing into the interior electrical panel. Extensive rust has accumulated at the bottom of the panel, with heavy corrosion formed along the left side of the enclosure. The corrosion has progressed to the bus bar and the breakers installed along that side of the panel.

The main breaker is specifically showing significant rust and deterioration. Considering the amount of water entering the panel and the visible corrosion already present throughout the equipment, the internal components and connection points of the main breaker may be significantly deteriorated as well.

Safety Concerns

The condition of the primary electrical service is a serious safety concern because the affected components are the main connection points supplying power to the entire home. These connections are showing evidence of water exposure, corrosion, heat discoloration, and significant deterioration.

Moisture entering electrical service equipment can contribute to corrosion, increased electrical resistance, overheating, arcing, breaker malfunction, and deterioration of electrical connections. The continued operation of severely deteriorated service equipment can increase the potential for electrical failure and further damage.

Because the water intrusion is entering through the overhead service, continuing through the meter enclosure, and then into the interior panel, the issue affects the home’s primary electrical service rather than being isolated to an individual branch circuit.

Recommended Overhead Service Replacement

Due to the extent of the water intrusion and deterioration throughout the existing overhead service, LPH recommends a complete 200-amp overhead electrical service replacement. Light corrosion is beginning to form on the bus bar, and the metal tabs on the backs of the breakers are showing signs of heat discoloration. These conditions can indicate deterioration at electrical connection points, which may increase resistance and contribute to additional heat buildup, poor electrical contact, or potential arcing over time. Replacing the subpanel would address these early signs of deterioration and provide a clean, reliable panel for the garage and future electrical needs.

LPH will replace the existing garage subpanel due to early signs of deterioration and heat-related wear within the panel. Light corrosion is beginning to form on the bus bar, and the metal tabs on the backs of the breakers are showing signs of heat discoloration.

LPH will remove the existing subpanel and install a new properly sized panel with new breakers as required. All connections will be properly torqued and the completed installation will be tested to verify safe and reliable operation.

Replacing the panel now addresses the early signs of corrosion and heat damage before they have an opportunity to progress into a more serious electrical issue, while also providing the garage with a clean, reliable panel for future electrical needs.

Moen Flo Smart Water Monitor & Shutoff, it’s a smart plumbing device that monitors the home’s water system and can automatically shut off the water if it detects a potential leak.

How Moen Flo works

The Flo device is installed on the home’s main water line. It continuously monitors things like:

* Water flow
* Water pressure
* Water usage patterns
* Potential leaks, including very small leaks that may otherwise go unnoticed

It can learn the household’s normal water-use patterns and identify unusual activity. If a significant leak is detected, the system can automatically shut off the home’s main water supply, helping limit water damage.

Main benefits

* Helps prevent major water damage: Automatic shutoff can stop or reduce flooding from a failed toilet supply line, washing machine hose, water heater, pipe, etc.
* 24/7 leak monitoring: The system monitors the plumbing even when nobody is home.
* Early leak detection: It can identify abnormal or continuous water usage before a small problem becomes a major one.
* Water usage awareness: Homeowners can see how much water the house is using and identify unusual consumption.
* Remote control: Through the Moen app, homeowners can monitor the system and, depending on the setup, turn the home’s water supply on or off remotely.
* Peace of mind: Particularly valuable for vacation homes, rental properties, or homeowners who travel frequently.
* Potential insurance benefits: Some insurers may offer discounts for approved water-leak detection/shutoff systems, although this varies by company and policy.

In simple terms: A Moen Flo acts like a 24/7 security system for your home’s plumbing. It watches the water system, alerts you to potential problems, and can shut the water off automatically to help protect the home.

e.336873551:
Technician performed water quality testing and found the home’s water hardness to be 18 grains per gallon (GPG) and the chlorine level to be 2.0 ppm. A hardness level of 18 GPG is considered hard water and can lead to calcium and magnesium scale buildup inside water heaters, plumbing fixtures, faucets, showerheads, and water-using appliances. Over time, this mineral buildup can reduce appliance efficiency, shorten equipment life expectancy, cause spotting on dishes and glassware, and leave soap residue on fixtures and surfaces. The presence of chlorine, while common in municipal water supplies, can contribute to dry skin and hair and may deteriorate rubber seals and gaskets within the plumbing system over time.

To improve water quality and help protect the home’s plumbing system, technician recommends installing a City Soft water treatment system. The system is designed to soften the water by removing the hardness minerals that cause scale buildup while also reducing chlorine levels throughout the home. Benefits of the system include improved soap and detergent performance, reduced spotting and scaling, softer-feeling water, and increased protection and efficiency of plumbing fixtures and water-using appliances.

The proposed installation location for the City Soft system is near the existing water mater to allow for efficient integration into the home’s main water distribution system. The softener’s backwash drain lines will be routed and connected to the existing main drain located near the water heater. The system also requires a dedicated electrical outlet for operation and regeneration cycles. An electrical outlet is provided. Once installed, the system will provide conditioned water to the entire home and help minimize the long-term effects of hard water and chlorine exposure on the plumbing system.

Technician will remove the unused drain piping in the basement near the water heater to clean up the existing plumbing and eliminate unnecessary piping.

This morning I arrived at the Snavely household to conduct their first annual electrical system and safety check. Upon performing a thorough evaluation of the homes main service I found several things worth noting. The most important finding in today’s visit is the presence of large quantities of rust affecting primarily the housing of the main breaker panel. I spent ample time trying to identify an exact source of this rusting, as the panel is only 9 years old. I was unable to pin point one specific source of moisture, which leads me to believe this rusting is a result of massive humidity and standing moisture in the basement. The basement is an unfinished cellar style basement with bare stone walls and floor. It is constantly damp, and in this case it seems it is leeching onto the basements equipment. As it stands the mechanical portions of the panel meaning the breakers, do not seem to be impacted by the rust, but there must be an immediate attempt to prevent further rust by running a dehumidifier or two in the basement and close to the panel. Being that this is our first electrical check I can not speak to the rate at which the rust is forming, but I can confirm that there is some signs of more recent condensation on the breaker panels shell. I have attached several photos of the corrosion in order for us to monitor the rate of deterioration as we continue to perform these checks annually. Otherwise, the only recommendations I had for Mrs. Snavely was the addition of a whole home surge protection device, and a dedicated circuit to prevent her washing machine from tripping.

If you have any questions related to todays visit please do not hesitate to contact us, thank you and take care!

i.331837352:
LPH completed a thorough electrical system check throughout the home, including an evaluation of the main electrical service, meter base, service entrance conductors, electrical panel, breakers, grounding and bonding, wiring, receptacles, switches, GFCI/AFCI protection, smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, visible junction boxes and connections, and the overall condition and operation of the home’s electrical equipment. LPH also checked for visible signs of overheating, corrosion, moisture intrusion, damaged or deteriorated components, improper wiring, and other conditions that could affect the safety, reliability, or proper operation of the electrical system.

The remainder of the home’s electrical system has been fully updated and is currently in great working order. LPH did not identify any significant concerns with the updated portions of the electrical system during today’s evaluation. The primary concern identified is with the aging exterior electrical service and evidence of moisture intrusion and corrosion associated with the existing service entrance.

Outside Service Replacement – Corrosion & Moisture Intrusion

LPH found visible corrosion where the neutral conductor exits the protective jacket as it enters the main electrical panel. The majority of the interior panel is clean, with rust staining concentrated at the base of the panel directly below where the service cable enters. This is an indication that moisture may be entering through the compromised service entrance rather than originating from within the panel itself.

LPH inspected the existing exterior meter base and found it to be an older, obsolete model that is showing its age. After removing the cover, a significant amount of rust buildup was observed inside the meter base, including corrosion around the meter lugs where the service entrance conductors are secured. The existing sealing at the top of the meter base is also old and deteriorated and may have provided an additional point of water entry.

A small tear was also identified in the upper portion of the service entrance cable. This creates another potential pathway for water to enter the cable jacket. Although the exposed portions of the neutral conductor inside the meter base appear relatively clean where they are able to dry, the greater concern is moisture becoming trapped inside the cable jacket where it can remain against the conductors and promote continued corrosion. Additional damage may also be present within the cable that cannot be fully evaluated until the existing cable is removed and dropped.

The neutral conductor is critical to maintaining proper voltage distribution throughout the home. If corrosion continues to weaken the neutral connection and the neutral were to fail, the home’s electrical system could experience an unstable or unbalanced voltage condition. This can result in some circuits receiving significantly more voltage than intended while others receive less, potentially causing serious damage to electronics, appliances, lighting, and other electrical equipment. Due to the visible corrosion, moisture concerns, aging meter base, deteriorated sealing, and compromised service cable, LPH recommends replacing the outside service before the condition can continue to deteriorate.

Complete Outside Service Replacement

LPH will remove the existing outside service and install a new code-compliant 100-amp exterior service. This will include:

* Removal of the existing obsolete meter base and outside service equipment.
* Cutting a new opening in the siding as needed to properly accommodate the new meter base.
* Installation of a new code-compliant 100-amp meter base.
* Installation of new service conductors protected within PVC conduit to protect them from future physical wear and weather exposure.
* Properly strapping the conduit to the home.
* Installation of a new PVC service head.
* Installation of a new code-compliant exterior emergency disconnect.
* Installation of new wiring from the meter base to the exterior disconnect.
* Continuation of the protected conduit run to the point where the service enters the basement.
* Installation of a new bonding bridge at the exterior service equipment.
* Relocation and lengthening of the grounding conductors as needed to properly terminate at the new exterior disconnect.
* Separation of the neutral and grounding conductors within the existing panel as required for the new service configuration.
* Proper bonding and grounding of the new service equipment.
* Sealing the new meter base and disconnect with silicone to help prevent future water intrusion.
* Sealing the service entrance where the new conduit and conductors enter the home.

This replacement will eliminate the compromised section of the existing service cable and replace the aging exterior equipment with a properly protected and weather-resistant service configuration. The new installation will significantly reduce the opportunity for future physical damage and water penetration while providing a safer, more reliable, and code-compliant outside service.

i.332644456:
LPH performed a comprehensive electrical system check throughout the home. During our evaluation, we inspected the electrical service, main electrical panel, breakers, grounding and bonding, accessible wiring, switches, receptacles, GFI protection, exterior electrical devices, weatherproofing of exterior devices, and accessible electrical equipment. We also checked for visible signs of age-related deterioration, loose or damaged connections, overheating, corrosion, physical damage, improper installations, and other conditions that could affect the safety, reliability, or performance of the home’s electrical system. The accessible electrical devices and circuits were evaluated for proper operation, and areas requiring repair, replacement, or additional protection were identified and discussed with the homeowner.

Findings & Recommendations

Aging Switches – Multiple Locations
Several existing switches throughout the home were found to be older devices utilizing back-stab style connections. The plastic molding on these switches is beginning to break away, indicating that the devices are reaching the end of their useful service life. Older back-stab connections can loosen over time, creating resistance and heat at the connection point and potentially leading to arcing or device failure.

LPH recommends replacing the affected switches with new devices utilizing secure connections to provide dependable operation and reduce the potential for future overheating or connection-related issues.

Exterior & Basement GFI Protection
LPH identified exterior receptacle locations requiring improved protection from moisture, including receptacles installed on the basement block wall where water and wall intrusion have previously been an issue.

LPH recommends installing new weather-resistant GFI devices at the applicable exterior and basement locations. Three exterior devices would also receive weatherproof bubble covers to provide additional protection from rain and moisture, including when cords are plugged in and the receptacles are being used.

Worn Interior Receptacles – 3 Locations
Three receptacles throughout the home were found to have heavily worn internal plug contacts and were struggling to securely hold plugs in place. Loose receptacle connections can result in poor electrical contact, heat buildup, intermittent operation, and premature wear on connected equipment.

LPH recommends replacing all three worn receptacles with new devices to provide secure and reliable connections.

Washing Machine GFI Protection
The washing machine receptacle was found without GFI protection.

LPH recommends adding GFI protection to the washer receptacle, providing additional protection against electrical shock should an electrical fault occur.

Upstairs Bedroom Ceiling Fans – 2 Locations
LPH provided an estimate to install two ceiling fans in the upstairs bedrooms. New wiring would be fished down to the existing switch locations, allowing the existing switched-receptacle configuration to be converted so the wall switches control the new ceiling fans.

This would provide convenient control of the new ceiling fans from the room entry while eliminating the need to rely on switched receptacles for fan operation.

Estimates & Homeowner Discussion

All findings, recommendations, and available repair options were reviewed in detail with the homeowner. At this time, the homeowner would like to take some time to consider the different estimates and determine how she would like to prioritize and budget the recommended electrical improvements along with the other areas of the home she is currently working on.

No additional work was authorized at this time beyond the evaluation. Today’s electrical system evaluation and all corresponding estimates will be sent to the homeowner via email for review and future planning.

Thank you for allowing LPH into your home today. We appreciate the opportunity to evaluate your electrical system and provide options to help keep your home safe, reliable, and up to date. We look forward to assisting with the recommended improvements when you are ready.

Grounding & Bonding

Whole-Home Surge Protection — Recommended Addition

e.335436778:
The home has recently been completely rewired and is equipped with brand-new electrical devices, LED lighting, appliances, and other modern electronics. Because of this recent investment, protecting the new electrical equipment from voltage surges is especially important.

Although the home was rewired recently, it just missed the cutoff requiring whole-home surge protection under the applicable code requirements. While it may not be mandatory for this installation, LPH strongly recommends adding whole-home surge protection as an additional layer of protection for the home’s new electrical system and equipment.

Modern electronics are significantly more sensitive to voltage fluctuations and surges than older equipment. In addition to large external surges, the home’s own mechanical and motor-driven equipment—such as HVAC systems, refrigerators, pumps, and other appliances—can create smaller downstream electrical surges when motors start and stop. These repeated micro-surges can place stress on sensitive electronic components, LED drivers, control boards, and other circuitry over time.

LPH recommends installing a whole-home surge protective device at the electrical panel to help divert damaging transient voltage away from the home’s branch circuits and connected equipment. This provides an additional level of protection against both internally generated transient surges and larger external events, such as utility disturbances or nearby lightning activity.

Premium Whole-Home Surge Protection
LPH will install a premium whole-home surge protection device at the home’s main electrical panel. This device is designed to protect the home’s electrical system and connected equipment from damaging voltage spikes and transient surges before they can travel throughout the home’s wiring.
Many homeowners think of lightning when they hear the term “surge,” but the majority of power surges actually originate inside the home. Everyday appliances such as air conditioners, refrigerators, heat pumps, furnaces, microwaves, dishwashers, washers, dryers, and even garage door openers create small electrical surges—known as microsurges—every time their motors cycle on and off. While each individual surge is small, thousands of these microsurges occur over time and gradually wear down the sensitive electronic components found in today’s modern appliances and equipment.
Whole-home surge protection helps absorb and divert these surges away from the home’s electrical system, reducing cumulative damage to expensive electronics and appliances. This is especially important in newer homes, where nearly every major appliance contains sophisticated circuit boards and microprocessors that are far more sensitive to voltage fluctuations than older equipment.
In addition to protecting against internally generated microsurges, whole-home surge protection also provides a critical first line of defense against larger surges originating from the utility company, switching events on the electrical grid, nearby lightning strikes, or power being restored after an outage.
Benefits of premium whole-home surge protection include:
	• Protects HVAC systems, refrigerators, ovens, dishwashers, washers, dryers, and other major appliances.
	• Helps safeguard sensitive electronics such as televisions, computers, gaming systems, networking equipment, and smart home devices.
	• Reduces the long-term effects of everyday microsurges that slowly degrade electronic components.

Many homeowners think of lightning when they hear the term “surge,” but the majority of power surges actually originate inside the home. Everyday appliances such as air conditioners, refrigerators, heat pumps, furnaces, microwaves, dishwashers, washers, dryers, and even garage door openers create small electrical surges—known as microsurges—every time their motors cycle on and off. While each individual surge is small, thousands of these microsurges occur over time and gradually wear down the sensitive electronic components found in today’s modern appliances and equipment.
Whole-home surge protection helps absorb and divert these surges away from the home’s electrical system, reducing cumulative damage to expensive electronics and appliances. This is especially important in newer homes, where nearly every major appliance contains sophisticated circuit boards and microprocessors that are far more sensitive to voltage fluctuations than older equipment.
In addition to protecting against internally generated microsurges, whole-home surge protection also provides a critical first line of defense against larger surges originating from the utility company, switching events on the electrical grid, nearby lightning strikes, or power being restored after an outage.
Benefits of premium whole-home surge protection include:

* Garbage Disposal: Install a GFCI receptacle under the kitchen sink to provide ground-fault protection for the garbage disposal and help protect against electrical shock in an area where water and electricity are in close proximity.

Adding GFCI protection in these locations improves the overall safety of the electrical system by helping quickly interrupt power if a ground-fault condition is detected, reducing the risk of electrical shock.

Premium Whole-Home Surge Protection
LPH will install a premium whole-home surge protection device at the home’s main electrical panel. This device is designed to protect the home’s electrical system and connected equipment from damaging voltage spikes and transient surges before they can travel throughout the home’s wiring.
Many homeowners think of lightning when they hear the term “surge,” but the majority of power surges actually originate inside the home. Everyday appliances such as air conditioners, refrigerators, heat pumps, furnaces, microwaves, dishwashers, washers, dryers, and even garage door openers create small electrical surges—known as microsurges—every time their motors cycle on and off. While each individual surge is small, thousands of these microsurges occur over time and gradually wear down the sensitive electronic components found in today’s modern appliances and equipment.
Whole-home surge protection helps absorb and divert these surges away from the home’s electrical system, reducing cumulative damage to expensive electronics and appliances. This is especially important in newer homes, where nearly every major appliance contains sophisticated circuit boards and microprocessors that are far more sensitive to voltage fluctuations than older equipment.
In addition to protecting against internally generated microsurges, whole-home surge protection also provides a critical first line of defense against larger surges originating from the utility company, switching events on the electrical grid, nearby lightning strikes, or power being restored after an outage.
Benefits of premium whole-home surge protection include:
	• Protects HVAC systems, refrigerators, ovens, dishwashers, washers, dryers, and other major appliances.
	• Helps safeguard sensitive electronics such as televisions, computers, gaming systems, networking equipment, and smart home devices.
	• Reduces the long-term effects of everyday microsurges that slowly degrade electronic components.
	• Can help extend the service life of modern appliances and equipment by reducing electrical stress on internal circuit boards.
	• Helps minimize the likelihood of costly repairs or premature equipment replacement due to surge damage.
	• Provides continuous protection for the entire home’s electrical system without relying solely on individual plug-in surge strips.
	• Offers added peace of mind during storms, utility switching events, and unexpected power outages.
As homes continue to rely on more connected technology and electronically controlled appliances, whole-home surge protection has become one of the most valuable upgrades for preserving the reliability, longevity, and performance of a home’s electrical equipment.

Premium Surge Protection Warranty & Replacement Coverage

The installed surge protection device also provides additional protection beyond the device itself. If the surge protector is ever sacrificed or fails as a result of a covered surge event, the device is backed by a lifetime warranty and coverage of up to $100,000 toward covered damage to the home’s electrical components and connected equipment, subject to the manufacturer’s warranty terms and conditions.

If the surge protector ever needs to be replaced under the warranty, the replacement device is provided at no charge. LPH will also handle the replacement installation for a $150 labor charge, helping make future warranty replacement straightforward and affordable for the homeowner.

This means the homeowner is not simply purchasing a surge protector—they are adding a long-term layer of protection to the home’s electrical system while also having manufacturer-backed coverage in the event of a significant surge.

As homes continue to rely on more connected technology and electronically controlled appliances, whole-home surge protection has become one of the most valuable upgrades for preserving the reliability, longevity, and performance of a home’s electrical equipment.

LPH performed a comprehensive electrical system check of the home. During the evaluation, LPH inspected the main electrical panel, breakers, wiring, grounding and bonding, receptacles, switches, GFCI protection, arc-fault protection, and visible electrical connections throughout the accessible areas of the home. LPH also checked for signs of overheating, arcing, corrosion, loose connections, damaged devices, improper installations, and other conditions that could affect the safety and reliability of the electrical system.

The electrical panel and overall electrical system were inspected for proper operation and general condition. The majority of the arc-fault breakers in the panel are in good condition; however, two older Cutler-Hammer arc-fault breakers showed noticeable signs of overheating. Black, sooty marks were present on the inside of the panel cover near these breakers, indicating that the breakers have been generating excessive heat under load. LPH discussed the importance of addressing these breakers to help prevent continued heat buildup, breaker failure, or potential damage to surrounding electrical components.

LPH also inspected the switches throughout the accessible areas of the home and identified one 3-way switch in the stairwell that was showing signs of arcing. This condition can create excessive heat and deterioration at the switch terminals and should be corrected to restore safe and reliable operation.

GFCI protection was also reviewed at applicable locations. LPH identified the washing machine receptacle and garbage disposal outlet as locations where additional GFCI protection can be provided. GFCI protection helps reduce the risk of electrical shock by quickly disconnecting power when a ground-fault condition is detected, which is particularly beneficial around appliances and areas where electricity may be exposed to moisture.

Options Reviewed with Homeowner

LPH reviewed the following options with the homeowner:

* Replace the two older Cutler-Hammer arc-fault breakers showing signs of overheating with new 15-amp arc-fault breakers with tails.
* Replace the arcing 3-way switch located in the stairwell.
* Add GFCI protection for the washing machine receptacle.
* Add GFCI protection for the garbage disposal outlet.

Homeowner-Approved Work

After reviewing the findings and available options, the homeowner elected to proceed with replacing the two affected arc-fault breakers with standard 15-amp breakers and replacing the arcing 3-way switch in the stairwell.

LPH addressed the identified overheating and arcing concerns as selected by the homeowner, helping restore safer and more reliable operation of these components. The additional GFCI protection options for the washing machine and garbage disposal were reviewed with the homeowner but were not selected at this time.

Today’s invoice will be emailed to the homeowner along with the completed electrical system evaluation for their records.

LPH completed an electrical system check throughout the home, including an evaluation of the main electrical service, outside meter base, service conductors, grounding and bonding, panel equipment, wiring, and various electrical devices throughout the home. During our evaluation, LPH identified several areas that could be addressed to improve the overall safety, reliability, and protection of the electrical system.

Primary Recommendation – Outside Electrical Service Replacement

The primary concern identified during today’s system check is the condition of the outside electrical service, which LPH found to be in critical condition and nearing complete failure.

There is an extremely heavy buildup of corrosion on the main neutral conductor inside the outside meter base. The aluminum conductor is fully coated with the byproduct of corrosion known as aluminum oxide. Aluminum oxide is not a reliable electrical conductor, and the severity of the deterioration combined with the moisture present at the service creates a serious concern for the integrity of the neutral connection.

The meter base is also showing significant corrosion from prolonged moisture exposure. Additional corrosion is present on the upper service cable, and the cable jacket where the conductors enter the meter base is currently wet. This indicates that the moisture-related deterioration has affected multiple portions of the service and is not isolated to one individual connection.

LPH considers this condition a serious electrical safety concern and the highest-priority recommendation from today’s evaluation. If the deteriorated neutral connection were to fail or become unstable, the home could experience an improper voltage balance between the two incoming phases. This can result in significant voltage fluctuations or voltage spikes throughout the home, potentially damaging electrical equipment, appliances, electronics, and sensitive circuit boards. A compromised service connection can also create excessive heat and an abnormal electrical current path, increasing the potential for an electrical failure or fire.

Due to the extent of the corrosion and moisture damage, LPH does not recommend attempting to repair only individual portions of the existing service. The service has reached a point where complete replacement is recommended as soon as possible to restore a reliable and properly protected electrical service.

The proposed service replacement will include removal of the existing deteriorated service equipment and conductors, installation of a new meter base and 200-amp exterior emergency disconnect, new properly sized service conductors, PVC protection from the service head through the exterior equipment and into the home, updated grounding and bonding, separation of neutrals and grounds within the main panel, sealing of exterior penetrations and equipment, reconnection of the utility-side service conductors with permanent compression crimps and new protective covers, and complete testing after power is restored.

This replacement will address the current deteriorated equipment while also providing additional protection against future moisture and UV exposure by enclosing the service conductors in PVC raceway and properly sealing the exterior portions of the installation.

LPH recommends completing the outside service replacement as soon as possible due to the current condition and the potential consequences of a service failure.

Additional Electrical Recommendations

During the system check, LPH also identified several opportunities to update individual electrical devices throughout the home. These included items such as loose or aging receptacles and switches, GFCI protection, and other device-related safety improvements.

LPH reviewed these recommendations with Jeff and discussed the purpose and benefits of addressing them. Jeff feels comfortable completing this specific device-related work himself, so no additional work was approved with LPH at this time.

While these individual device recommendations are worth addressing, the outside electrical service remains the primary concern from today’s evaluation due to the severity of the corrosion, moisture exposure, and potential for service failure.

Follow-Up

The homeowner will not be back at the home until September 26th. LPH will schedule a time to call back after his return so we can go over the findings and recommendations in further detail and answer any additional questions.

At this time, the estimate for the outside service replacement will be emailed to Jeff along with today’s electrical system evaluation for review.

Thank you for allowing LPH into your home and for the opportunity to evaluate your electrical system. We look forward to servicing you again in the future.

e.338915870:
Critical Electrical Service Condition

LPH found the home’s outside electrical service to be in critical condition and nearing complete failure. There is an extremely heavy buildup of corrosion on the main neutral conductor inside the outside meter base. The aluminum conductor is fully coated with the byproduct of corrosion, known as aluminum oxide.

Aluminum oxide is not a reliable electrical conductor. Because of the extent of the deterioration and the moisture present within the service equipment, the electrical connection is becoming increasingly dependent on the remaining conductive path through the damaged area. This creates a serious and unpredictable condition where the neutral connection could fail or become unstable.

If the main neutral connection were to fail, the electrical system could lose its ability to properly balance the voltage between the two incoming phases. This can result in significant voltage fluctuations or voltage spikes throughout the home, potentially damaging or destroying sensitive electrical equipment, appliances, electronics, and circuit boards. A compromised service connection can also create excessive heat and an abnormal path for electrical current, creating a serious fire and electrical safety hazard.

The meter base itself shows substantial corrosion consistent with prolonged moisture exposure. The upper service cable also has corrosion present, and the cable jacket where the conductors enter the meter base is currently wet. These conditions indicate that moisture has been affecting multiple components of the service rather than being isolated to one repairable connection.

Why Full Service Replacement Is Required

Due to the extent of deterioration, this is not a situation where replacing or repairing individual components would provide a reliable long-term solution. Multiple portions of the service have been compromised by moisture and corrosion. LPH recommends a complete replacement of the affected service equipment and conductors, from the service head where the connection is made to the utility lines through the equipment entering the home.

The replacement will provide a new, properly protected service and eliminate the deteriorated components currently creating the safety concern.

Full Scope of Work

LPH will:

* Shutdown of the electrical service and cut the existing connections at the top of the service to cap and disconnect the conductors coming from the utility pole.
* Remove the existing service head.
* Remove the existing upper service cables secured to the brick wall.
* Remove the existing exterior meter base and the service conductors feeding the home’s panel.
* Install a new meter base and a new 200-amp emergency exterior disconnect to provide the required means of shutting off power to the home from outside.
* Completely seal the new exterior equipment and penetrations with silicone to help prevent future moisture intrusion.
* Install new PVC raceway from the service head to the meter base and from the meter base through the exterior disconnect and into the home.
* Fully enclose the new service conductors in PVC, protecting them from direct exposure to rain, moisture, and UV rays and reducing the potential for future deterioration.
* Install new 200-amp, 3-wire service conductors from the service head to the meter base and through to the exterior disconnect as required for the service configuration.
* Relocate the main service disconnecting point to the new exterior disconnect.
* Extend the existing grounding conductors from the main panel by properly crimping the existing conductors to the required length and routing them through the exterior wall to the new disconnect.
* Drill through the exterior wall as necessary to bring the grounding conductors into the disconnect.
* Install a new grounding bar inside the exterior disconnect to properly terminate the grounding conductors.
* Install new 200-amp, 4-wire conductors from the exterior disconnect into the home’s main panel.
* Separate the neutral and grounding conductors within the main panel.
* Install a new grounding bar in the main panel and remove the existing neutral-to-ground bonding connection, since the main panel will no longer serve as the first means of disconnecting the service.
* Install a bonding bridge on the exterior of the home to provide a proper connection point for additional systems, such as telephone, cable, or other exterior grounding/bonding connections.
* Seal exterior PVC penetrations and piping with silicone to provide additional protection against moisture intrusion.
* Reconnect the conductors at the top of the service using permanent compression crimps and install new protective covers.
* Restore power and test the electrical system to confirm the new service is properly energized and operating as intended.

Safety & Long-Term Protection

This replacement is intended to address the immediate safety concern created by the severely deteriorated service, while also providing a properly protected 200-amp service configuration designed to prevent the new conductors and connections from being exposed to the same environmental conditions that contributed to the existing deterioration.

Because the service supplies the entire home, failure at this point can affect every electrical circuit and piece of equipment in the house. LPH recommends addressing this condition as an emergency electrical repair rather than continuing to operate the home with the existing deteriorated service.

LPH Electrical System Check

LPH performed an electrical system evaluation beginning at the main electrical service and panel, continuing through the accessible branch circuits, receptacles, switches, grounding and bonding system, and exterior electrical devices. During the inspection, LPH identified several conditions that should be addressed to improve the safety, reliability, and long-term performance of the electrical system.

Main Electrical Panel — Challenger 100 Amp Panel

Upon inspection, LPH found the home is currently equipped with an older 100-amp Challenger electrical panel that is approaching the end of its expected service life. Challenger equipment has a history of concerns involving breaker overheating, loose electrical connections, arcing, and breakers failing to trip properly when overcurrent protection is required.

While LPH was inspecting and tightening the electrical connections, a noticeable amount of soot/discoloration was able to be wiped from the wiring connected to the older Challenger breakers. This type of residue can be an indication that the connection or breaker has been experiencing excessive heat under load. Because heat and loose connections can progressively damage electrical components, this condition should not be ignored.

Recommendation — Replace 100 Amp Challenger Panel

LPH recommends replacing the existing 100-amp Challenger panel with a new Premium Eaton CH electrical panel.

The new Eaton CH panel would provide a modern enclosure and new breakers, eliminating the aging Challenger equipment and the associated concerns with continuing to operate the existing panel. The replacement would provide improved reliability, modern overcurrent protection, and additional peace of mind for the homeowner.

The Eaton CH equipment is also backed by the manufacturer’s warranty for the life of the device, providing long-term protection and value. Replacing the panel is the most comprehensive long-term solution rather than continuing to maintain aging Challenger equipment that is already showing signs of excessive heat.

⸻

Electrical Service Grounding — Improper Grounding Configuration

During the inspection, LPH also found that the home’s electrical service grounding system has not been installed correctly.

The existing system is relying on the home’s underground water piping as the grounding electrode, but the grounding conductor is not properly configured as one continuous connection through the water meter. The existing installation connects the grounding conductor to a water pipe in the basement, with a separate jumper installed across the water meter.

This configuration does not provide the proper continuous grounding connection to the underground water piping.

LPH also found that the electrical service is missing a dedicated grounding electrode/ground rod. A properly installed grounding system is an important part of the home’s electrical safety system because it provides a path for fault current and helps stabilize the electrical system during abnormal conditions and electrical surges.

Recommendation — Correct Grounding and Bonding

LPH recommends correcting the existing grounding system by installing the grounding electrode system properly, including a dedicated ground rod, and correcting the water service grounding connection so the grounding conductor is installed as one continuous connection to the water meter and properly jumped to the other side.

While correcting the grounding system, LPH would also bond the home’s gas piping as required to ensure the metallic gas piping is properly connected to the home’s grounding and bonding system.

This correction would bring the home’s grounding and bonding system up to current safety standards and provide a much more reliable path for fault current.

⸻

Basement Washer Receptacle — No GFCI Protection

LPH found that the receptacle serving the washing machine is currently not GFCI protected.

The receptacle is located in an unfinished basement and is mounted against a stone wall. Because of the basement environment, there is an increased possibility of moisture exposure. LPH also observed corrosion beginning to develop around the existing electrical boxes and mounting locations.

Recommendation — Replace Washer Receptacle

LPH recommends replacing the existing washer receptacle with a weather-resistant GFCI receptacle.

GFCI protection is designed to monitor the electrical current leaving and returning through the circuit. If the device detects an unintended path to ground, such as through a person or damaged equipment, it can quickly disconnect power to help reduce the risk of electrical shock.

Because the washing machine represents a higher-use appliance and can be exposed to moisture or internal ground faults, providing GFCI protection is an important safety upgrade.

At this time, LPH recommends addressing the washer receptacle specifically rather than replacing every basement receptacle.

⸻

Exterior Receptacle — Corrosion and Lack of Weather-Resistant Protection

LPH also inspected the exterior receptacle and found that it is an older, non-weather-resistant device with visible corrosion around the area where electrical devices are plugged into the receptacle.

Exterior electrical devices are exposed to rain, humidity, condensation, and other environmental conditions. The existing receptacle does not provide the level of protection recommended for an exterior location.

Recommendation — Replace Exterior Receptacle

LPH recommends replacing the existing exterior receptacle with a weather-resistant GFCI receptacle.

This replacement would provide the necessary GFCI protection for an exterior location while also providing a device specifically designed to withstand outdoor environmental conditions. The upgrade will help reduce the risk of electrical shock caused by water intrusion and deterioration of the existing receptacle.

⸻

Stairwell Switch — Electrical Arcing

LPH found that the switch located on the right side of the stairwell leading to the third floor is visibly arcing when being turned on and off.

Arcing occurs when electricity jumps across a gap rather than flowing cleanly through the switch contacts. Continued arcing can generate excessive heat and can damage the internal components of the switch, wiring, or surrounding electrical box.

Recommendation — Replace Arcing Switch

LPH recommends replacing the existing switch due to the observed arcing.

Replacing the switch will eliminate the damaged/arcing device and restore reliable switching operation while reducing the potential for continued heat buildup and electrical damage.

Many homeowners think of lightning when they hear the term “surge,” but the majority of power surges actually originate inside the home. Everyday appliances such as air conditioners, refrigerators, heat pumps, furnaces, microwaves, dishwashers, washers, dryers, and even garage door openers create small electrical surges—known as microsurges—every time their motors cycle on and off. While each individual surge is small, thousands of these microsurges occur over time and gradually wear down the sensitive electronic components found in today’s modern appliances and equipment.
Whole-home surge protection helps absorb and divert these surges away from the home’s electrical system, reducing cumulative damage to expensive electronics and appliances. This is especially important in newer homes, where nearly every major appliance contains sophisticated circuit boards and microprocessors that are far more sensitive to voltage fluctuations than older equipment.
In addition to protecting against internally generated microsurges, whole-home surge protection also provides a critical first line of defense against larger surges originating from the utility company, switching events on the electrical grid, nearby lightning strikes, or power being restored after an outage.

	• Can help extend the service life of modern appliances and equipment by reducing electrical stress on internal circuit boards.

	• Provides continuous protection for the entire home’s electrical system without relying solely on individual plug-in surge strips.
	• Offers added peace of mind during storms, utility switching events, and unexpected power outages.

Water pressure can affect the wear and tear on all the plumbing in the home.

i.334380213:
Today, we returned for the second day of the exterior excavation and interior repipe.

On Day 1, we excavated approximately five feet below grade and began trenching toward the street, where we located the existing 6-inch terracotta sewer line for our connection. Within five feet of the house, we installed a new 4-inch PVC house trap through a 6-inch sleeve. The connection was sealed using a 6-inch-by-4-inch fernco, and the walls on both the interior and exterior foundation walls were sealed with hydraulic cement. After positioning the house trap, we laid a 6” stone bed below where the pipe will be installed and we continued installing the new sewer lateral to the existing 6-inch terracotta line, and added a two-way tee clean out near the street. Once the lateral was completed, we prepared the system for an air test, allowing the inspection to be moved up to Date 1. An East Lampeter Township inspector examined the installation, and the work passed inspection. Following the inspection, we covered the new sewer lateral with 12”inches of stone and secured the excavation with construction fencing for the night. 

Inside the basement, we installed new sanitary drain piping along the basement wall all properly strapped and connected it to the existing stack. We also installed new branch drain lines for the water softener and the new laundry pump connections. A new water-softener discharge line was ran and neatly secured along the basement ceiling.

On Day 2, we made minor adjustments to the piping in the basement and completed the exterior backfill. The disturbed area was raked to a rough grade, and the jobsite was cleaned to the best condition possible.

All completed work was tested and confirmed to be functioning properly with no leaks. We reviewed the completed work with the customer and collected all final signatures. Job complete.

i.334638391:
LPH Electrical System Check – Findings, Options & Completed Work

LPH performed an electrical system check of the home, evaluating the accessible electrical equipment, wiring, devices, switches, receptacles, GFCI protection, and areas of concern identified by the homeowner. During the evaluation, LPH reviewed the upstairs bathroom exhaust fan and lighting controls, the disconnected bedroom receptacle wiring located in the attic, and the kitchen receptacle located below the island.

Upstairs Bathroom – Bath Fan & Lighting Controls

LPH found two existing bathroom fans installed at the same ceiling location. Both fans were wired together; however, one of the existing fan units had previously had its internal components removed and was effectively being used as a junction point for the electrical wiring. There were six wires using the remaining fan enclosure as a junction, which is not an appropriate long-term method of enclosing and protecting electrical connections.

Option: LPH recommended removing the existing fan assemblies, properly separating the wiring, and relocating the electrical connections into a new approved junction box. LPH would then install a new Panasonic Whisper bath fan and reconnect the existing ductwork and wiring as appropriate. A new combination of single-pole switches would also be installed to allow the bathroom exhaust fan/light and vanity lighting to operate independently, providing improved ventilation and more convenient control of the bathroom lighting.

Completed: The homeowner approved this option. LPH removed both existing bath fans from the ceiling, separated the six wires that had been using the existing fan as a junction point, and placed the wiring connections into a new junction box. Once the wiring was properly secured and enclosed, LPH cut the required opening and installed the new Panasonic Whisper bath fan. The existing ductwork and wiring were reconnected, and the new switching was installed to separately control the bath fan/light and vanity lights. The completed installation was tested and confirmed to be operating properly.

Bedroom Receptacle – Restore Power

LPH found an existing bedroom receptacle that had been left without power, with the associated wiring located in the attic. The existing wiring originated from a junction box and included a dead-ended section that was no longer providing power to the receptacle.

Option: LPH recommended properly terminating the existing dead-ended wiring in an approved junction box and running new wiring from the nearby existing feed to restore power to the bedroom receptacle. This provides a properly enclosed and accessible connection rather than leaving unused or disconnected wiring exposed in the attic.

Completed: The homeowner approved this option. LPH accessed the existing junction box in the attic and pulled the bedroom receptacle wiring from that location. The existing dead-ended wire was placed into an additional approved junction box, and new wiring was run from the other junction box to restore the bedroom receptacle. The completed wiring was secured, enclosed, tested, and confirmed to be operating properly.

Kitchen Receptacle – GFCI Protection

LPH evaluated the kitchen receptacle located below the kitchen island. Although this receptacle is not serving a countertop location, an appliance was plugged into it and the existing circuit does not have an equipment grounding conductor.

Option: LPH recommended installing GFCI protection at this location. A GFCI does not create an equipment grounding path on an ungrounded circuit, but it does provide an additional layer of protection by monitoring the flow of electricity and quickly interrupting power when an imbalance is detected. This can help reduce the risk of electrical shock, particularly where an appliance is being used.

Completed: The homeowner approved this option. LPH installed the GFCI receptacle, tested its operation, and confirmed that the GFCI protection was functioning properly.

Completion

The homeowner reviewed the recommended options with LPH and approved all of the proposed work. All approved work was completed during today’s visit, and the installations were tested and confirmed to be operating properly at the completion of the service.

Today’s invoice and electrical evaluation will be emailed to the homeowner for their records.

Thank you for allowing LPH into your home. We appreciate the opportunity to serve you and look forward to servicing you again in the future.

i.334793110:
LPH Electrical System Check — Storm Damage & Complete Electrical Service Replacement

Reason for Inspection

LPH arrived at the property to perform a comprehensive inspection of the home’s electrical service following multiple tree falls that caused significant physical damage to the property’s exterior electrical service.

The purpose of the inspection was to evaluate the condition of the electrical equipment, document the extent of the damage, determine whether the affected components remain safe and suitable for continued use, and identify the repairs and required code upgrades necessary to restore the electrical system.

⸻

Main Electrical Panel — Evidence of Recent Water Intrusion

LPH began the inspection at the home’s main electrical panel. Upon arrival, visible moisture and water were present on the breaker handles. After removing the panel cover, clear evidence of water intrusion was found inside the electrical enclosure.

Fresh corrosion was visible on the exposed bare neutral conductor where the existing service cable enters the panel. The pattern of water intrusion indicates that water was entering through the damaged service cable and traveling downward through the electrical equipment.

Water was observed traveling down the center of the enclosure, directly through the area containing the main breakers and along the bus assembly before collecting at the bottom of the panel.

The corrosion pattern is consistent with this recent water intrusion. Fresh rust formation was concentrated at the lower portion of the enclosure where water had collected, providing physical evidence of water entering the enclosure and subsequently pooling at the bottom.

LPH removed the breakers from the panel to further evaluate the extent of the moisture exposure. Moisture was found retained between the breakers, and water could actually be shaken out of the breaker assemblies. This confirms that the water intrusion extended beyond the interior of the panel enclosure and directly affected the electrical breakers themselves.

Due to the direct exposure of the panel components and breakers to water, these components can no longer be considered reliable for continued service.

⸻

Exterior Electrical Service — Physical Damage From Tree Falls

LPH then inspected the home’s exterior electrical service. Significant physical damage was found throughout the service entrance.

The upper service drop has multiple heavy gouges, tears, and openings in the exterior jacket of the service cable. The damage is concentrated in the areas where the service cable was pulled away from the metal straps securing it to the home.

The location and appearance of these damaged areas are consistent with the service cable being subjected to substantial pulling force from the fallen trees. The damaged portions of the cable have compromised the protective outer jacket, leaving openings through which water can enter the service conductors.

This damage is not limited to normal aging or deterioration. The physical damage is concentrated at the locations where the service was forcibly displaced from its original attachment points.

⸻

Meter Base — Structural Damage & Active Water Entry

Further inspection of the meter base revealed significant damage at the top of the enclosure.

A large opening and cracking were found where the service enters the top of the meter base. The surrounding material has been visibly damaged and separated, creating a substantial opening into the electrical equipment.

This opening provided a direct path for rainwater to enter the meter base following the physical damage to the service.

Upon opening the meter base, LPH observed water actively present inside the enclosure. Water could be seen dripping down the neutral conductor and continuing toward the lower service drop.

This observed water path corresponds directly with the route by which water was able to travel from the damaged exterior service into the home’s main electrical panel.

The meter base was found to be heavily saturated with moisture, with water actually spilling from the enclosure when the cover was opened.

Significant corrosion was also visible at the service lugs and electrical connection points inside the meter base. These connections are critical components of the home’s electrical service, and their exposure to water and subsequent corrosion has compromised the condition of the equipment.

⸻

Extent of Damage

Based on the complete inspection, the damage extends across multiple interconnected components of the home’s electrical service.

Affected components include:

* Upper service entrance cable.
* Lower service entrance cable.
* Service head and exterior service components.
* Meter base and service entrance openings.
* Service lugs and electrical connections.
* Main electrical panel enclosure.
* Main breaker assembly.
* Interior bus assembly.
* Branch circuit breakers.
* Grounding and bonding components.

The physical damage to the exterior service created openings that allowed water to enter the electrical equipment. LPH was able to observe evidence of this water migration from the exterior service, through the meter base, into the service conductors, and ultimately into the main electrical panel.

The presence of fresh corrosion, standing water, moisture inside breakers, and active water dripping through the service equipment demonstrates that the affected components have sustained direct water exposure.

⸻

Complete Electrical Service Replacement

Due to the extent of the physical damage and water exposure, LPH recommends replacement of the complete electrical service rather than attempting to replace or repair individual components.

The affected equipment is interconnected as part of the home’s service, and replacing only isolated sections would leave other water-damaged and physically compromised components in place.

LPH would replace the damaged electrical service with new service equipment, including:

* New exterior meter base.
* New outside emergency/service disconnect.
* New service head.
* Complete replacement of the damaged upper and lower service entrance conductors.
* New service entrance connections and associated exterior equipment.
* New main electrical panel and breakers.
* Updated grounding and bonding system.
* Whole-home surge protection.

⸻

Main Electrical Panel — Replacement Options

As part of the complete electrical service replacement, the existing water-damaged main electrical panel and all affected breakers will be replaced.

LPH can provide the homeowner with two service/panel options:

Option 1 — 30-Space Eaton CH Panel

LPH would install a new 30-space Eaton CH electrical panel with new breakers as required for the home’s existing electrical service.

This panel will replace the existing water-damaged panel and provide a new, reliable enclosure and breaker system for the home’s electrical circuits.

Option 2 — 42-Space Eaton CH Panel With 200-Amp Service Upgrade

If the homeowner elects to upgrade the home’s electrical service to 200 amps, LPH would install a new 42-space Eaton CH electrical panel sized for the upgraded service.

The 42-space panel provides additional circuit capacity and room for future electrical needs, while the 200-amp service provides the home with increased available electrical capacity compared with the existing service.

The 42-space Eaton CH panel would be installed as part of the complete 200-amp service upgrade, including the appropriately sized service equipment, service entrance conductors, meter base, emergency disconnect, grounding and bonding system, and associated mandatory code upgrades.

⸻

Mandatory Code Upgrades Associated With Service Replacement

Because the electrical service is being completely replaced, the new installation will need to meet the applicable current electrical requirements. The following items are therefore mandatory code upgrades associated with the new service installation, rather than optional improvements.

New Exterior Emergency Disconnect

LPH will install a new exterior emergency/service disconnect. This will establish the required first means of disconnect for the home’s electrical service and provide emergency personnel with an accessible means of disconnecting power to the residence from outside the home.

Grounding System Relocation & New Bonding

LPH will relocate the home’s grounding system to the new exterior service disconnect and install a new exterior bonding bridge.

The grounding and bonding system will be configured as part of the new service so that the service disconnect properly establishes the grounding reference for the home’s electrical system.

Separation of Grounds & Neutrals

The new main electrical panel will be configured with the grounded (neutral) conductors and equipment grounding conductors properly separated.

The new exterior service disconnect will serve as the first means of disconnect, allowing the downstream main panel to be configured appropriately for a service disconnect located outside the home.

Whole-Home Surge Protection

LPH will install whole-home surge protection as part of the new electrical service installation.

The surge protective device will be installed at the electrical service to help protect the home’s wiring, electrical equipment, appliances, and connected electronics from transient voltage surges entering through the electrical system.

Installing surge protection during the service replacement provides the home with an additional layer of protection while the electrical service is being completely rebuilt.

Service Labeling & Final Inspection

LPH will provide the required service identification and labeling associated with the new installation.

The completed electrical service will be subject to the applicable electrical inspection requirements. LPH will complete the installation and associated mandatory code upgrades so the new service can be properly inspected.

⸻

Conclusion

The inspection found substantial physical damage to the home’s electrical service following multiple tree falls, including damaged service conductors, displaced and torn service cable jackets, a significantly damaged meter base, and compromised service connections.

The resulting openings allowed water to enter the electrical service. During LPH’s inspection, water was still present inside the meter base and was observed traveling down the service conductors toward the main electrical panel. The panel and breakers showed direct evidence of this water intrusion, including fresh corrosion, pooled water, and moisture retained inside the breaker assemblies.

The damage is therefore not isolated to one component. The meter base, service conductors, service head, main panel, breakers, and associated service connections have all been affected.

LPH recommends a complete electrical service replacement due to the extent of the physical and water damage.

The homeowner will have the option of replacing the existing panel with a 30-space Eaton CH panel or upgrading the home’s electrical service to 200 amps with a 42-space Eaton CH panel.

As part of either service replacement, the applicable mandatory code upgrades will be completed, including the exterior emergency disconnect, updated grounding and bonding configuration, proper separation of grounds and neutrals, required service labeling, and whole-home surge protection.

The completed installation will remove the damaged and water-compromised electrical equipment and provide the home with a new, properly configured electrical service that can be inspected and approved under the applicable current electrical requirements.

Front Lawn Landscape Lighting — Storm Damage

In addition to the electrical service damage, LPH found that the home’s front lawn landscape lighting system also sustained physical damage from falling tree limbs during the storm event. A total of four low-voltage landscape light fixtures were impacted and damaged.

LPH tested the existing 12-volt low-voltage landscape lighting wiring and confirmed that the wiring remains operational and is capable of supplying the replacement fixtures.

LPH would replace the four storm-damaged landscape light fixtures with four new homeowner-supplied 12-volt landscape lights. The existing operational low-voltage wiring would be utilized to reconnect and restore each affected lighting location. This will return the front lawn landscape lighting system to its pre-damage operating condition while reusing the existing wiring that was confirmed to remain functional.

All estimates will be emailed to the homeowner for review. Thank you.
