Reason for Inspection

LPH arrived at the property to perform a comprehensive inspection of the home’s electrical service following multiple tree falls that caused significant physical damage to the property’s exterior electrical service.

The purpose of the inspection was to evaluate the condition of the electrical equipment, document the extent of the damage, determine whether the affected components remain safe and suitable for continued use, and identify the repairs and required code upgrades necessary to restore the electrical system.

⸻

Main Electrical Panel — Evidence of Recent Water Intrusion

LPH began the inspection at the home’s main electrical panel. Upon arrival, visible moisture and water were present on the breaker handles. After removing the panel cover, clear evidence of water intrusion was found inside the electrical enclosure.

Fresh corrosion was visible on the exposed bare neutral conductor where the existing service cable enters the panel. The pattern of water intrusion indicates that water was entering through the damaged service cable and traveling downward through the electrical equipment.

Water was observed traveling down the center of the enclosure, directly through the area containing the main breakers and along the bus assembly before collecting at the bottom of the panel.

The corrosion pattern is consistent with this recent water intrusion. Fresh rust formation was concentrated at the lower portion of the enclosure where water had collected, providing physical evidence of water entering the enclosure and subsequently pooling at the bottom.

LPH removed the breakers from the panel to further evaluate the extent of the moisture exposure. Moisture was found retained between the breakers, and water could actually be shaken out of the breaker assemblies. This confirms that the water intrusion extended beyond the interior of the panel enclosure and directly affected the electrical breakers themselves.

Due to the direct exposure of the panel components and breakers to water, these components can no longer be considered reliable for continued service.

⸻

Exterior Electrical Service — Physical Damage From Tree Falls

LPH then inspected the home’s exterior electrical service. Significant physical damage was found throughout the service entrance.

The upper service drop has multiple heavy gouges, tears, and openings in the exterior jacket of the service cable. The damage is concentrated in the areas where the service cable was pulled away from the metal straps securing it to the home.

The location and appearance of these damaged areas are consistent with the service cable being subjected to substantial pulling force from the fallen trees. The damaged portions of the cable have compromised the protective outer jacket, leaving openings through which water can enter the service conductors.

This damage is not limited to normal aging or deterioration. The physical damage is concentrated at the locations where the service was forcibly displaced from its original attachment points.

⸻

Meter Base — Structural Damage & Active Water Entry

Further inspection of the meter base revealed significant damage at the top of the enclosure.

A large opening and cracking were found where the service enters the top of the meter base. The surrounding material has been visibly damaged and separated, creating a substantial opening into the electrical equipment.

This opening provided a direct path for rainwater to enter the meter base following the physical damage to the service.

Upon opening the meter base, LPH observed water actively present inside the enclosure. Water could be seen dripping down the neutral conductor and continuing toward the lower service drop.

This observed water path corresponds directly with the route by which water was able to travel from the damaged exterior service into the home’s main electrical panel.

The meter base was found to be heavily saturated with moisture, with water actually spilling from the enclosure when the cover was opened.

Significant corrosion was also visible at the service lugs and electrical connection points inside the meter base. These connections are critical components of the home’s electrical service, and their exposure to water and subsequent corrosion has compromised the condition of the equipment.

⸻

Extent of Damage

Based on the complete inspection, the damage extends across multiple interconnected components of the home’s electrical service.

Affected components include:

* Upper service entrance cable.
* Lower service entrance cable.
* Service head and exterior service components.
* Meter base and service entrance openings.
* Service lugs and electrical connections.
* Main electrical panel enclosure.
* Main breaker assembly.
* Interior bus assembly.
* Branch circuit breakers.
* Grounding and bonding components.

The physical damage to the exterior service created openings that allowed water to enter the electrical equipment. LPH was able to observe evidence of this water migration from the exterior service, through the meter base, into the service conductors, and ultimately into the main electrical panel.

The presence of fresh corrosion, standing water, moisture inside breakers, and active water dripping through the service equipment demonstrates that the affected components have sustained direct water exposure.

⸻

Complete Electrical Service Replacement

Due to the extent of the physical damage and water exposure, LPH recommends replacement of the complete electrical service rather than attempting to replace or repair individual components.

The affected equipment is interconnected as part of the home’s service, and replacing only isolated sections would leave other water-damaged and physically compromised components in place.

LPH would replace the damaged electrical service with new service equipment, including:

* New exterior meter base.
* New outside emergency/service disconnect.
* New service head.
* Complete replacement of the damaged upper and lower service entrance conductors.
* New service entrance connections and associated exterior equipment.
* New main electrical panel and breakers.
* Updated grounding and bonding system.
* Whole-home surge protection.

⸻

Main Electrical Panel — Replacement Options

As part of the complete electrical service replacement, the existing water-damaged main electrical panel and all affected breakers will be replaced.

LPH can provide the homeowner with two service/panel options:

Option 1 — 30-Space Eaton CH Panel

LPH would install a new 30-space Eaton CH electrical panel with new breakers as required for the home’s existing electrical service.

This panel will replace the existing water-damaged panel and provide a new, reliable enclosure and breaker system for the home’s electrical circuits.

Option 2 — 42-Space Eaton CH Panel With 200-Amp Service Upgrade

If the homeowner elects to upgrade the home’s electrical service to 200 amps, LPH would install a new 42-space Eaton CH electrical panel sized for the upgraded service.

The 42-space panel provides additional circuit capacity and room for future electrical needs, while the 200-amp service provides the home with increased available electrical capacity compared with the existing service.

The 42-space Eaton CH panel would be installed as part of the complete 200-amp service upgrade, including the appropriately sized service equipment, service entrance conductors, meter base, emergency disconnect, grounding and bonding system, and associated mandatory code upgrades.

⸻

Mandatory Code Upgrades Associated With Service Replacement

Because the electrical service is being completely replaced, the new installation will need to meet the applicable current electrical requirements. The following items are therefore mandatory code upgrades associated with the new service installation, rather than optional improvements.

New Exterior Emergency Disconnect

LPH will install a new exterior emergency/service disconnect. This will establish the required first means of disconnect for the home’s electrical service and provide emergency personnel with an accessible means of disconnecting power to the residence from outside the home.

Grounding System Relocation & New Bonding

LPH will relocate the home’s grounding system to the new exterior service disconnect and install a new exterior bonding bridge.

The grounding and bonding system will be configured as part of the new service so that the service disconnect properly establishes the grounding reference for the home’s electrical system.

Separation of Grounds & Neutrals

The new main electrical panel will be configured with the grounded (neutral) conductors and equipment grounding conductors properly separated.

The new exterior service disconnect will serve as the first means of disconnect, allowing the downstream main panel to be configured appropriately for a service disconnect located outside the home.

Whole-Home Surge Protection

LPH will install whole-home surge protection as part of the new electrical service installation.

The surge protective device will be installed at the electrical service to help protect the home’s wiring, electrical equipment, appliances, and connected electronics from transient voltage surges entering through the electrical system.

Installing surge protection during the service replacement provides the home with an additional layer of protection while the electrical service is being completely rebuilt.

Service Labeling & Final Inspection

LPH will provide the required service identification and labeling associated with the new installation.

The completed electrical service will be subject to the applicable electrical inspection requirements. LPH will complete the installation and associated mandatory code upgrades so the new service can be properly inspected.

⸻

Conclusion

The inspection found substantial physical damage to the home’s electrical service following multiple tree falls, including damaged service conductors, displaced and torn service cable jackets, a significantly damaged meter base, and compromised service connections.

The resulting openings allowed water to enter the electrical service. During LPH’s inspection, water was still present inside the meter base and was observed traveling down the service conductors toward the main electrical panel. The panel and breakers showed direct evidence of this water intrusion, including fresh corrosion, pooled water, and moisture retained inside the breaker assemblies.

The damage is therefore not isolated to one component. The meter base, service conductors, service head, main panel, breakers, and associated service connections have all been affected.

LPH recommends a complete electrical service replacement due to the extent of the physical and water damage.

The homeowner will have the option of replacing the existing panel with a 30-space Eaton CH panel or upgrading the home’s electrical service to 200 amps with a 42-space Eaton CH panel.

As part of either service replacement, the applicable mandatory code upgrades will be completed, including the exterior emergency disconnect, updated grounding and bonding configuration, proper separation of grounds and neutrals, required service labeling, and whole-home surge protection.

The completed installation will remove the damaged and water-compromised electrical equipment and provide the home with a new, properly configured electrical service that can be inspected and approved under the applicable current electrical requirements.

i.334862130: We were called out to evaluate why both exhaust fans were not functioning. Upon arrival, we were met with Sadie and her tenant to let us into the apartment and address their main concern. We started our evaluation for bathroom exhaust fan and their corresponding switches to assess voltage readings and physical condition. We noticed that both switches were functioning correctly and sending proper voltages to the unit. We also confirmed that each unit was receiving proper voltage, which led us to the conclusion that both bathroom fan motors failed. We located the model number for each fan to see if it was possible to replace the internals or if the entire assembly needed to be replaced. Upon a research, we discovered that the existing model is discontinued and the entire assembly would need to be swapped with its updated counterparts. We also noticed that both bathroom exhaust fans are sharing the same 4 inch vent pipe, which is also conjoined with the dryer vent. This presents a concern with humid air backfeeding into the other appliances, which not only could damage them, but also create cavities for the dryer lint to sit and get moist from humid air. We provided an package to replace both units and install one single vent for both fans w/ a Y duct adapter or installing two individual vents for each unit. Installing two solitary vents for each unit is the best for performance and efficiency, but will include having two vents installed on the exterior of the home. The next best option would be installing one vent with a Y duct adapter to prevent backflow, which is a middle ground, but lacks the performance and efficiency of the first venting option. The second bathroom fan package includes just replacing both bathroom exhaust fans with the new counter parts and reusing the existing vent system. This option is not recommended due to the concerns listed above, but could be taken care of if desired. We presented these options to Sadie prior to leaving today. Sadie opted to have these solutions emailed to her to review and make the decision at a later time. We thank you for choosing LPH to evaluate your electrical needs, and we look forward to servicing you in the future.

i.335044890:
LPH completed a comprehensive electrical system check of the home. During the evaluation, we reviewed the electrical service and meter equipment, exterior service conductors and connections, the main electrical panel, breakers, grounding and bonding, wiring and visible connections, receptacles and switches, GFCI protection, and other accessible electrical components. We also looked for signs of water intrusion, corrosion, overheating, loose or deteriorated connections, damaged devices, and other conditions that could affect the safety, reliability, or proper operation of the electrical system.

Findings – Outside Electrical Service

During the system check, LPH found evidence of water penetration into the existing outside electrical service. Corrosion is present along the upper service drop as it enters the meter base and continues down the lower service drop toward the interior panel. Water intrusion and corrosion can deteriorate electrical conductors and connections over time, potentially increasing resistance and heat and creating a risk of electrical failure or arcing.

Water entry has also reached the interior electrical panel. Dried drip marks and evidence of water collecting were found above the main breaker, with rust developing on the breaker rivets. Because the main breaker has been exposed to water contamination, LPH recommends replacement rather than continuing to rely on a compromised component.

The homeowner approved the recommended service replacement, and the work has been scheduled for Thursday, September 24th.

LPH will complete a full service replacement to bring the installation up to current applicable electrical requirements. The work will include new service cables, a new service head, a new 100-amp exterior emergency disconnect, service wiring enclosed in conduit, a new meter base, a four-wire connection from the exterior disconnect to the interior panel, relocation of the grounding connections to the exterior disconnect, installation of a new grounding bar in the interior panel, separation of the neutral and grounding conductors, and replacement of the water-contaminated main breaker. Exterior components and entry points will also be properly sealed with silicone to help prevent future water intrusion.

This approach addresses the underlying water intrusion and corrosion rather than simply replacing individual damaged components. A complete service replacement will provide new conductors, connections, and protective equipment while improving the overall safety and reliability of the electrical service.

GFCI Replacements – Completed Today

LPH also identified four GFCI devices requiring attention. The homeowner approved the replacements, and LPH replaced four GFCI receptacles today: one in the bedroom, two in the kitchen that had failed, and one in the living room. Each replacement was tested after installation and confirmed to be operating properly.

All findings and recommended options were discussed with the homeowner. The remaining estimates, including the approved service replacement, along with today’s electrical system evaluation, will be emailed to the homeowner for their records and review.

Thank you for allowing LPH into your home today. We appreciate the opportunity to service your home and look forward to assisting you again in the future.

e.335910716:
Moen Flo (often called Moen Flo by Moen) is a smart water-monitoring and leak-detection system for your home. It installs on your main water line and continuously monitors water flow and pressure.

Key benefits

* 💧 Leak detection: Identifies unusual water usage and can alert you to potential leaks—even small, continuous leaks.
* 🚰 Automatic shutoff: If it detects a potentially serious leak, the system can automatically shut off your home’s water supply, helping prevent major water damage.
* 📱 Smartphone alerts: You can monitor water use and receive notifications through the Moen app.
* 📊 Water-usage tracking: Shows how much water your household is using and can help identify unusually high consumption.
* 🏠 Protection while you’re away: Particularly useful when you’re traveling because the system can monitor your plumbing even when you’re not home.
* 🧪 Daily health tests: The system periodically checks your plumbing for abnormal flow patterns that could indicate a leak.
* 💰 Potential insurance savings: Some homeowners may qualify for discounts on homeowners insurance, although this depends on the insurer and policy.

Is it worth it?

It’s especially attractive if you have a finished basement, expensive flooring, an older plumbing system, or frequently leave your home unattended. The automatic shutoff can potentially save you from a very expensive water-damage event.

(If there is not an outlet available for the Moen Flo to plug into further charges may apply)

LPH arrived to begin the annual electrical system check. Upon arrival, no electrical concerns/questions were reported prior to our electrical inspection.

We began our evaluation at the main electrical/distribution panel. This is where we assessed the internal conditions, age, connections and voltage readings. During this inspection, most of the inspected parameters meet the required threshold for a healthy panel.

We discovered there are multiple conductors landed on one of the GFI breakers, which presents two concerns. One of them being the increased chance of loose connections since the breaker is not designed to handle two conductors simultaneously. The second is the capacity for this breaker and each circuit is much less.

Next, we inspected all of the protective systems for personnel and equipment in the home such as the smoke detectors, GFI protection devices, and the grounding system. First, we discovered that the water meter does meet today’s grounding standards to protect against any leakage of electricity from traveling on the pipes. The next was confirmation that all of the existing smoke detectors and carbon monoxide detectors are installed in the right locations and up-to-date. Lastly, we identified an area with missing GFI protection, which is for the washer. All other devices in the home were tested and functioning properly prior to leaving today. We did identify multiple areas with plug-in night light units. We left an option to install nightlight/outlet combo units to replace the existing systems at any of the homeowners locations. This option is to only alleviate the extra plug space but still allow nightlight capabilities.

We provided options to remedy all of our electrical recommendations, which was presented today. All of the options that were not approved will be emailed along with the electrical evaluation form and invoice for today’s visit. We thank you for allowing us in your home to service you and we look forward to servicing you in the future.

Out to home today for the yearly plumbing system check. Upon arrival to the home, there was one concern. Homeowner states they have noticed that the water has not been as soft as they remember. They are noticing dry skin for multiple people inside the home. Started by performing a water test at the kitchen faucet. Found that the water softener is working properly at reducing hardness and chlorine inside the home. Inquired about water usage inside the home if it had changed at all recently. The homeowner stated that they had other people move in recently and their water usage as increased from 4 persons to 7 persons. Performed inspection of water softener unit and found system nearly due for the next regeneration cycle within the next few days. With homeowners approval, adjusted timer on the unit from 12 days to 10 days. Increasing the frequency of regeneration cycles will refresh the filtration bed and better provide soft water inside the home. Advised homeowner that with more frequent regeneration cycles, they will also increase their salt usage. Homeowner understands and will keep an eye on the brine tank with the new adjustment.

From there, performed the full home plumbing inspection. Performed flush of water heater system during visit. Tested water pressure inside the home to be at 100 PSI. Recommended and safe water pressure ranges from 40-60. Found that the home is already equipped with a Pressure reducing valve, however the unit has failed. Recommended replacement of valve to reduce water pressure to safe operating pressure to prevent premature failure of components in the plumbing system. Relating to the water pressure inside the home, found the laundry faucet to be air hammering when running hot water. Air hammering could be caused purely from the high water pressure, however there may also be a faulty component inside the faucet. Provided pricing for replacement due to age of fixture. Also identified corrosion at both main shut off valves. Recommended replacement of valves to ensure reliability of valves if there is an emergency or if service needs done to plumbing system. Lastly, found some minor leaks at the shower faucet upstairs and an outdoor faucet in the garage. 

Went over all recommendations with homeowner. Pricing provided today is valid for 60 days. Thank you for trusting LPH.

e.340776707:
Homeowner mentioned a rust spot on the existing water heater. Technician investigated the area and found that the rust spot is being caused by leaking galvanized water pipe fittings located directly above the water heater. The galvanized piping is supplying the exterior hose bib.

To complete the repair, Technician would need to shut off the water supply to the home and open the plaster ceiling in the basement to access the existing galvanized piping and fittings. Technician would remove the deteriorated galvanized fittings and piping, as well as the existing exterior hose bib. Technician would then install a new Woodford freeze-resistant hose bib and reconnect the water supply piping using PEX to copper connections. This repair would help eliminate the existing leak and replace the deteriorated galvanized components with new plumbing materials.

Technician performed water quality testing and found the home’s water hardness to be 5 grains per gallon (GPG) and the chlorine level to be .5 ppm. A hardness level of 5 GPG is considered hard water and can lead to calcium and magnesium scale buildup inside water heaters, plumbing fixtures, faucets, showerheads, and water-using appliances. Over time, this mineral buildup can reduce appliance efficiency, shorten equipment life expectancy, cause spotting on dishes and glassware, and leave soap residue on fixtures and surfaces. The presence of chlorine, while common in municipal water supplies, can contribute to dry skin and hair and may deteriorate rubber seals and gaskets within the plumbing system over time.

To improve water quality and help protect the home’s plumbing system, technician recommends installing a City Soft water treatment system. The system is designed to soften the water by removing the hardness minerals that cause scale buildup while also reducing chlorine levels throughout the home. Benefits of the system include improved soap and detergent performance, reduced spotting and scaling, softer-feeling water, and increased protection and efficiency of plumbing fixtures and water-using appliances.

The proposed installation location for the City Soft system is near the existing water heater. The cold water inlet would connect to the cold water main approximately 25’ away. The softener’s backwash drain lines will be routed and connected to the existing main drain located behind the washer machine at the proposed installation area. The system also requires a dedicated electrical outlet for operation and regeneration cycles. The home’s electrical panel is located approximately 20 feet away, and an outlet will need to be installed and provided at the equipment location prior to or as part of the installation. Once installed, the system will provide conditioned water to the entire home and help minimize the long-term effects of hard water and chlorine exposure on the plumbing system.

This afternoon I arrived at the Miller household to perform his annual electrical system and safety check. Mr. Miller informed us that he did not wish to have his entire home checked and just had a concern he wished to have addressed. Mr. Miller showed us to an outlet with intermittent power. This outlet was partially backstabbed, and its connection had come loose. We replaced the outlet during todays visit, and also provided an option to replace all other backstabbed switches and outlets in order to prevent future problems. 

Upon performing a thorough evaluation of their homes main electrical service, I noted that Mr. Miller has a “Challenger” brand panel in his home. I informed Mr. Miller that the brand itself has been deemed by the NEC as uninsurable, as well as having a total loss of the companies Underwriters Laboratories (UL) listing. This company by a court of law was ordered to halt all manufacturing and production of their systems, and divest the rights to their company. What this means is that due to numerous known hazards resulting in equipment failure and potential fire hazards, these panels and breakers are no longer allowed to be manufactured or installed in homes. The style of breakers in this panel, known as (breaker type), were constructed poorly. This failed design has been the root cause of innumerable cases of critical failure events such as electrical fires, and or massive damage to home circuits, with some breakers having a 60%-80% failure to trip rate in the event of an electrical overcurrent. For the reasons listed, and secondarily the load centers age, I have provided an option for replacement of the main breaker panel.

i.335262120:
LPH performed a comprehensive electrical system check throughout the home. Our evaluation began at the main electrical service and electrical panel and continued through the accessible branch-circuit wiring, grounding and bonding, receptacles, switches, GFI protection, and exterior electrical devices.

The purpose of the system check is to evaluate the overall condition, safety, functionality, and protection of the home’s electrical system while identifying any areas that may benefit from repair, replacement, or future improvement.

Main Electrical Service & Panel

LPH inspected the home’s main electrical service and electrical panel, including the panel enclosure, breakers, conductor terminations, bus connections, grounding and bonding, circuit organization, and overall condition of the equipment.

Branch Circuitry & Wiring

LPH inspected accessible branch-circuit wiring and electrical connections throughout the home for proper installation, conductor sizing, condition, signs of overheating, loose connections, damage, or other potential electrical concerns.

Grounding & Bonding

LPH inspected the accessible grounding and bonding components of the electrical system to verify that the system has the appropriate means of providing a safe path for fault current and allowing protective devices to operate as intended.

GFI Protection

LPH checked the home’s GFI protection in the applicable areas and tested accessible GFI devices for proper operation.

The home has GFI protection installed throughout the required areas, as well as additional GFI protection in areas where it provides an optional additional level of electrical safety.

Interior Receptacles & Switches

LPH inspected the accessible interior receptacles and switches throughout the home, including their general condition, mounting, operation, and visible wiring connections.

During the inspection, LPH observed that several of the existing switches utilize backstab/stab-in wire connections that are beginning to loosen. While opening one of the existing switch boxes, LPH also observed that the plastic housing of one of the switches was beginning to crack. Deterioration of the switch housing can allow additional movement at the connection points and contribute to premature loosening of the existing stab-in connections.

Exterior Electrical Devices

LPH inspected the accessible exterior receptacles and their associated protection. The exterior receptacles have appropriate weather-resistant protection to help protect the devices and electrical connections from moisture and outdoor exposure.

Safety Equipment — Overall Condition

LPH found the home’s electrical safety equipment to be in great shape overall. The home has already received significant electrical safety upgrades, including modern GFI protection, properly protected exterior receptacles, and upgraded electrical devices.

The home’s electrical safety system is well equipped to protect the occupants and electrical equipment under normal operating conditions. The recommendations identified below are primarily intended to address the homeowner’s desired improvements, improve convenience and functionality, and add additional protection to the home’s electrical equipment.

LPH Recommendations

1. Install Four Ceiling Fan-Rated Boxes & Wiring

LPH would install four ceiling fan-rated electrical boxes in the upstairs bedrooms. The boxes would be installed from accessible locations in the attic and properly secured to the framing to support the new ceiling fans.

New wiring would be run from each ceiling fan location down the wall to the existing switch boxes in the bedrooms.

The existing switches currently control switched receptacles. LPH would convert those receptacles to remain powered at all times and repurpose the existing wall switches to control the new ceiling fans.

This configuration allows the homeowner to maintain convenient wall-switch control of each ceiling fan while allowing the existing receptacles to operate as standard, continuously powered receptacles.

2. Premium Whole-Home Surge Protection

LPH recommends installing a premium whole-home surge protective device at the home’s main electrical panel.

Whole-home surge protection provides an additional layer of protection against transient voltage events before they can travel throughout the home’s electrical system. These events can originate from external sources such as utility switching, electrical grid disturbances, nearby lightning activity, or power restoration following an outage.

Surges can also originate within the home when motor-driven equipment such as HVAC systems, refrigerators, heat pumps, furnaces, washers, dryers, pumps, microwaves, and garage door openers cycle on and off.

Modern appliances, LED drivers, electronic controls, circuit boards, and smart-home equipment are particularly sensitive to these voltage fluctuations. Repeated transient events can place electrical stress on these components over time.

A whole-home surge protective device helps divert these transient voltages away from the home’s branch circuits and connected equipment, helping protect the homeowner’s investment and potentially reducing premature electronic component failure.

Benefits include:

* Helps protect major appliances and HVAC equipment.
* Helps protect televisions, computers, gaming systems, networking equipment, and smart-home devices.
* Helps reduce electrical stress on sensitive electronic components.
* Helps protect modern LED drivers and electronically controlled equipment.
* Provides protection throughout the home’s electrical system rather than relying solely on plug-in surge strips.
* Adds an additional layer of protection during storms, utility events, and power interruptions.
* Can provide greater peace of mind and help protect the homeowner’s investment in modern electrical equipment.

The installed premium surge protection device also includes manufacturer-backed warranty and replacement coverage, subject to the manufacturer’s terms and conditions.

3. Replace Existing Switches With Decorator-Style Switches

LPH recommends replacing the existing switches throughout the home with new decorator-style switches.

This recommendation addresses the loose stab-in connections and the deteriorating switch housing observed during the inspection. The new switches would be properly terminated using their screw-terminal connections rather than relying on the existing stab-in connections.

This provides a more secure connection, helps reduce premature wear, and gives the home a consistent, updated appearance.

4. Upgrade Office Electrical Boxes

LPH would also remove the existing single-gang electrical box in the office and replace it with a larger two-gang box on the back wall with the window, while the existing box is removed we would drill through the adjacent stud using the opening and add outlet locations in the 2 bays to the left using the same method to drill through the studs. Adding 8 total plug locations to be used on the back wall of the office.

This provides additional room for future electrical devices and offers the homeowner a convenient and cost-effective way to add additional receptacles without having to do more extensive wire fishing from above.

5. Additional Office Receptacles — Optional

At the homeowner’s request, LPH can also install additional receptacle locations in the office by fishing new wiring down from accessible attic locations.

This would allow the homeowner to place receptacles in locations that are most convenient for desks, electronics, computers, and other equipment.

Additional estimates can be provided for any specific receptacle locations the homeowner would like to add.

Overall System Assessment

LPH found the home’s electrical safety equipment to be in great overall condition, with substantial modern electrical upgrades already in place. The home has appropriate GFI protection, additional GFI protection in optional areas, properly protected exterior receptacles, and modern electrical devices.

The recommendations identified during today’s system check are primarily focused on improving functionality, convenience, reliability, and protection while addressing the homeowner’s specific electrical needs.

LPH recommends the four ceiling fan installations, replacement of the existing switches with properly terminated decorator-style switches, expansion of the office electrical boxes, optional additional office receptacles, and installation of premium whole-home surge protection.

These improvements would allow the homeowner to further enhance an already well-upgraded electrical system while adding convenience and an additional level of protection for the home’s electrical equipment.

Premium Whole-Home Surge Protection

LPH would install a premium whole-home surge protection device at the home’s main electrical panel. The device is designed to protect the home’s electrical system and connected equipment from damaging voltage spikes and transient surges before they can travel throughout the home’s wiring.

Many homeowners think of lightning when they hear the term “surge,” but electrical surges can also originate within the home. Everyday appliances such as air conditioners, refrigerators, heat pumps, furnaces, microwaves, dishwashers, washers, dryers, and garage door openers can create smaller transient voltage events, commonly referred to as microsurges, as their motors and electrical components cycle on and off.

While an individual event may be relatively small, these occurrences happen repeatedly over the life of the equipment. Over time, repeated electrical stress can contribute to premature wear of sensitive electronic components, particularly the circuit boards, control modules, and microprocessors found in modern appliances and electronics.

Whole-home surge protection helps absorb and divert these transient voltages, reducing the amount of electrical stress that reaches the home’s branch circuits and connected equipment.

The surge protective device also provides an additional layer of protection against larger external events, including utility switching events, electrical disturbances, nearby lightning activity, and voltage spikes associated with power being restored following an outage.

Benefits of whole-home surge protection include:

* Helps protect HVAC systems, refrigerators, ovens, dishwashers, washers, dryers, and other major appliances.
* Helps safeguard sensitive electronics such as televisions, computers, gaming systems, networking equipment, and smart-home devices.
* Reduces the cumulative effects of repeated transient voltage events.
* Helps reduce electrical stress on sensitive electronic components and control boards.
* May help extend the useful service life of modern appliances and electronic equipment.
* Helps reduce the potential for costly repairs or premature equipment replacement caused by surge-related damage.
* Provides protection at the electrical panel for the home’s connected circuits rather than relying solely on individual plug-in surge strips.
* Provides additional peace of mind during storms, utility switching events, and unexpected power interruptions.

As homes continue to rely more heavily on electronically controlled appliances and connected technology, whole-home surge protection is a valuable upgrade for protecting the homeowner’s investment and improving the long-term reliability of the home’s electrical equipment.

i.335309270:
The existing Rheem 75-gallon power vent water heater was installed on 12/17/2019 and was found to have a failed thermal release device. The thermal release device is a safety component designed to respond to excessive temperatures within the combustion chamber. When excessive heat causes the device to fail or activate, it closes the fresh-air intake damper as a safety measure. This restricts the combustion air supply and prevents the burner from maintaining a flame, resulting in the water heater not operating properly.

Technician recommends replacing the failed thermal release device and testing the water heater to verify proper operation. After replacement, the technician will confirm that the fresh-air intake damper is functioning correctly and that the burner is able to ignite and remain lit.

Water heater is not under warranty.

I found no rust, corrosion, or oxidization on any of the wiring, or panel housing itself. The panel is reading proper voltage of at least 240V and all breakers are tightened and properly sized. The external portion of the service consisting of the meter base and service wiring is in good and serviceable condition with no signs of deterioration or damage that could allow for failures. The rest of the homes electrical systems were all functioning and providing appropriate power outputs with no faults. The homes life safety devices consisting of smoke/ carbon monoxide detectors as well as GFCI receptacles, were up to code and in working order. For all of the reasons listed, I had no recommendations for Mrs. Jones at the time of my departure aside from the addition of 1 smoke detector in the in use bedroom. All systems were tested and functioning properly. Thank you for allowing us to complete your annual electrical system check. We appreciate the opportunity to help ensure your homes electrical systems remain safe, reliable, and efficient. If you have any questions, please don’t hesitate to reach out. i.335375826:
We were called out to complete the annual electrical system check for Paul. Upon arrival, Paul stated that he did not want the entire home checked but instead wanted his concern that he was dealing with inspected and evaluated. Paul reported that roughly within the past year, he had the garage circuit trip multiple times. Within the same year, he had this wire re-ran from the electrical panel to a junction box in the shed and then ran in conduit, the whole length above ground to the garage. Paul reported a fitting that would pop apart occasionally, and he would have to manually put back together, which we re-glued and solidified prior to leaving today. 

After our full evaluation of the electrical panel, wire and conduit, and light switches and outlets in the garage. We did not identify any major concern or culprit on why this system is tripping. We came to the conclusion that the breaker itself could be starting to fail and provide provided options to replace it. We also identified that the system is not GFI protected, which is highly recommended. We provided an option to install a new GFI breaker and new devices in the garage to properly protect this system and provide electrical devices with the one year warranty. However, upon installing the GFI breaker, we noticed that this breaker would consistently trip immediately. We took apart the entire circuit as far as we can get access to and did not notice any immediate concerns that would cause this breaker to trip. We then took apart the wires at the junction box location in the shed, and the breaker was still consistently tripped. We then opted to put in a normal breaker which is functioning correctly and all devices in the garage are working properly. If any other issues occur, we informed Paul to inform us ASAP so we can address this. We thank you for allowing us in your home to service you and we look forward to servicing in the future.

e.335848688:
A water softener can provide several benefits, especially in homes with hard water:

* Reduces calcium and mineral buildup in pipes, water heaters, faucets, and fixtures.
* Extends the life of plumbing and appliances by reducing scale buildup.
* Improves water heater efficiency by limiting mineral deposits that can reduce heating performance.
* Helps soap and detergent work better, so less may be needed for cleaning.
* Leaves skin feeling softer and can reduce the dry, tight feeling caused by hard water.
* Makes hair feel cleaner and softer by reducing mineral residue.
* Reduces water spots and scale on sinks, shower doors, faucets, and dishes.
* Can help protect clothing by reducing mineral deposits that can make fabrics feel stiff or look dull.
* Improves overall water quality and comfort throughout the home.

For this particular situation, the biggest benefits to emphasize would be protecting the water heater and plumbing from further calcium buildup, improving efficiency, and extending the life of the home’s water-using appliances.

Performed cooling system check on split AC unit. Please see attached evaluation form for system readings and photos. There were a few areas of concern documented on today’s visit, which were gone over with the customer:

A. There is no float or wet switch on the air handler in the attic to prevent water damage to ceilings in the event of a condensate blockage
B. Indoor coil and blower have significant dust buildup, showing up as low airflow in my temperature readings. 
C. Microbial growth is present inside the air handler, on wiring and the blower
D. Contactor on the outdoor unit has notable burn marks.

For these concerns I recommended the following actions:

A. Install a float switch in the secondary drain port of the coil and a wet switch in the drain pan under the unit to shut it down in case of a condensate issue
B. Clean the indoor blower and coil
C. Replace the contactor
D. Install an electronic air filter to better clean the air and keep dust from the system. 
E. Install a germicidal UV to sterilize the existing microbial growth and prevent any further buildup, as well as neutralize microbes in the homes air. 

I also did a test on the minisplit to ensure refrigerant pressures were within expected parameters. Discussed adding a second system option to the SPP.

i.336002600: We were called out to evaluate why the light fixture would flicker when turning off/in the off position. Upon arrival, we’ve met with Erik who informed us of the situation and the location of the issue. We then started our thorough evaluation at the fixture and the light switch that controls this fixture. We were also informed by Erik that he wanted the switch replaced due to it being broken, and the fixture raised another 6 inches. First we started by taking the fixture down to assess the wiring condition and voltage readings at this location. We received the proper voltages going to these wires and into the existing fixture. We reconfigured the wiring by locating which wire controls what portion of the light socket and matching that to the wires coming through the ceiling. From this point, we left the light on while we provided an option to replace the broken switch. This option was approved and completed today. However, when the new switch was installed, we immediately identified that the problem reoccurred and this LED lightbulb struggled to function in the on position. When we installed an incandescent lightbulb in this fixture, it was functioning correctly and as intended. With all of our testing, our research shows that the LED lightbulb itself is the problem due to the low quality internals. We highly recommend Phillips LED counterpart which are top quality bulbs and components. Is there any other questions or concerns, reach out at your earliest convenience. We thank you for allowing us in your home to service your electrical needs and we look forward to servicing you in the future.

LPH was called out today after the homeowner reported that the thermostat screen went blank twice during the night of 09/02/26.

During the inspection, LPH found that the air filter was dirty and restricting airflow. LPH also observed that the air handler was sweating and found the condensate drain line to be clogged.

The air handler is equipped with two safety switches designed to prevent water from accumulating in the drain pan. LPH explained to the homeowner that restricted airflow can cause the system to sweat, which may activate one of the safety switches. Additionally, a backed-up condensate drain line can activate the second safety switch, causing the system to shut down.

LPH replaced the dirty air filter and cleared the clogged condensate drain line. A full system diagnostic was then performed. At the time of service, the system was operating properly, and all functions were working as intended.

LPH arrived to begin the annual electrical system check. Upon arrival, no electrical concerns/questions were reported prior to our electrical inspection.

We began our evaluation at the main electrical/distribution panel. This is where we assessed the internal conditions, age, connections and voltage readings. During this inspection, most of the inspected parameters meet the required threshold for a healthy panel. However, there are a few recommendations we assessed during this inspection. 

First we noticed that this electrical system is currently within the “end of life” range, which means the longevity is in question. Lastly, there’s no system put in place to protect appliances/electronics from spikes of electric which target the sensitive components inside these units. A whole home surge protection device is recommended if the homeowners were interested in  protecting their main utility equipment with a one time investment unit.

Next, we inspected all of the protective systems for personnel and equipment in the home such as the smoke detectors, GFI protection devices, and the grounding system. First, we discovered that the water meter does meet today’s grounding standards to protect against any leakage of electricity from traveling on the pipes. The next was confirmation that all of the existing smoke detectors and carbon monoxide detectors are installed in the right locations and up-to-date. Lastly, we identified an areas with missing GFI protection, which for the washer in the garage. All other devices in the home were tested and functioning properly prior to leaving today.

We provided options to remedy all of our electrical recommendations, which was presented today. All of the options that were not approved will be emailed along with the electrical evaluation form and invoice for today’s visit. We thank you for allowing us in your home to service you and we look forward to servicing you in the future.

LPH arrived on site to investigate why the ceiling lighting in the kitchen was not operating. Upon inspection of the electrical panel, LPH found a tripped breaker and reset it. The homeowner had already removed the light fixtures to investigate the issue prior to LPH’s arrival.

After resetting the breaker, LPH tested the wiring and confirmed that power was properly restored and the wiring was operational. LPH then investigated further to determine what may have caused the breaker to trip.

During the investigation, LPH found that one of the existing electrical boxes had become extremely loose due to the mounting screws rusting out from previous water damage. The box was properly re-secured using new screws to eliminate movement and provide a secure mounting point for the light fixture.

At the second location, LPH found that the wiring was not contained within an electrical box. LPH installed a new pancake electrical box, securely fastening it in place and positioning it flush with the surrounding surface so the light fixture can be properly installed. The existing wiring was also carefully taped where the insulation had begun to deteriorate, providing additional protection to the wiring.

Both locations were fully tested after the repairs, and LPH confirmed that the wiring and electrical connections were operating properly without causing the breaker to trip. These corrections address the loose and unsecured conditions found during the investigation and help provide a safer, more reliable installation going forward.

The homeowner will reinstall the kitchen light fixtures. Today’s invoice will be emailed to the homeowner for their records.

Thank you for choosing LPH!

i.336231963:
Arrived on site to continue the second day of excavation. The previous day, we excavated from the house toward the street and exposed the existing sewer lateral. A 4-inch transition sewer pipe was located near the street and was found to be in good condition, allowing us to make our connection prior to the gas main.
Installed a new 4-inch PVC house trap within 5 feet from the foundation wall. The 6” & 4” pvc going through the foundation was sealed using a 6” x 4” Fernco connection underground to help prevent water and debris from entering the home. Both sides of the foundation wall were properly sealed with hydraulic cement. During excavation, a small section of the existing water service at the wall of the house was unfortunately damaged. The line was repaired and routed back into the home through a new 1-1/2-inch sleeve, providing additional protection for the water service at the foundation. A new angle meter valve and meter union were also installed. The sleeve was sealed on the exterior with a rubber Fernco connection, and both the interior and exterior foundation walls were sealed with hydraulic cement. We continued installation of the new sewer lateral using SDR-35 from the house trap to the existing transition connection. A two-way tee cleanout was installed for future service access. The sewer line was encased in crushed stone and prepared for inspection.
      Today, we returned and performed an air test on the new work we installed outside. The installation was inspected by LASA and passed inspection. Following approval, the exposed sewer lateral was covered with crushed stone and the excavation was backfilled, with the soil compacted approximately every 2 feet. Inside the home, we disconnected and removed the existing water heater and installed a new Rheem 50-gallon electric water heater on lintels, cutting out corroded section of pipe above we installed the unit with a new expansion tank and isolation valves. All completed work was tested and functioning properly with no leaks present. The customer was shown the completed work, final payment was collected, and all required signatures were obtained.

Thank you for trusting Lancaster Plumbing & Heating Services.

LPH completed a Cooling System Check on a 6-year-old heat pump. During the inspection, LPH identified several issues. The air handler and heat pump coil were found to be dirty, and the disconnect for the heat pump is missing its cover.

LPH recommends performing a thorough cleaning of the air handler and heat pump coil, as well as replacing the disconnect to ensure the system operates safely, efficiently, and reliably.

e.338914496:
Technician performed water quality testing and found the home’s water hardness to be 6 grains per gallon (GPG) and the chlorine level to be .5 ppm. A hardness level of 6 GPG is considered hard water and can lead to calcium and magnesium scale buildup inside water heaters, plumbing fixtures, faucets, showerheads, and water-using appliances. Over time, this mineral buildup can reduce appliance efficiency, shorten equipment life expectancy, cause spotting on dishes and glassware, and leave soap residue on fixtures and surfaces. The presence of chlorine, while common in municipal water supplies, can contribute to dry skin and hair and may deteriorate rubber seals and gaskets within the plumbing system over time.

To improve water quality and help protect the home’s plumbing system, technician recommends installing a City Soft water treatment system. The system is designed to soften the water by removing the hardness minerals that cause scale buildup while also reducing chlorine levels throughout the home. Benefits of the system include improved soap and detergent performance, reduced spotting and scaling, softer-feeling water, and increased protection and efficiency of plumbing fixtures and water-using appliances.

The proposed installation location for the City Soft system is near the existing water heater to allow for efficient integration into the home’s main water distribution system. The softener’s backwash drain lines will be routed and connected to the existing main drain located behind the water heater at the proposed installation area. The system also requires a dedicated electrical outlet for operation and regeneration cycles. A outlet is provided. Once installed, the system will provide conditioned water to the entire home and help minimize the long-term effects of hard water and chlorine exposure on the plumbing system.

i.336413736:
Electrical System Check & Loss of Power Repair

LPH arrived at the home in response to a loss-of-power concern. Upon arrival, LPH tested the electrical panel and confirmed that the breakers and power at the panel were operating properly. We then identified which portions of the home were not receiving power and confirmed that the entire basement circuit was affected, starting at the panel GFCI.

Troubleshooting & Circuit Tracing

LPH began troubleshooting at the Panel GFI receptacle that would not reset due to a fault somewhere downstream on the circuit. Because this circuit was extensively interconnected throughout the basement, LPH systematically traced the wiring through multiple junction boxes and branch connections.

The basement circuit was found to supply approximately eight light fixtures as well as multiple receptacles serving important equipment, including the sump pump, condensate pump, dehumidifier, basement mini refrigerator, and crawl space lighting.

LPH separated and tested the wiring at multiple junction points to isolate the source of the fault. After extensive circuit tracing, we identified a branch that traveled through several lighting junction boxes before continuing into the main crawl space. Further investigation led into a secondary crawl space that appeared to contain wiring leading toward an exterior receptacle.

Exterior Receptacle — Water Intrusion

LPH located an exterior GFI receptacle associated with the basement circuit. The receptacle was equipped with an improper cover for the location, and the weather-rated electrical box was found to contain a significant amount of water. The box and cover had not been properly sealed, allowing moisture to enter the electrical enclosure and cause the downstream GFI to trip.

LPH removed the affected device and cover, dried and cleared the electrical box of moisture, and installed a new duplex receptacle. Because the entire circuit was already protected by GFI protection upstream, additional GFI protection at this location was not required.

LPH also installed a properly rated wet-location in-use bubble cover and resealed the exterior box and cover with silicone to help prevent future water intrusion.

GFI Protection — Exterior & Bathroom Receptacles

The homeowners also reported ongoing issues with the exterior GFI and two bathroom GFI receptacles. Investigation found that the circuit had originally been configured with one GFI device providing protection for the downstream receptacles. Additional GFI devices had subsequently been installed at multiple locations by another electrician.

This configuration caused multiple GFI devices to trip together when a fault occurred, requiring the homeowner to locate and reset multiple devices before power could be restored.

LPH corrected the GFI wiring configuration so that each GFI receptacle trips independently at its respective location. The master bathroom GFI was intentionally left with load-side wiring because it is being used to provide GFI protection to the additional receptacle within that bathroom.

Restoration & Testing

After identifying and correcting the source of the fault, LPH reassembled all junction boxes that had been opened during troubleshooting and securely reconnected the circuit wiring. All affected light fixtures, receptacles, the basement GFI receptacle, junction boxes, and electrical panel cover were properly refastened and restored.

Power was then returned to the basement circuit. LPH tested the entire affected circuit, including the newly installed exterior receptacle, and confirmed that the exterior receptacle properly trips the upstream basement GFI protection as intended.

All repaired and affected electrical components were tested and confirmed to be operating properly at the completion of the service.

Payment was collected at the completion of today’s service. Tonight’s invoice will be emailed directly to the homeowner.

Thank you for allowing LPH into your home. We appreciate the opportunity to diagnose and correct this electrical issue and look forward to servicing you again in the future.

The homeowner reported that there was no hot water coming from the existing Bradford White 80-gallon electric water heater. The technician verified that the water heater was manufactured in 2020 and remains under warranty through 2030.

Upon inspection, the technician found that the 30-amp double-pole Square D breaker had tripped. The technician reset the breaker and tested the water heater’s heating elements. The upper heating element was drawing approximately 19.6 amps at 242 VAC and tested within normal operating range. The lower heating element was drawing approximately 4.4 amps at 242 VAC and showed an open line when resistance was tested. This indicates that the lower heating element has failed and requires replacement.

The technician recommends replacing both the upper and lower heating elements, along with both thermostats, to restore proper operation and ensure the water heater is operating reliably. The replacement components should be verified for compatibility with the existing Bradford White water heater and warranty requirements.

LPH arrived to begin the annual electrical system check. Upon arrival, the homeowner reported that they had a lightning strike the tree in front of their home and shop. They stated that they lost a car charger and a light fixture, but had no other severe damage to the electrical system. 

We began our evaluation at the main electrical/distribution panel. This is where we assessed the internal conditions, age, connections and voltage readings. During this inspection, most of the inspected parameters meet the required threshold for a healthy panel. However, there are a few recommendations we assessed during this inspection. 

First we discovered that there are multiple locations where more than one wire is landed under one breaker termination screw, which increases the chance of loose connections. Second we noticed that this electrical system is currently past the “end of life” range, which means the longevity is in question. The sub electrical panel in the shop is the old Sylvania/Zinsco style that is really outdated and a safety concern. We also noticed that the feeder wire going to the subpanel is not the right style and is not properly protected against physical damage. Lastly, there’s no system put in place to protect appliances/electronics from spikes of electric which target the sensitive components inside these units. A whole home surge protection device is recommended if the homeowners were interested in  protecting their main utility equipment with a one time investment unit.

Next, we inspected all of the protective systems for personnel and equipment in the home such as the smoke detectors, GFI protection devices, and the grounding system. First, we discovered that the water does not need to be grounded due to being a well system. The next was confirmation that all of the existing smoke detectors and carbon monoxide detectors are installed in the right locations and up-to-date. All other devices in the home were tested and functioning properly prior to leaving today.

We provided options to remedy all of our electrical recommendations, which was presented today. All of the options that were not approved will be emailed along with the electrical evaluation form and invoice for today’s visit. We thank you for allowing us in your home to service you and we look forward to servicing you in the future.

LPH arrived to begin the annual electrical system check. Upon arrival, Ryan reported he wanted a quote for a new outside outlet on the exterior side of the home where the guest bedroom sits. We informed Ryan that we can pull power off of the existing bedroom outlet to power the new exterior receptacle on that same side, but cautioned him to be aware of what all he uses this outlet for. 

We began our evaluation at the main electrical/distribution panel. This is where we assessed the internal conditions, age, connections and voltage readings. During this inspection, all of the inspected parameters meet the required threshold for a healthy panel. However, there are a few recommendations we assessed during this inspection. 

First we discovered that two sets of breakers that contain shared wire circuits, that need to have a different style of breaker installed for proper protection. Lastly, there’s no system put in place to protect appliances/electronics from spikes of electric which target the sensitive components inside these units. A whole home surge protection device is recommended if the homeowners were interested in  protecting their main utility equipment with a one time investment unit.

Next, we inspected all of the protective systems for personnel and equipment in the home such as the smoke detectors, GFI protection devices, and the grounding system. First, we discovered that the water meter does meet today’s grounding standards to protect against any leakage of electricity from traveling on the pipes. The next was confirmation that all of the existing smoke detectors and carbon monoxide detectors are installed in the right locations and up-to-date. All other devices in the home were tested and functioning properly prior to leaving today.

We provided options to remedy all of our electrical recommendations, which was presented today. The electrical panel correction option was approved by the homeowner and completed today. Both new breakers were installed and working properly prior to leaving today. One year worry free parts and labor warranty will be included for these two breakers. All of the options that were not approved will be emailed along with the electrical evaluation form and invoice for today’s visit. We thank you for allowing us in your home to service you and we look forward to servicing you in the future.

Upon arrival, tech met with Justin. He stated he was having a backup into the laundry tub when he does a load of laundry. Tech ran the laundry tub and had him flush a toilet on the first floor multiple times. We found that after a few minutes, it started to backup. Tech explained that it was a main line backup. Tech made several passes and ran 75’ of cable which would put us in the main line. Tech was unable to restore flow. Tech used his camera to try and locate where the line was running. We knocked on a few doors to see if anyone was experiencing any backups. One lady stated that she did have a backup about a year ago and American water company came to the home, installed a cleanout in her backyard and jetted the common line. We took a look in the riser pipe and found it to be backed up. Justin called the city and American water. American water arrived onsite as tech was leaving. e.340378813:
Technician performed water quality testing and found the home’s water hardness to be 5 grains per gallon (GPG) and the chlorine level to be . 5 ppm. A hardness level of 16 GPG is considered hard water and can lead to calcium and magnesium scale buildup inside water heaters, plumbing fixtures, faucets, showerheads, and water-using appliances. Over time, this mineral buildup can reduce appliance efficiency, shorten equipment life expectancy, cause spotting on dishes and glassware, and leave soap residue on fixtures and surfaces. The presence of chlorine, while common in municipal water supplies, can contribute to dry skin and hair and may deteriorate rubber seals and gaskets within the plumbing system over time.

To improve water quality and help protect the home’s plumbing system, technician recommends installing a City Soft water treatment system. The system is designed to soften the water by removing the hardness minerals that cause scale buildup while also reducing chlorine levels throughout the home. Benefits of the system include improved soap and detergent performance, reduced spotting and scaling, softer-feeling water, and increased protection and efficiency of plumbing fixtures and water-using appliances.

The proposed installation location for the City Soft system is near the existing water heater. The water softener inlet would come from the water meter approximately 20’ away. The softener’s backwash drain lines will be routed and connected to the existing main drain located near the water meter. The system also requires a dedicated electrical outlet for operation and regeneration cycles. The home’s electrical panel is located approximately 20 feet away, and an outlet will need to be installed and provided at the equipment location prior to or as part of the installation. Once installed, the system will provide conditioned water to the entire home and help minimize the long-term effects of hard water and chlorine exposure on the plumbing system.

i.336989544:
LPH arrived to begin the annual electrical system check. Upon arrival, the homeowners reported some outlets in the dining room were not working. After a thorough evaluation, we discovered that the outlet is damaged and allowing the hot wire to touch the ground wire. We recommend the replacement of this outlet as preventative maintenance. We disconnected this outlet from the circuit to allow the rest of them to work. The homeowners also inquired on having some recessed lighting installed in the dining room, living room and 2nd floor hallway. We provided options to do so and informed them that plaster will need to be cut and all repairs are homeowners responsibility.

We began our evaluation at the main electrical/distribution panel. This is where we assessed the internal conditions, age, connections and voltage readings. During this inspection, all of the inspected parameters meet the required threshold for a healthy panel.

However, we discovered that there’s no system put in place to protect appliances/electronics from spikes of electric which target the sensitive components inside these units. A whole home surge protection device is recommended if the homeowners were interested in  protecting their main utility equipment with a one time investment unit.

Next, we inspected all of the protective systems for personnel and equipment in the home such as the smoke detectors, GFI protection devices, and the grounding system. First, we discovered that the water meter does meet today’s grounding standards to protect against any leakage of electricity from traveling on the pipes. The next was identifing the existing smoke detectors in the home are either missing or out of date since 2024. All other devices in the home were tested and functioning properly prior to leaving today.

We provided options to remedy all of our electrical recommendations, which was presented today. All of the options that were not approved will be emailed along with the electrical evaluation form and invoice for today’s visit. We thank you for allowing us in your home to service you and we look forward to servicing you in the future.

e.337326697:
Technician was shown the electrical breaker panel and the location of the well pump and pressure tank outside in the well house. Upon inspection of the well house, Technician noticed the door was left wide open and the pressure tank was tipped over. Technician repositioned the pressure tank into an upright position and secured it so it is sitting flat and cannot tip over.

Technician then inspected the electrical panel and found the existing Square D Homeline 15-amp double-pole breaker in the off/tripped position. Technician turned the breaker on and checked the voltage entering the pressure switch, which measured approximately 244 VAC.

Technician ran water from the boiler drain to operate the well pump and checked the pump’s electrical readings. The well pump was drawing approximately 5.19–5.26 amps and tested at approximately 6.9 ohms for continuity. These readings indicate the well pump is operating properly.

Technician then checked the continuity of the existing well wire from the electrical panel to the pressure switch. The expected resistance should be approximately 0–0.5 ohms; however, the existing well wire measured approximately 12–14 ohms. These readings indicate the existing well wire is compromised and should be replaced.

The existing Square D Homeline 15-amp double-pole breaker should also be replaced with a properly sized Square D Homeline double-pole breaker.

Technician recommends replacing the existing underground well wire from the electrical panel to the pressure switch. Technician will trench a new path for the well wire from the electrical panel located in the bedroom to the well house, approximately 60 feet away. New electrical conduit will be installed to provide additional protection for the new well wire. Technician will also replace the existing 15-amp double-pole breaker with a 30-amp double-pole breaker.

The findings indicate the compromised well wire and tripped breaker are the reason for the loss of water. Technician also determined that the pressure tank being tipped over is likely related to groundwater rising inside the well house. The increased water level can cause the pressure tank to become buoyant and potentially cause the pressure switch to come into contact with water.

With the replacement of the well wire, Technician recommends relocating the pressure tank and electrical pressure switch higher on the plywood wall inside the well house. This will help keep the electrical components and pressure tank above potential groundwater levels and reduce the risk of future water exposure.

Technician will need to remove a portion of the drywall around the electrical panel in the bedroom to complete the electrical work. LPH is not responsible for drywall repairs or landscaping restoration following completion of the installation.

Technician attempted to contact the homeowner multiple times to provide an update regarding the findings and condition of the well pump system, as well as the applicable dispatch fee. Technician was unable to reach the homeowner and left a message.

The current issue is a cracked evaporator coil drain pan that is leaking water. At this time, the replacement drain pan is not expected to be available until October. We would also enlarge and modify the return box to improve airflow and ensure the new system receives the proper amount of return air for efficient operation.

On the outdoor portion of the system, we would replace the existing equipment with a new condenser, new equipment pad, and new electrical disconnect as part of the installation.

Based on our discussion and the home’s needs, I put together three different replacement options for the homeowner to consider. All three options are backed by our 10-year parts and 10-year labor warranty for added peace of mind.

A water softener removes hardness minerals—mainly calcium and magnesium—from your water. Its main benefits are:

* Reduces limescale buildup in pipes, faucets, showerheads, kettles, and water heaters.
* Helps appliances last longer, especially water heaters, dishwashers, and washing machines.
* Improves soap and detergent performance, so you may need less for washing and cleaning.
* Reduces soap scum and mineral spots on showers, sinks, dishes, and glassware.
* Makes laundry feel softer and can reduce mineral residue on fabrics.
* Makes cleaning easier because hard-water deposits form less readily.
* Can improve water-heater efficiency by limiting scale buildup on heating elements.

The softener also gets rid of any chlorine in the water. Chlorine is snare for consumption and absorbs into skin when showering, washing hands, etc. homeowner has been telling technician about all the issues and technician 100% believes that the main issue is the water quality.
e.337837321:
A pressure reducing valve (PRV) regulates incoming water pressure and keeps your home’s plumbing at a safer, more consistent pressure. Tech tested water pressure and found it to be 83psi. Most fixtures and plumbing components are only rated to 75psi

Benefits of a PRV

* Protects plumbing fixtures — Reduces stress on faucets, toilets, shower valves, and appliances.
* Prevents pipe damage — Excessive water pressure can contribute to leaks and premature pipe failure.
* Extends appliance life — Helps protect water heaters, washing machines, dishwashers, and ice makers.
* Reduces water consumption — Lower pressure can reduce the amount of water used at fixtures.
* Reduces water hammer — Can help minimize banging or knocking in plumbing lines.
* Provides consistent pressure — Keeps household water pressure from fluctuating

Installed new 240 volt condensate pump onto system. Previously, there was none. There was a substantial amount of water on the floor and inside the return plenum. 

Break down of work flow for today:
-Disconnected unit from power at breaker panel 
-Ran wire for condensate into air handler
-Landed two in line fuses on each leg of outgoing power to each leg of the condensate pump
-Grounded pump
-Ran thermostat wire and broke R on thermostat with safety switch on condensate
     -This means should the condensate pump overfill, the unit will shut off to prevent leakage 
-Ran vinyl tubing from outside along the line set to the pump 
-Secured tubing with hose clamp and electrical tape along line set
-Had to remove silicon caulk around the outside termination, resealed this hole when finished
-Restored power to unit, filled condensate pump with water to test operation. Everything is working properly at this time
-Vacuumed and cleaned surrounding area of water and rust as well as inside return plenum

Finally, performed system check. Everything is operating properly and within spec at this time. Measurements taken can be referred to on the system evaluation form.

Comprehensive Plumbing System Inspection

The technician arrived at the home and completed a comprehensive plumbing system safety inspection. The technician inspected the plumbing throughout the home, including fixtures, drain components, stopper assemblies, and other accessible plumbing-related equipment. The technician also cleaned the stopper assemblies as needed and reviewed the plumbing system with the homeowner. The homeowner was present and accompanied the technician throughout the inspection. During the inspection, the technician identified two major concerns that should be addressed.

1. Water Quality – High Chlorine Levels and Hard Water

The homeowner’s water was found to have approximately 4 parts per million (PPM) of chlorine(4 times the amount that a pool has). Chlorine is a chemical and it is unsafe to absorb/consume.
