The home is also experiencing hard water, which is contributing to mineral staining throughout the home. Hard water can result in mineral buildup on plumbing fixtures and can negatively affect water-using appliances and plumbing components over time. The technician recommends installing a water softener to address the home’s water-quality concerns. A properly sized treatment system can help reduce mineral buildup, improve water quality, protect plumbing fixtures and appliances, and potentially extend the service life of plumbing components throughout the home. Also improves the well being of the homeowner. 

2. Sewer Line Cracks and Basement Leakage

During the inspection, the technician identified two cracks in the existing sewer line. When plumbing fixtures are used, wastewater is leaking through these damaged areas and into the basement. As a temporary measure, the technician applied electrical tape around the cracked sections to help reduce the amount of leakage until a permanent repair or replacement can be completed. This is only a temporary measure and is not considered a permanent repair. The technician also noted that the sewer line has already undergone multiple previous spot repairs. Due to the existing condition and history of repairs, additional isolated repairs may only provide temporary relief, and other sections of the sewer line may continue to deteriorate. For a long-term solution, the technician recommends evaluating the sewer line for complete replacement or a more comprehensive repair, depending on the overall condition and accessibility of the piping.

i.337578696: This morning I arrived at the Peters household to conduct their annual electrical system and safety check. Upon performing a thorough evaluation of the homes main electrical service, I found no major discrepancies. However, I did identify a set of three breakers which are what we refer to as double tapped. When a breaker is double tapped, especially if it is not specifically rated to be, It can make it difficult to secure a firm connection on both wires, over time, and if left unmaintained, these wires can begin to loosen and cause potential arcing or burning. Now, during todays visit I made sure to tightly secure the three breakers terminal screws, and saw no signs of electrical failure, but it is still accepted universally as malpractice and does not conform with NEC standards for safety. I have provided an option to replace these three breakers with properly rated tandem breakers in order to mitigate any potential failures down the road. The only other option I provided was for the replacement of 3 expired combination detectors in the home. The panel and the rest of the homes devices appeared to be in good and serviceable condition otherwise. If you have any questions or concerns, please do not hesitate to contact us. The first thing we were shown was how the outside hose faucet leaks when it is turned on and even worse when water is turned on. The second thing that was brought to our attention had to do with a leak at the kitchen faucet and the final thing that was brought to our attention was that a part of the handle for the tub/shower temperature control had broken. A lot of what we saw today and the issues the tenants are having, have to do with age of equipment coupled with the hard water. 

In addition to what was brought to our attention the technician discovered that there are still galvanized steel water lines that run from the basement up to the bathroom on the second floor. There is a good possibility that they run a good portion of the way, before transitioning over to copper. With what we can see in the basement the galvanized should be replaced in order to avoid any major leak issues. We did discover a few spots on the galvanized where there had been previous leaks, which usually means they are weak spots that are prone to future leaks. 

Before coming across that concern, we were evaluating the electric water heater. We learned that existing water heater is 18 years old and the lower element is no longer producing the amps it should be when heating the water. The fittings on the water lines coming to and from the unit are also showing signs of a slow seeping leak. 

While evaluating the tub/shower valve we discovered it to be difficult to turn on and off. We also looked at the concern of the tenant and discovered that the trim piece for the temperature control had come off. While attempting to put it back together we determined that the tabs that help lock it into place had broken. Everything else in the bathroom is operating as it should at the present time.

i.337677353:
LPH completed the relocation and installation of the dedicated dryer circuit for the upstairs kitchen pantry. LPH first removed the existing three-wire, ungrounded fabric Romex dryer circuit that ran from the electrical panel through the basement joists and up the wall to the previous dryer location. The existing wiring was completely removed from all accessible locations, eliminating the need for the old circuit to remain in place or be extended through an additional junction box.

The existing single-gang metal dryer box was pried away from the stud and removed from the plaster wall. LPH then enlarged the existing opening to accommodate a new two-gang old-work electrical box. New three-wire cable with a grounding conductor was installed by drilling through the basement joists and creating a new pathway up through the wall. The new cable was routed through the joists and fished up the wall into the newly prepared opening in the pantry.

The new wiring was placed into the two-gang box, and the box was securely mounted and clamped into the wall. At the electrical panel, LPH installed the new circuit wiring using the proper connector and landed the circuit on a new 2-pole, 30-amp breaker after removing two unused breakers to create the necessary space. The panel cover was reinstalled and the panel was relabeled to identify the new dryer location.

At the pantry, LPH installed the new flush-mount dryer receptacle and cover plate, completing the new dedicated dryer connection.

LPH also replaced the existing washing machine receptacle with a new 20-amp weather-resistant, tamper-resistant GFCI receptacle. This provides GFCI protection for the washing machine connection while also providing improved protection against moisture and accidental contact.

During the work, LPH also identified an issue with the dryer appliance connection. The dryer did not have a proper connector where the appliance cable entered the unit, and the dryer cord had been incorrectly installed with the grounding and neutral conductors bonded incorrectly. LPH opened the rear access panel, installed the proper 3/4-inch connector, and corrected the appliance wiring so the neutral conductors were properly connected together and the grounding conductor was properly bonded to the dryer housing.

Once all work was completed, power was restored and both the new dryer receptacle and washing machine GFCI were tested and confirmed to be operating properly. The electrical panel was relabeled, all work areas were swept and vacuumed, and LPH reviewed the completed work with the homeowner.

e.337938894:
Existing laundry drain is currently discharging into the sump pump pit, with the sump pump then discharging into the main sanitary drain line. Per IPC requirements, sump pumps are intended to discharge groundwater and should discharge to an approved location outside the home. Laundry wastewater is considered gray water and should be discharged into the sanitary drainage system.

Technician recommends installing a dedicated laundry pump to properly discharge the laundry gray water into the main sanitary drain line. The laundry pump discharge piping will connect to the existing sump pump discharge piping leading to the main sanitary drain. A dedicated electrical outlet is already provided for the laundry pump.

The laundry pump will also require a properly installed vent. The vent piping will exit through the back of the home and continue vertically along the exterior wall, terminating near the roof.

The existing sump pump discharge will be modified so that it terminates above the sump pump pit and exits toward the back of the home, providing an appropriate discharge location for the groundwater collected by the sump pump

The existing 2nd floor hallway bathroom lavatory faucet is showing significant corrosion due to moderately hard water. The corrosion has affected the overall condition and appearance of the faucet. Technician recommends replacing the existing lavatory faucet to prevent further deterioration and restore proper function and appearance.

Technician performed water quality testing and found the home’s water hardness to be 6 grains per gallon (GPG). A hardness level of 6 GPG is considered hard water and can lead to calcium and magnesium scale buildup inside water heaters, plumbing fixtures, faucets, shower heads, and water-using appliances. Over time, this mineral buildup can reduce appliance efficiency, shorten equipment life expectancy, cause spotting on dishes and glassware, and leave soap residue on fixtures and surfaces. The presence of chlorine, while common in municipal water supplies, can contribute to dry skin and hair and may deteriorate rubber seals and gaskets within the plumbing system over time.

To improve water quality and help protect the home’s plumbing system, technician recommends installing a City Soft water treatment system. The system is designed to soften the water by removing the hardness minerals that cause scale buildup while also reducing chlorine levels throughout the home. Benefits of the system include improved soap and detergent performance, reduced spotting and scaling, softer-feeling water, and increased protection and efficiency of plumbing fixtures and water-using appliances.

The proposed installation location for the City Soft system is near the existing water heater to allow for efficient integration into the home’s main water distribution system. The softener’s backwash drain lines will be routed and connected to the existing main drain located behind the water heater at the proposed installation area. The system also requires a dedicated electrical outlet for operation and regeneration cycles. The home’s electrical panel is located approximately 15 feet away, and an outlet will need to be installed and provided at the equipment location prior to or as part of the installation. Once installed, the system will provide conditioned water to the entire home and help minimize the long-term effects of hard water and chlorine exposure on the plumbing system.

The homeowner had a spare fuse on hand that we replaced, and we reset the breaker in the main panel as well. All units were back in operation. 

We began our evaluation at the main electrical/distribution panel. This is where we assessed the internal conditions, age, connections and voltage readings. During this inspection, most of the inspected parameters meet the required threshold for a healthy panel. However, there are a few recommendations we assessed during this inspection. 

First we discovered that there are multiple locations where more than one wire is landed under one breaker termination screw, which increases the chance of loose connections. Second we noticed that this electrical system is currently within the “end of life” range, which means the longevity is in question. This main electrical/distribution panel is also maxed out and most newer circuit or electrical equipment could not be installed within this existing panel. Lastly, there’s no system put in place to protect appliances/electronics from spikes of electric which target the sensitive components inside these units. A whole home surge protection device is recommended if the homeowners were interested in  protecting their main utility equipment with a one time investment unit.

Next, we inspected all of the protective systems for personnel and equipment in the home such as the smoke detectors, GFI protection devices, and the grounding system. First, we discovered that the water meter does not meet today’s grounding standards to protect against any leakage of electricity from traveling on the pipes. The next that there are no smoke or CO detectors in home. Lastly, we identified an areas with missing GFI protection, which is the kitchen. All other devices in the home were tested and functioning properly prior to leaving today.

We provided options to remedy all of our electrical recommendations, which was presented today. All of the options that were not approved will be emailed along with the electrical evaluation form and invoice for today’s visit. i.337744096:
Performed heating system check on 13 year old gas furnace. Please see attached system evaluation form for measurements and photos. Customer stated that there was an intermittent noise coming from the furnace. I ran the system in heating and cooling modes and could not replicate the noise. Blower spins freely and has no debris on it. No oil leaks on the motor. Capacitor tested normally. The only thing of note on this concern was the filter was very much plugged. There is a possibility the coil froze at one point from this, but I could not replicate this occurrence to prove it. I asked customer to record the noise if it happens again. 

During my inspection I found 2 areas of concern on the furnace:
A. Heavy oxidation on the igniter
B. Extreme rust on parts of the heat exchanger, with one of the lower bends exhibiting rust patterns indicating a near future failure. 

Combustion analysis was within expected range and the rust spots, while dark, do not appear to penetrate the heat exchanger wall yet. We discussed replacing the igniter, replacing the igniter and the heat exchanger, or replacing the furnace. Customer opted for Option B, Igniter and Heat exchanger, and we will be back on Friday to perform this work.

e.340840399:
A Moen Flo is a smart water-monitoring and leak-detection system made by Moen. It is typically installed on the main water line entering a home and monitors the home’s water use and plumbing system.

What it does

* 💧 Monitors water usage: Tracks how much water your home is using and can identify unusual patterns.
* 🚨 Detects leaks: It can recognize continuous or abnormal water flow that may indicate a leak.
* 🛑 Can shut off the water: Depending on the system and configuration, it can automatically stop the home’s water supply when it detects a potentially serious leak.
* 📱 Provides alerts: The accompanying app can notify you about suspected leaks, excessive water use, or other plumbing issues.
* 🏠 Helps prevent water damage: A small leak can eventually cause significant damage to floors, walls, ceilings, and belongings. Early detection is the primary benefit.

Why it is important

The biggest value of a Moen Flo is preventing or reducing water damage before you notice a problem yourself. A traditional plumbing leak might continue for hours—or even days—while nobody is home. A smart shutoff system can detect the abnormal flow and alert you, and in appropriate circumstances shut off the supply.

It can also help you understand your home’s water consumption, potentially making it easier to spot waste or plumbing problems.

i.337992648:
During today’s electrical system evaluation, LPH identified extensive evidence of water intrusion and resulting corrosion affecting multiple components of the underground electrical service, including the exterior meter base and interior electrical panel.

The exterior meter base has a film of corrosion present across the meter base lugs and neutral bar, with corrosion visible throughout the affected components. The meter base also shows evidence that water has entered the enclosure and collected in the bottom.

Additional evidence of water entry was found at the interior electrical panel. Corrosion is present along the top portion of the panel, with dried drip marks extending down the interior of the enclosure and along the conductors leading to the breakers. A dried water stain is also present where water appears to have previously pooled on top of the two breakers located at the upper portion of the panel. Rust is present on several breaker screws, along with additional rust spots on the panel enclosure and cover.

The paper circuit labeling inside the panel and on the panel cover shows significant evidence of having been exposed to moisture. Portions of the paper have visible water damage, and mold has formed on the affected labeling. Several copper conductors connected to breakers also have small areas of green oxidation consistent with moisture exposure.

LPH compared today’s findings with the electrical system inspection performed last year. These conditions were not documented during the previous inspection. Based on the extent and pattern of the corrosion, dried drip marks, water staining, oxidation, and other evidence present throughout the service equipment, the damage appears to have occurred more recently than the previous inspection.

Safety Concerns

The extent of the water-related damage makes this a serious electrical safety concern. Electrical equipment is designed to operate in a dry environment, and moisture inside service equipment can contribute to corrosion, deterioration of electrical connections, increased electrical resistance, overheating, arcing, breaker malfunction, and failure of electrical components.

Of particular concern is that evidence of moisture is present at multiple points within the electrical service rather than being isolated to a single component. Water has affected the meter base, service equipment, panel enclosure, breakers, wiring, and electrical connections. Continued operation of equipment with this level of moisture-related deterioration creates an increased risk of electrical malfunction and further damage.

Because some of the affected components are part of the home’s primary electrical service, the concern extends beyond an individual receptacle or branch circuit. The service equipment is responsible for safely distributing electrical power throughout the home, making the condition of these components especially important.

Recommended Corrective Work

Due to the considerable evidence of water intrusion affecting multiple components of the electrical service, LPH recommends replacing the affected service equipment and associated wiring to restore the system to a safe, properly protected, and code-compliant condition.

The recommended service replacement would include:

* Required electrical inspections and coordination of the electrical service shutdown.
* Removal of the existing exterior meter base and installation of a new meter base.
* Proper sealing of the new meter base to help prevent future water intrusion.
* Installation of a new exterior emergency disconnect.
* Installation of new conduit from the exterior disconnect into the home.
* Sealing of the disconnect, meter base, conduit, and all electrical entry points into the home.
* Reconfiguration of the interior panel as a subpanel, with the grounding system properly established at the service disconnect.
* Installation of the required bonding bridge.
* Installation of new four-wire conductors from the exterior disconnect to the interior panel.
* Installation of whole-home surge protection.

Additional evidence of water entry was found at the interior electrical panel. Corrosion is present along the top portion of the panel, with dried drip marks extending down the interior of the enclosure and along the conductors leading to the breakers. A dried water stain is also present where water appears to have previously pooled on top of the two breakers located at the upper portion of the panel. Rust is present on several breaker screws, along with additional rust spots on the panel enclosure and cover.

The paper circuit labeling inside the panel and on the panel cover shows significant evidence of having been exposed to moisture. Portions of the paper have visible water damage, and mold has formed on the affected labeling. Several copper conductors connected to breakers also have small areas of green oxidation consistent with moisture exposure.

LPH compared today’s findings with the electrical system inspection performed last year. These conditions were not documented during the previous inspection. Based on the extent and pattern of the corrosion, dried drip marks, water staining, oxidation, and other evidence present throughout the service equipment, the damage appears to have occurred more recently than the previous inspection.

Safety Concerns

The extent of the water-related damage makes this a serious electrical safety concern. Electrical equipment is designed to operate in a dry environment, and moisture inside service equipment can contribute to corrosion, deterioration of electrical connections, increased electrical resistance, overheating, arcing, breaker malfunction, and failure of electrical components.

Of particular concern is that evidence of moisture is present at multiple points within the electrical service rather than being isolated to a single component. Water has affected the meter base, service equipment, panel enclosure, breakers, wiring, and electrical connections. Continued operation of equipment with this level of moisture-related deterioration creates an increased risk of electrical malfunction and further damage.

Because some of the affected components are part of the home’s primary electrical service, the concern extends beyond an individual receptacle or branch circuit. The service equipment is responsible for safely distributing electrical power throughout the home, making the condition of these components especially important.

Recommended Corrective Work

Due to the considerable evidence of water intrusion affecting multiple components of the electrical service, LPH recommends replacing the affected service equipment and associated wiring to restore the system to a safe, properly protected, and code-compliant condition.

i.338004334: We were called out to evaluate why the home’s electric was not functioning correctly. Upon arrival, we spoke with Eugene to identify his main concerns and the location of his concerns. Eugene stated that when he would run his microwave, it would bog down pretty heavy and affect the lights in the kitchen. He also stated that his fridge in the basement would do the same thing and he wanted to know what was going on. We did a thorough evaluation starting at the main electrical panel where we assessed irregular voltage readings at the main breaker and at each individual breaker from this point. We received 128 V from one phase to neutral and 110 V from the other phase to neutral. We then had Eugene start his microwave and immediately noticed that the same phase the microwave was on, dropped to 110 V while the other phase spiked past 130V. This leads us to the conclusion that the neutral wire feeding this house is bad. We then began to search where the neutral wire has failed, whether it was PPL’s powerline or the homeowners service wire (that was older and brittle) on the home. After a thorough evaluation, we discovered that the neutral wire on the homeowner side of the connection is bad and received the same irregular voltages, as when we tested inside the main panel. We confirmed this by testing PPL voltage while under load and when the power is turned off, and the voltage was steady during both instances. We provided multiple solutions to remedy the exterior service wire but also provided option options to replace the electrical panel whether it’s the 100 amp counterparts or the 200 amp upgrade. Eugene opted to go with the 100 amp replacement prior to leaving today. We also re-crimped the neutral wire today to allow the home to function correctly until we can come back and replace the entire wire. After doing so the voltages were reading normal even during a heavier load. We thank you for trusting us to evaluate your electrical concern and provide solutions to remedy this concern. We look forward to servicing you in the future.

Out to home today for a leak around the base of a newly installed smart toilet fixture. System was installed approximately a month ago by another contractor. They have been out several times with various issues with the system. Leakage has occurred in the ceiling of the bathroom downstairs. Homeowners are requesting reinstalling the smart toilet fixture to ensure system functions and does not leak. 

Performed evaluation of system and found out that the fixture is not properly secured to the floor. Toilet is missing the side mounts that should secure the toilet the floor. Homeowners were able to find some leftover hardware from the original install. At the time, we were unsure if that was all of the hardware needed to complete the install. Homeowners approved reinstallation of smart toilet. Made homeowners aware that if any hardware was missing, LPH will not be able to complete the installation. They understood and approved repairs today. 

Started by draining down system and disconnecting water and power to unit. Removed fixture and found wax seal to be of alignment and leaking. Cleaned up mounting surfaces and inspected flange. Found flange to be in good condition at this time. Pulled up instructions from the manufacture to ensure proper installation. Found that we are missing necessary mounting hardware to complete installation. The template and measurements for installing the bracket were also missing. Based on abnormal directions and missing measurements, suggested returning the toilet and purchasing a different brand unit. Had discussion with homeowner on how to proceed. 

Homeowners decided they would like LPH to install a temporary toilet in the hall bathroom. They will then work on exchanging their smart toilet fixture for another unit. Once the new unit has arrived, they will reach out to schedule another appointment to install their new fixture. Then they would like the temporary fixture installed in their 3rd floor bathroom. Went over pricing for all necessary work. Homeowners approved installation of new comfort height elongated fixture in the 2nd floor bathroom today. 

Supplied and installed new gerber toilet including new supply line and mounting hardware. Upon completion of installation, tested for leaks and proper function. Once system had been checked for leaks, sealed around base using clear silicone. Advised homeowners to avoid usage of fixture for 12 hours to allow sealant to fully cure before usage of fixture. One year guarantee given on work performed today. Remaining pricing provided today is valid for 60 days. While onsite, also spoke about the benefits of our partnership plan. We also confirmed that this receiver has gone bad, by bypassing the receiver and sending power straight to the fan, and all components for the fan were functioning correctly at this time. We provided an option to replace the ceiling fan remote kit and receiver, which is approved and completed today. The new receiver/remote kit was tested and working correctly prior to leaving today. i.338296616: During today’s consultation, the homeowner advised the technician that the existing shower was installed approximately 45 years ago and that the shower drain has been experiencing leakage for several years. With their approval, tech used drain equipment from the trap out and was able to restore flow. Tech had them flush a toilet and run a bathtub for approximately 10 minutes to ensure the line was open. We then performed a video inspection and came across deteriorating cast iron pipe that had buildup and holding water in multiple spots. It transitions to pvc at the foundation. The inside pvc is holding water as well. Tech explained the severity of the pipe and strongly suggest a sewer line replacement to avoid any future backups. Tech presented a solution. They are going to look over and discuss the option tonight. Tech will follow-up tomorrow. Due to the condition of the pipe, there is no warranty for the work performed today. e.340918416:
The main-floor powder room lavatory drain shows signs of corrosion on the existing chrome-plated P-trap. The hot emergency shutoff valve also shows signs of corrosion. Technician recommends replacing the existing P-trap and replacing both the hot and cold emergency shutoff valves to help prevent future leaks and ensure the lavatory water connections and drain are in good working condition.

Technician performed water quality testing and found the home’s water hardness to be 5 grains per gallon (GPG) and the chlorine level to be 2.0 ppm. A hardness level of 5 GPG is considered hard water and can lead to calcium and magnesium scale buildup inside water heaters, plumbing fixtures, faucets, showerheads, and water-using appliances. Over time, this mineral buildup can reduce appliance efficiency, shorten equipment life expectancy, cause spotting on dishes and glassware, and leave soap residue on fixtures and surfaces. The presence of chlorine, while common in municipal water supplies, can contribute to dry skin and hair and may deteriorate rubber seals and gaskets within the plumbing system over time.

To improve water quality and help protect the home’s plumbing system, technician recommends installing a City Soft water treatment system. The system is designed to soften the water by removing the hardness minerals that cause scale buildup while also reducing chlorine levels throughout the home. Benefits of the system include improved soap and detergent performance, reduced spotting and scaling, softer-feeling water, and increased protection and efficiency of plumbing fixtures and water-using appliances.

The proposed installation location for the City Soft system is near the existing water heater to allow for efficient integration into the home’s main water distribution system. The softener’s backwash drain lines will be routed and connected to the existing main drain located behind the water heater at the proposed installation area. The system also requires a dedicated electrical outlet for operation and regeneration cycles. The home’s electrical panel is located approximately 40 feet away, and an outlet will need to be installed and provided at the equipment location prior to or as part of the installation. Once installed, the system will provide conditioned water to the entire home and help minimize the long-term effects of hard water and chlorine exposure on the plumbing system.

A new fresh-air intake would be installed and terminated outside near the existing exhaust location. The tankless water heater condensate would drain into a condensate pump. The condensate pump discharge would then connect to the existing 2” PVC drain near the water heater location to properly dispose of the condensate.

The existing gas piping would need to be increased to 1” near the gas meter location to provide the proper volume of gas required for the tankless water heater. A new gas connection would then be routed to the tankless water heater as required.

A designated electrical outlet would be required for the tankless water heater and condensate pump. The electrical connection would provide the necessary power for the equipment and allow the condensate pump to operate properly during tankless water heater operation.

Technician recommends addressing the gas, venting, combustion air, condensate, and electrical requirements as part of the tankless water heater installation to ensure the new system operates properly and according to manufacturer specifications and applicable codes.

e.339616962:
2nd Floor Hallway Bathroom: The double lavatory pop-up assemblies are not functioning properly. The left pop-up assembly is unable to operate the plunger to properly stop and hold water in the sink, while the right pop-up assembly is missing the plunger mechanism. Technician recommends replacing both lavatory pop-up assemblies to restore proper operation and drainage control. Emergency valves for the lav faucet on the right show some corrosion. Technician performed water quality testing and found the home’s water hardness to be 16 grains per gallon (GPG) and the chlorine level to be 1.0 ppm. A hardness level of 16 GPG is considered hard water and can lead to calcium and magnesium scale buildup inside water heaters, plumbing fixtures, faucets, showerheads, and water-using appliances. Over time, this mineral buildup can reduce appliance efficiency, shorten equipment life expectancy, cause spotting on dishes and glassware, and leave soap residue on fixtures and surfaces. The presence of chlorine, while common in municipal water supplies, can contribute to dry skin and hair and may deteriorate rubber seals and gaskets within the plumbing system over time.

To improve water quality and help protect the home’s plumbing system, technician recommends installing a City Soft water treatment system. The system is designed to soften the water by removing the hardness minerals that cause scale buildup while also reducing chlorine levels throughout the home. Benefits of the system include improved soap and detergent performance, reduced spotting and scaling, softer-feeling water, and increased protection and efficiency of plumbing fixtures and water-using appliances.

The proposed installation location for the City Soft system is near the existing water heater. The inlet for the water softener would be routed from the water meter to the water heater room inside the duct work chase. The softener’s backwash drain lines will be routed and connected to the existing main drain located behind the water heater at the proposed installation area. The system also requires a dedicated electrical outlet for operation and regeneration cycles. During the original evaluation, LPH identified corrosion along the upper service drop where it entered the meter base, as well as deterioration along the lower service connection between the meter and interior panel. Water had also entered the interior electrical panel, with dried drip marks and a visible water-settling area directly above the main breaker. Rust was developing on the main breaker’s rivets, indicating that the breaker had been exposed to water contamination.

LPH completed the full outside service replacement, including:

* Installed new service entrance conductors.
* Installed a new service head.
* Installed a new 100-amp exterior emergency disconnect.
* Installed new conduit to properly protect and contain the service wiring.
* Installed a new meter base.
* Installed a new four-wire feeder from the exterior disconnect to the interior panel.
* Relocated the grounding connections to the exterior service disconnect.
* Installed a new grounding bar in the interior panel.
* Separated the neutral and equipment grounding conductors within the interior panel.
* Replaced the water-contaminated main breaker.
* Sealed the exterior service components and electrical entry points with silicone to help prevent future water intrusion.
* Completed the required grounding and bonding connections associated with the new service installation.
* Tested the completed service and electrical system to verify proper operation.

This replacement addressed the underlying water intrusion and corrosion by rebuilding the affected service rather than simply replacing individual deteriorated components. The new installation provides properly protected service conductors and connections while establishing the appropriate separation of neutral and grounding conductors between the exterior service disconnect and interior panel.

LPH completed the work, tested the system, and confirmed the electrical service was operating properly upon completion.

Payment was collected in full for today’s services. Today’s invoice will be emailed to the homeowner for their records.

Thank you for allowing LPH into your home today. It was a pleasure talking with you, and I look forward to servicing you again in the future.

Thank you for trusting LPH with your plumbing needs. We strive to provide professional, high-quality service on every visit, and your feedback helps us continue improving.

We would greatly appreciate hearing about your experience with the technician who served you today. Your feedback regarding the quality of work performed, communication, professionalism, and overall service is extremely valuable to us.

Thank you again for choosing LPH. We truly appreciate your business and the opportunity to serve you!

Technician performed a thorough plumbing system inspection on all accessible plumbing fixtures throughout the home to evaluate overall operation, drainage, water flow, and visible plumbing conditions. During the inspection, technician identified a few concerns within the plumbing system and discussed recommended solutions with the homeowner to address the issues found. Technician reviewed available repair and improvement options to help maintain proper system performance and prevent future plumbing problems.

e.338943402:
The existing 2nd-floor hallway bathroom tub spout with diverter is not diverting the water fully to the shower head, causing water to continue flowing from the tub spout while the shower is in use. Technician recommends replacing the tub spout with a new tub spout and diverter to ensure proper water flow to the shower head and reliable operation.

The existing main water shut-off valve is leaking from the packing nut. The home also has galvanized water piping that transitions back to copper, along with several isolation valves that are not functioning properly and cannot reliably shut off the water supply. Technician recommends replacing the leaking main water shut-off valve and the non-functioning isolation valves to restore proper water shut-off and isolation throughout the plumbing system. The water will need to be shut off at the curb stop in order to complete the valve replacements.

Technician performed water quality testing and found the home’s water hardness to be 12 grains per gallon (GPG) and the chlorine level to be 2.0 ppm. A hardness level of 12 GPG is considered hard water and can lead to calcium and magnesium scale buildup inside water heaters, plumbing fixtures, faucets, showerheads, and water-using appliances. Over time, this mineral buildup can reduce appliance efficiency, shorten equipment life expectancy, cause spotting on dishes and glassware, and leave soap residue on fixtures and surfaces. The presence of chlorine, while common in municipal water supplies, can contribute to dry skin and hair and may deteriorate rubber seals and gaskets within the plumbing system over time.

To improve water quality and help protect the home’s plumbing system, technician recommends installing a City Soft water treatment system. The system is designed to soften the water by removing the hardness minerals that cause scale buildup while also reducing chlorine levels throughout the home. Benefits of the system include improved soap and detergent performance, reduced spotting and scaling, softer-feeling water, and increased protection and efficiency of plumbing fixtures and water-using appliances.

The proposed installation location for the City Soft system is near the existing water main valve to allow for efficient integration into the home’s main water distribution system. The softener’s backwash drain lines will be routed and connected to the existing main drain located behind the washer machine. The system also requires a dedicated electrical outlet for operation and regeneration cycles. The home’s electrical panel is located approximately 20 feet away, and an outlet will need to be installed and provided at the equipment location prior to or as part of the installation. Once installed, the system will provide conditioned water to the entire home and help minimize the long-term effects of hard water and chlorine exposure on the plumbing system.

Technician performed water quality testing and found the home’s water hardness to be 19 grains per gallon (GPG) and the chlorine level to be 1.0 ppm. A hardness level of 19 GPG is considered hard water and can lead to calcium and magnesium scale buildup inside water heaters, plumbing fixtures, faucets, showerheads, and water-using appliances. Over time, this mineral buildup can reduce appliance efficiency, shorten equipment life expectancy, cause spotting on dishes and glassware, and leave soap residue on fixtures and surfaces. The presence of chlorine, while common in municipal water supplies, can contribute to dry skin and hair and may deteriorate rubber seals and gaskets within the plumbing system over time.

To improve water quality and help protect the home’s plumbing system, technician recommends installing a City Soft water treatment system. The system is designed to soften the water by removing the hardness minerals that cause scale buildup while also reducing chlorine levels throughout the home. Benefits of the system include improved soap and detergent performance, reduced spotting and scaling, softer-feeling water, and increased protection and efficiency of plumbing fixtures and water-using appliances.

The proposed installation location for the City Soft system is near the existing water heater. The cold inlet to the water softener would be supplied from the water meter in the craft room and run in the chase to the location of the water softener approximately 40’ away. The softener’s backwash drain lines will be routed and connected to the existing main drain located behind the water heater at the proposed installation area. The system also requires a dedicated electrical outlet for operation and regeneration cycles. The home’s electrical panel is located approximately 5 feet away, and an outlet will need to be installed and provided at the equipment location prior to or as part of the installation. Once installed, the system will provide conditioned water to the entire home and help minimize the long-term effects of hard water and chlorine exposure on the plumbing system.

Today I was called out due the homeowner experiencing an issue with the hot water heater not functioning properly. The plumbers had previously inspected the system and verified that all plumbing components were functioning properly, which prompted today’s electrical inspection.

I began troubleshooting at the main electrical panel and immediately noticed an arcing sound coming from the hot water heater breaker. After removing the panel cover, I found that the white hot leg of the 240V circuit supplying the hot water heater was very loose and showed signs of burning.

I removed the damaged section of wire and properly secured and tightened all connections. After completing the repair, power was restored to the hot water heater, and it began heating properly. All voltage and amp readings are within spec as well reading approximately 18-19 amps. 

LPH waited several minutes to confirm that the water temperature increased, and hot water was restored. Based on the findings and successful testing, I am confident that this repair has corrected the issue. If you have any additional questions or concerns, please do not hesitate to contact us.

LPH was recently at the property to diagnose an error code 70 on the existing Rinnai tankless water heater, indicating a suspected faulty PC board. The tankless water heater was originally installed by LPH on 04/05/2019. Technician replaced the PC board; however, additional error codes returned after the repair.

The most recent error codes are 11 (ignition failure), 17 (Venturi), and 71 (gas valve solenoid). Technician contacted Rinnai technical support to further diagnose the issue. After troubleshooting, Rinnai technical support determined that the gas valve solenoid is not operating properly. Technician recommends replacing the gas valve to restore proper operation of the tankless water heater.

Technician also inspected the Venturi and found a significant amount of dust and debris buildup, including cat litter dust. The fresh-air intake for the tankless water heater is currently drawing combustion air from the basement rather than directly from the exterior. This allows dust and debris from the basement environment to be drawn into the unit and can contribute to buildup on internal components.

Technician also inspected and cleaned the flame rods, which were found to be heavily soiled. Keeping the combustion air intake clean and properly supplied with exterior air will help reduce the amount of dust and debris entering the tankless water heater and help maintain proper operation.

If the water heater provides another code, homeowner will let LPH know and move forward with replacing the gas valve.

The kitchen faucet is not in good working condition, and the hot water was flowing slightly slower than the cold water. Technician explained that the existing water piping is galvanized steel and is prone to corrosion and rust buildup over time.

Today, the technician inspected the kitchen faucet and found the aerator completely restricted with sediment that had broken free from the existing galvanized water piping. The technician also inspected the 2nd-floor hallway bathroom tub/shower valve. The newly installed cartridge was not allowing hot water to fully pass through the valve. Technician replaced the cartridge with another new cartridge and flushed the water lines; however, the hot water still does not fully pass through the cartridge.

The 2nd-floor hallway bathroom lavatory faucet aerator was also inspected and found to contain sediment. Brown, rust-colored water was observed when the water supply was turned back on and the lines were flushed. The sediment and discoloration are consistent with corrosion inside the existing galvanized water piping. As galvanized piping ages, the interior can corrode and accumulate rust and sediment. Pieces of this corrosion can break free and travel through the water lines, restricting faucet aerators, cartridges, and other plumbing fixtures and affecting proper water flow.

Technician recommends replacing the existing galvanized water piping throughout the home with new PEX piping. Replacing the galvanized piping would eliminate the deteriorating water piping as a source of rust and sediment and provide a more reliable water distribution system. Premium Whole-Home Surge Protection

LPH will install a premium whole-home surge protection device at the home’s main electrical panel. This device is designed to protect the home’s electrical system and connected equipment from damaging voltage spikes and transient surges before they can travel throughout the home’s wiring.

Many homeowners think of lightning when they hear the term “surge,” but a significant amount of surge activity actually originates inside the home. Everyday appliances such as air conditioners, refrigerators, heat pumps, furnaces, microwaves, dishwashers, washers, dryers, and garage door openers can create small electrical surges, commonly referred to as microsurges, when their motors and electronic controls cycle on and off. While these individual events are small, repeated voltage fluctuations can contribute to electrical stress on sensitive electronic components over time.

Modern appliances and electronics increasingly rely on circuit boards, microprocessors, and other sensitive electronic components. Whole-home surge protection helps absorb and divert transient surges, reducing the amount of electrical stress placed on these components.

The surge protector also provides protection against larger external surge events, including utility switching, power-grid disturbances, nearby lightning activity, and voltage spikes that can occur when power is restored following an outage.

Benefits of premium whole-home surge protection include:

* Helps protect HVAC equipment, refrigerators, ovens, dishwashers, washers, dryers, and other major appliances.
* Helps safeguard televisions, computers, gaming systems, networking equipment, smart-home devices, and other sensitive electronics.
* Helps reduce the cumulative effects of everyday electrical transients and microsurges.
* Helps reduce electrical stress on modern appliance circuit boards and electronic controls.
* Can help reduce the potential for costly repairs or premature equipment replacement caused by surge damage.
* Provides protection at the home’s electrical panel rather than relying solely on individual plug-in surge strips.
* Provides an added layer of protection during storms, utility switching events, and unexpected power outages.

Premium Surge Protection Warranty & Replacement Coverage

The installed surge protection device also provides protection beyond the surge protector itself. If the surge protector is sacrificed or fails as a result of a covered surge event, the device is backed by a lifetime warranty and up to $100,000 in covered damage protection for eligible home electrical components and connected equipment, subject to the manufacturer’s warranty terms and conditions.

If the surge protector requires replacement under the manufacturer’s warranty, the replacement device is provided at no charge. LPH will handle the replacement installation for a $150 labor charge, helping make a future warranty replacement straightforward and affordable.

LPH stands behind the completed smoke detector installation with a 10-year parts warranty and 1-year labor warranty, in addition to the lifetime warranty provided with the whole-home surge protection device, subject to applicable manufacturer terms and conditions.

Upon arrival, tech met with Victoria. She stated she started hearing a gurgle from the second floor bathtub when she flushes the toilet but all drains are flowing. Tech flushed the toilet and heard the gurgle. Tech went outside to the trap and listened while she flushed again. Tech could hear the flush but there wasn’t a proper flow of water come down the pipe. Tech presented a video inspection. With her approval, we performed a video inspection of the main line. We came across terra-cotta pipe that had separations at all connections and some water being held. Tech had her flush the toilet again but only had some water flow past his camera not a heavy rush like there should be. Tech had her flush the downstairs toilet while watching the camera and noticed some blockage flush out of the cast iron pipe. We then filled the tub up and let the water drain out. We observed a heavy flow of water. She flushed the toilet again and the gurgle was gone. Tech explained that she had a soft blockage somewhere in the branch line and by dumping a heavy load of water it helped flush it out. Tech flushed the toilet and few more times with no gurgle. Tech did present a few options for replacement. She does not want to move forward at the moment. She does not want tech or the office to connect her regarding the options presented. She might be ready to move forward after the new year. We agreed that tech will follow-up in January. Thanks for trusting Lancaster plumbing and heating.

e.340874580:
Technician performed water quality testing and found the home’s water hardness to be 5 grains per gallon (GPG) and the chlorine level to be . 5 ppm. A hardness level of 16 GPG is considered hard water and can lead to calcium and magnesium scale buildup inside water heaters, plumbing fixtures, faucets, showerheads, and water-using appliances. Over time, this mineral buildup can reduce appliance efficiency, shorten equipment life expectancy, cause spotting on dishes and glassware, and leave soap residue on fixtures and surfaces. The presence of chlorine, while common in municipal water supplies, can contribute to dry skin and hair and may deteriorate rubber seals and gaskets within the plumbing system over time.

To improve water quality and help protect the home’s plumbing system, technician recommends installing a City Soft water treatment system. The system is designed to soften the water by removing the hardness minerals that cause scale buildup while also reducing chlorine levels throughout the home. Benefits of the system include improved soap and detergent performance, reduced spotting and scaling, softer-feeling water, and increased protection and efficiency of plumbing fixtures and water-using appliances.

The proposed installation location for the City Soft system is near the existing water heater. The water softener inlet would come from the water meter approximately 20’ away. The softener’s backwash drain lines will be routed and connected to the existing main drain located near the water meter. The system also requires a dedicated electrical outlet for operation and regeneration cycles. The home’s electrical panel is located approximately 20 feet away, and an outlet will need to be installed and provided at the equipment location prior to or as part of the installation. Once installed, the system will provide conditioned water to the entire home and help minimize the long-term effects of hard water and chlorine exposure on the plumbing system.
